nytimes.com.title: Nobel Prizes 2026: What to Know
nytimes.com.text:
The 2026 Nobel Prizes are being awarded this week, starting with the announcement of the prize for physiology or medicine on Monday.
Every October, committees in Sweden and Norway name Nobel laureates in a variety of prizes related to science, literature and economics, as well as peace work. Six prizes in total are awarded.
Laureates will receive their medals, prize money and diplomas in Stockholm and Oslo in December.
Here is a quick guide to this year’s prizes.
What are the Nobel Prizes?
Six Nobel Prizes are awarded every year, each recognizing an individual’s or an organization’s groundbreaking contribution in a specific field. Prizes are given for physiology or medicine, physics, chemistry, economic sciences, literature and peace work, the last of which often draws the most attention because of the fame of the people and groups nominated.
This year, there were 287 candidates for the Nobel Peace Prize — 208 individuals and 79 organizations, the Nobel committee said. Last year, the institute received 338 nominations. The highest number ever received was 376 candidates, in 2016. (Here’s how those nominations work.)
Previous Nobel Peace Prize recipients include Kailash Satyarthi and Malala Yousafzai (2014); President Barack Obama (2009); Nelson Mandela and F.W. de Klerk (1993); the 14th Dalai Lama, Tenzin Gyatso (1989); and Mother Teresa (1979).

cnn.com.title: Democrats release midterms ad featuring family of Epstein victim Virginia Giuffre
cnn.com.text: The campaign arm working to elect House Democrats released a political advertisement on Monday featuring the family of Virginia Giuffre, who was the first victim of Jeffrey Epstein to go public with allegations of abuse. The advertisement was released in support of Democratic candidate Jessica Killin, who is facing incumbent Republican Rep. Jeff Crank in Colorado’s 5th Congressional District. It features a brother and sister-in-law of Giuffre, who died by suicide last year, speaking directly to camera and criticizing Crank for not meeting with them while lawmakers were considering votes to release files related to the late sex offender. “My sister, Virginia, was one of Jeffrey Epstein’s victims,” Giuffre’s brother Sky Roberts said in the ad. “She spent her life trying to expose the truth. After she died, we promised to carry on her fight.” Giuffre’s sister-in-law, Amanda Roberts, continued: “But our own congressman, Jeff Crank, refused to meet with us. Then, when he had the chance to expose the truth and release the Epstein files, he repeatedly voted to cover them up.” The ad ends with the two meeting with Killin over cups of coffee. Crank’s campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment. He last year had declined to sign a bipartisan discharge petition, which would have forced a vote to release thousands of files related to Epstein on the House floor. Later, joining nearly every other member of Congress, Crank voted to pass the Epstein Files Transparency Act, which compelled the government to release extensive files pertaining to its investigations into Epstein. “I have consistently supported transparency and accountability regarding the business dealings, investigation, and prosecution of Jeffrey Epstein,” Crank said in a statement at the time. Giuffre accused Epstein of trafficking her and forcing her to have sex with his friends. She alleged Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor sexually assaulted her when she was a teenager. Mountbatten-Windsor, formerly Prince Andrew, has repeatedly denied claims of abuse. Epstein died by suicide while facing sex trafficking charges in 2019, spurring conspiracy theories and continuing intrigue related to his relationships with powerful men, including President Donald Trump and former President Bill Clinton. Both Trump and Clinton have said they cut off their relationships with Epstein years ago and denied having knowledge of his crimes. Colorado’s 5th Congressional District, which is made up of Colorado Springs and its suburbs, was once considered a reach for Democrats but may now be in play. Crank is serving in his first term after winning in 2024 by about 13 points.

cnn.com.title: Their jobs were among the first to be changed by AI. Now some are trying to avoid it
cnn.com.text: In 2024, software engineer Laura Housh began using AI as a helper for coding and other tasks. Two years later, Housh says she has a love-hate relationship with AI. “I’ve tried to use it for coding, and I just can’t get behind it,” she said. AI can provide direction or serve as a second set of eyes, she said, but added that it lacks the context to be truly useful. Housh isn’t the only one who thinks AI isn’t all that it’s cracked up to be. Six in 10 tech workers who participated in a new survey say they try to avoid using AI, according to Stack Overflow, a popular question-and-answer site for programmers. The results of  Stack Overflow’s 100-question survey, which includes responses from 30,000 software developers in 169 countries, were shared exclusively with CNN ahead of their Tuesday publication. Software engineers have been at the forefront of the AI shift as one of the first industries to embrace the technology. Both tech giants and startups are increasingly using AI to write code, and “software developer” was ranked as the job most poised to be transformed by AI in an Indeed Hiring Lab report last year. The survey’s results, like Housh’s experience, provide a glimpse at what that transition has been like for some developers, painting a mixed picture of both rising adoption and uncertainty about how the technology is reshaping their professions. The Stack Overflow survey showed that 65% of responders use coding assistants or agents. Last year, Google’s research division published a survey of 5,000 tech professionals from around the world and found that 90% said they use AI in their job — a 14% increase from 2024. But job unhappiness among respondents in Stack Overflow’s survey has also grown compared to last year. Nearly one in three said they are not happy in their current roles, compared to 28.4% last year. About 45% described themselves as “complacent” with their jobs and only 22.3% are “happy.” The biggest factors among those who are complacent or unhappy are burnout, tech fatigue, economic uncertainty and a lack of clarity about upward mobility in their role. Many of those anxieties would exist regardless of AI. But the fast pace of AI advancement has “augmented” some of those concerns, according to Stack Overflow CEO Prashanth Chandrasekar. “People have to completely retool their jobs, and so it is quite unnerving for folks to know exactly how much of what they’re doing will be automated,” Chandrasekar told CNN. Software developers are grappling with concerns that are more nuanced than whether their jobs will be replaced, according to Chandrasekar. Senior programmers may feel the skills they’ve honed are no longer as relevant, he said. Entry-level workers are expected to operate as if they have three years of experience since “the bar has been raised” because of AI. Tech workers often use their spare time to learn the latest coding tools, he said. AI has its limitations Housh says she’s familiar with the pressures of learning and keeping up with AI. She said she watches AI-focused videos and reads platform documentation in her personal time — and she still struggles to keep up. “It’s taxing because you have a lot of noise saying, ‘Do this, do this, do this, or you’ll get left behind,’” she said. For programmers like Housh and Audrey Eschright, a software engineer with 20 years of experience, it’s not about a lack of desire to embrace the new technology. Rather, the problem is that AI agents have neither the broad general knowledge of an experienced developer nor the job-specific context of a longtime employee. That can cause friction and more fatigue for developers, said Housh. What’s more, using AI instead of writing code manually can leave developers out of the loop of the solution, Eschright said. “Writing code is how you solve problems,” said Eschright. “As a software engineer, the process of figuring out what a system does is to change it.”  This sentiment is also captured in Stack Overflow’s survey results. A little more than 74% of respondents said AI is useful for implementing code, and about 72% said it’s helpful for debugging — but only 34.4% say AI is useful for other job functions like communication and design. The survey showed that just 6.6% trust AI with important decisions. And about 78% said that source attribution is important when checking AI-generated code. Developers are particularly careful about trusting AI today because the stakes are higher as more companies move AI projects from the pilot phase to mainstream use, according to Chandrasekar. A January report from Deloitte found 54% of the 3,200-plus business and IT leaders it surveyed expected to move 40% or more of their AI experiments into production in the next three to six months. “I don’t like losing control; I like critical thinking and curiosity,” said Housh. “It’s just so important to be more curious than ever.”

cnn.com.title: What James Talarico told a pro-defund the police group in 2020
cnn.com.text: In late summer 2020, as protests over the murder of George Floyd spread across the country, Texas Democratic state Rep. James Talarico told a group of young progressive activists that it was “rich” that “defund the police” was considered taboo when Texas had spent decades defunding public schools and health services. “As an educator, it’s always rich to me that ‘defund the police’ is considered off-limits in our political debate, when defunding health services, defunding public education has been the stated policy of our state government for decades now,” Talarico told activists with Texas Rising, a progressive advocacy group that at the time was explicitly calling for police departments to be defunded and for greater investment in community-based alternatives. Talarico, who was responding to a question on how to talk to unfamiliar audiences about the idea of investing in communities instead of policing, acknowledged that the “defund” slogan itself was getting a hostile reaction in his swing district, which he noted had not elected a Democrat since he was a child. “You know, a hashtag like defund the police is getting people all riled up in my community,” Talarico said. But when people are asked whether armed police officers should respond to minor traffic accidents or mental-health crises, Talarico said, “Most people kind of understand that that’s not what we should be using police officers for.” The previously unreported remarks offer a window into how Talarico approached the fraught “defund the police” debate at the height of the 2020 protests: avoiding endorsing the politically thorny slogan while also arguing that voters could be persuaded to support some of the changes being advocated by activists if they were described in more concrete terms. Now running for the US Senate, Talarico’s campaign calls it a “flat-out lie” that he ever supported defunding the police and points to his votes for state appropriations bills that increased funding for law enforcement. And in a statement to CNN, Talarico’s campaign reiterated his opposition to defunding police. “James did not call for and does not support defunding the police, and he strongly supports Texas law enforcement and first responders,” spokesperson JT Ennis said. “That’s why James has voted to send billions of dollars to local law enforcement, in addition to advocating for better-funded mental health resources so that cops don’t have to respond to mental health emergencies that could be handled by a counselor.” Talarico’s campaign told CNN that his Texas Rising comments were meant to criticize Republicans who attack the phrase “defund the police” while supporting cuts to other public priorities. The campaign said his later comments argued against the phrase itself and instead proposed specific policies that it said did not involve defunding the police. Talarico’s public record and rhetoric on policing is more nuanced than that categorical denial suggests. From 2019 through at least 2022, Talarico repeatedly backed arguments and policies associated with the broader movement to rethink policing, including limiting police power, investing more heavily in social services and community-based alternatives, and one time explicitly arguing for spending less on policing and prisons. He also proposed sending “highly trained crisis interventionists” to some emergencies. Many of those comments came at the height of the “defund the police” movement, when the phrase had no single accepted meaning. While some activists tied it to abolishing or dramatically reducing traditional policing, others used the slogan to describe redirecting police funding toward mental healthcare, housing, education and other social services. The slogan quickly took on a political life of its own, becoming fodder for Republican attacks against a supposed far-left agenda item supported by Democrats. In 2020, then-Sen. Kamala Harris, before she was tapped as Joe Biden’s vice presidential pick, praised the movement for forcing a debate over whether large police budgets reflected the right priorities. Others in 2020, such as Abdul El-Sayed, now the Democratic nominee for Senate in Michigan, made a similar case for redirecting police spending toward public services and explicitly embraced the “defund the police” slogan. Talarico often made arguments that overlapped with Harris’ interpretation, even as he stopped short of explicitly embracing the phrase itself. In his 2020 call with pro-defund activists, Talarico praised protesters in the Black Lives Matter movement for pushing elected officials to rethink the role of government and policing. “We always expect protesters to be nonviolent,” he said on his Texas Rising call. “What happens if we expect our government to be nonviolent? What does that question open up in terms of possibility?” He said “the voices in the street, particularly Black and brown voices” were pushing those in power to “expand our moral imagination” and live up to the country’s “stated ideals.” A high-stakes Senate campaign Now, as his Senate campaign seeks to appeal to a broader electorate, Talarico has moderated his image and said many of his 2020 comments “missed the mark.” He has walked back his support for youth transgender rights and other progressive causes as he faces scandal-plagued Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton in a tight race that could help determine which party controls the Senate next year. Talarico had questioned greater reliance on police even before Floyd’s death. In 2019, he criticized efforts to increase police presence in schools without comparable investments in mental health professionals, arguing that more officers could contribute to what he called a “culture of violence.” His rhetoric became more sweeping in the weeks after Floyd’s murder in May 2020. In a May Facebook exchange, Talarico said he and other lawmakers would “continue to push anti-racist legislation that limits police power,” while promoting healthcare, education and economic justice in communities of color. In another exchange on the same post, Democratic state Rep. Shawn Thierry called for police to “put down the weapons & kneel alongside Black citizens” and asked when they would be “brought to heel” over what she described as brutality, killings and abuses of police power. Talarico liked the comment and replied, “I couldn’t agree more,” adding that he was committed to work with Thierry “to make the imagery you described a reality.” That next month, after the release of footage surrounding the death of Javier Ambler II during a 2019 arrest in Williamson County, Texas, Talarico called for replacing the existing policing system. “Our system of policing is deeply broken,” he said. “We must replace it with something new and something better.” Talarico’s campaign told CNN, “This quote is taken out of context. It refers to reality TV shows on policing.” Talarico’s campaign also said his Facebook comments were referring to legislation like what later became Javier Ambler’s Law, a bipartisan law sponsored by Talarico that barred Texas law enforcement agencies from contracting with reality television shows. Asked directly about defunding the police by the local publication Honest Austin in September 2020, Talarico reiterated the same argument his campaign said had been taken out of context, saying, “Our system of policing is deeply broken. We must replace it with something new and something better,” before questioning whether armed officers were needed for every emergency. “What if we stopped bringing a gun to every emergency?” Talarico said. “What if we called a three-digit number to summon highly trained crisis interventionists to address a problem in our neighborhood? What if we made rehabilitation, reconciliation, and restoration our operating principles?” “We need to invest in community-based solutions that cure the societal ills that we ask the police to treat: poverty, homelessness, substance abuse, mental health disorders,” Talarico continued. “We must empower our communities, not police them. Only then will we have true public safety.” Talarico’s campaign told CNN he was arguing for better funding for mental health resources so police don’t have to respond to mental health emergencies that could be handled by a counselor. The situation around Austin The debate was also playing out in real time in Austin, where city leaders approved a budget in August 2020 that cut roughly $150 million from the police department. Talarico praised Austin’s local leaders during the same period and criticized Republican Gov. Greg Abbott’s efforts to punish cities that reduced police funding. He also praised efforts to end what he called the “over-policing” of communities of color, saying police violence against people of color has its roots in slavery and Jim Crow. Talarico’s campaign told CNN he was “discussing the hypocrisy of the state government trying to tell local governments how to run their municipalities when conservatives are supposed to believe in small government.” Talarico’s campaign also contributed $2,500 in June 2020 to the Austin Justice Coalition, which was advocating cuts to Austin’s police budget and redirecting money toward social services and to “defund” the police department. The donation became an issue in his reelection campaign after Republicans accused him of helping to defund police. Talarico dismissed the attack as “fearmongering” and defended the contribution, describing the Austin Justice Coalition as “a well-respected civil rights organization in our community that champions educational equity, economic opportunity, and police reform.” In 2021, Talarico campaigned against Austin’s Proposition A, which would have required the city to maintain at least two police officers for every 1,000 residents and would have forced the hiring of hundreds of additional officers. Talarico urged voters to defeat the measure, arguing instead that “true public safety” required investment in communities. Austin voters ultimately rejected the proposal by wide margin. And in 2022, Talarico connected reduced spending on policing and prisons with greater spending on social programs. “If we took just half of what we spent on wars, prisons, and policing, and spent it on education, healthcare, and jobs, we could make prisons obsolete,” Talarico said at a graduation ceremony for incarcerated students. “Research tells us that expanding Medicaid reduces crime, increasing SNAP benefits reduces crime, education reduces crime, clean air and clean water reduces crime. A less violent government leads to a less violent society.”

cnn.com.title: Nobel Prize in medicine awarded to trio for technique that helps decode mysteries of the brain
cnn.com.text: The 2026 Nobel Prize in physiology or medicine has been awarded to three scientists – Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel – for their work developing a technique to decode the inner workings of the brain. This method – known as optogenetics – acts as a “light-sensitive switch,” allowing scientists to “map which cells are responsible for which function” in the brain, said Anna Wedell, a member of the Nobel Prize committee, which announced the prestigious honor in Sweden on Monday. German researchers Hegemann, 71, and Nagel, 73, discovered a protein in algae, known as channelrhodopsin, before American scientist Deisseroth, 54, “transformed the protein into a light-controlled switch for nerve cells,” the committee said in a statement. That work has “laid the foundation for a new era in neuroscience,” the committee added. By using this method, researchers can identify and even control the neural circuits that govern “specific memories, feelings, and behaviors relevant for neurological and psychiatric disorders.” All three laureates were “very surprised” when they learned of their prize shortly before the public announcement, said the committee’s secretary-general Thomas Perlmann. “Karl Deisseroth was very tired when he answered, he was definitely asleep, but he woke up … All three said the same thing, that they thought it was absolutely wonderful to receive the prize with the other two,” Perlmann noted when announcing the prize. The award highlights the “profound impact of a field that has fundamentally changed how scientists understand the brain and nervous system,” said David Pendlebury, head of research analysis at Clarivate’s Institute for Scientific Information, in a statement. “The Nobel Committee’s recognition underscores the extraordinary influence of this work, which has transformed neuroscience by enabling researchers to use light to precisely control and study neural activity,” Pendlebury added. ‘A new era in neuroscience’ The discovery began with Hegemann’s curiosity about the behavior of single-celled algae known as Chlamydomonas, which are able to swim towards a light source. In the early 2000s, he and Nagel discovered channelrhodopsin, a protein found on the surface of Chlamydomonas that is unusually both light-sensitive and generates electrical impulses. Regardless of which cell they put the protein in, those cells became light sensitive. Deisseroth, who worked in a psychiatric clinic before becoming a neurosurgeon, built on their discovery by introducing the gene that codes the protein into the nerve cells of rats. By illuminating the nerve cells, he was able around 2007 to control the movement of mouse whiskers. The work marked the infancy of the field of optogenetics, which now means that researchers can understand which nerve cells in the brain control different functions. For example, the Nobel committee said scientists have since identified neural circuits that govern pain, social behaviors, thirst, food consumption, reward and attention. Finding a way to learn about the role of specific brain regions in mental functions “transformed how we study malfunctioning circuits in mental disorders,” said Andrea Benucci, a professor in biology and experimental psychology at Queen Mary University of London, in an email. “The ability to activate or silence neurons in the brain using laser light has opened the door to unprecedented precision,” Benucci told CNN. The hope is optogenetics will lead to new medical treatments as well as a deeper understanding of psychiatric and neurological disorders such as depression, anxiety, schizophrenia, Alzheimer’s disease and Parkinson’s disease. Researchers in optogenetics are attempting to restore vision in people who have become blind due to retinitis pigmentosa, a disease that destroys the eye’s rods and cones. “When they inserted a channelrhodopsin-like protein in the retina of a blind person, the person regained some vision. Using special glasses emitting light, the person was able to discern and grasp objects on a table,” according to a release from the Nobel committee. Another area of research seeks to harness optogenetics to improve cochlear implants for hearing loss. The three laureates will equally split the 12 million Swedish krona ($1,200,000) prize pot. Four more Nobel Prizes – physics, chemistry, literature and peace – will be awarded later this week, before the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Science is awarded next Monday. This story and its headline has been updated with additional reporting.

cnn.com.title: How Mai Atafo’s tailored vision is reshaping African fashion
cnn.com.text: From his razor-sharp bespoke tailoring and luxury bridal wear to creating red-carpet looks for some of Africa’s biggest stars, Nigerian fashion designer Mai Atafo has built a brand around exclusivity. Now, he is immersed in preparations for a Lagos fashion show coming later this month. After pulling off an outstanding 90-minute show in Lagos in 2023, that had 800 people sitting front row, with 50 models wearing 83 outfits and walking on six lanes, he plans on outdoing himself this October. “It’s got to be bigger, better,” he told CNN’s Larry Madowo in Lagos. Naomi Campbell Having a standout fashion show is on brand for Atafo, who in April 2019 had supermodel Naomi Campbell, a long-time champion of African design, grace his runway during the ARISE Fashion Week show in Lagos. It came as a surprise to him. Atafo was getting ready for the event when the show’s director told him that Campbell would be walking in his show. “I didn’t have anything made for her,” Atafo recalled. He hastily rearranged his show, with Campbell opening it. The moment she hit the runway, “the crowd just goes crazy,” Atafo said. For the finale, she walked with Atafo and kissed his cheek. “I’m like, ‘Oh, did I get a kiss too from Naomi Campbell?’ Oh my god!” he added In an interview with CNN in April 2019, days before the ARISE fashion show, Campbell talked about her love for Africa and her desire to help its creatives gain international recognition for their work. “It makes me proud to say I’m wearing an African designer,” she said. “Our great world of fashion has ignored this continent. … For me, Africa is very rich in so many ways and has been so untapped… and so this is the time.” The clientele As chief creative officer of his eponymous fashion brand ATAFO, whose designs embody the idea of sartorial elegance, he hopes to one day be viewed as an equal to that select group of luxury designers whose brands are identified by a single name: Versace, Valentino and Gucci. Atafo’s clientele includes some of Nigeria’s most prominent politicians, celebrities and business leaders, many of whom visit his Lagos store to get custom-made designs. Media mogul Mo Abudu, singers Yemi Alade and Tiwa Savage and “Big Brother Naija” host Ebuka Obi-Uchendu have all been seen in ATAFO. Actor and singer Banky Wellington and his wife, actress Adesua Etomi, are both friends and clients. “He’s made some of the most important pieces my wife and I have ever worn, including our wedding outfits,” Wellington said in a message to CNN. “I genuinely believe he is one of the finest designers we’ve encountered anywhere in the world,” Wellington added, praising Atafo’s craftsmanship and attention to detail. “He has that rare ability to understand who you are, what the moment requires, and then create something that feels distinctly like you while still carrying his signature.” In August 2021, South African actress Thuso Mbedu wore a beautiful red tulle gown designed by Atafo to the Hollywood Critics Association Awards, where she received the TV Breakout Star Award for “The Underground Railroad.” A month later, The Hollywood Reporter recognized Atafo as being part of a wave of international designers grabbing the attention of Hollywood’s most prominent stylists and celebrities. Beyond the recognition for his creativity, Atafo has been invited to speak at the Africa Business Conference at Harvard University multiple times. “That made me feel like I was doing something right. It’s moments like that or moments that my garments are showcased at the Africa Fashion exhibition at [London’s] Victoria and Albert Museum, which moves on to the Brooklyn Museum, which is moving to Paris. … They’re really, really good moments. I cherish them,” he said. A new career Atafo, who holds a master’s degree in information systems and technology, did not set out to be a fashion designer — he only wanted to have his own unique style. He joked that If he was starting out in the Instagram era, he would “probably be a fashion influencer, because it was about me wearing clothes and looking good, not necessarily making people look good. I didn’t want anyone [else] to look good, I wanted to look the best.” He said that he took his first steps into design because in those early days, his long arms meant that he had to alter the suits and shirts he bought, sometimes removing cuffs and replacing sleeves with ones in a different fabric. “I used to do all those tricks … And that’s how the journey started,” he said. For the past 16 years, Atafo has been perfecting his craft, attending fashion school in Italy and becoming certified as a tailor at the Savile Row Academy. He even had his team trained by a master tailor from Saville Row, the London street known for bespoke tailoring that’s popular with celebrities, politicians and royalty. And since most of his clients are from the upper echelon of Nigerian society, Atafo wanted to bring that standard to them. He said: “We [Africans] do this thing where we go, like ‘it’s good enough for here,’ and for me that’s not the standard. It has to be good enough for everywhere. “The world is a global village … I can be walking anywhere in the world right now and someone will see my suit, and I go like ‘I made it and I made it in Africa’ — and that’s something I want to be proud of.”

cnn.com.title: Anthropic expected to IPO despite market uncertainty, AI slowdown calls
cnn.com.text: Wall Street is gearing up for Anthropic’s expected mega initial public offering, a major test of investors’ appetite for one of the AI industry’s leading firms. Just weeks ago, its CEO called for an industry-wide slowdown over growing safety concerns. The IPO could take place as soon as November, according to the Wall Street Journal. Anthropic’s IPO has been highly anticipated after the company announced in June that it confidentially filed to go public. Anthropic could raise as much as $100 billion in an IPO that would value the company at around $2 trillion, according to the Journal. The seismic sums would vault Anthropic into the top 10 most valuable companies in the world. Anthropic’s IPO would mark a major milestone in the AI boom that has enveloped markets in recent years. But the journey to the IPO has been messy, and there have been delays. Anthropic’s plans have been muddled by questions about AI regulation and safety risks. Former employees, as well as CEO Dario Amodei, have raised concerns in recent weeks, spurring an industry-wide call to slow down AI development to better manage risks. Tech leaders, including Amodei, signed an accord at the White House last week to “self-police” the development of AI. Meanwhile, the outlook for all potential IPOs has grown complicated in recent months. The market has grown more uncertain as interest rates are on the rise. Bond yields have surged in recent weeks, pushing up borrowing costs, as traders adjust to the Iran war energy shock and central banks raising rates. Some companies have gotten cold feet. Oura, a tech company that makes wearable health tracking rings, said it would go public this fall before announcing last week that it would delay its debut due to market uncertainty. Holtec Nuclear, an energy company, also recently suspended its planned IPO, citing poor sentiment impacting the stock market. And OpenAI announced it would delay its IPO until next year because of AI safety concerns. “You’ve got rising rates. You’ve got the war in Iran. You’ve got the sort of shakier economy ex-AI,” Heath Terry, head of AI investment research at Citi, told CNN. “I think that’s what’s sort of created uncertainty.” “IPOs need a stable market environment, they need positive investor sentiment, and with that sort of unstable broader economic landscape, that makes it a lot more difficult,” Terry said, speaking broadly about IPOs and not specific companies. Still, Anthropic is reportedly moving forward with its plans to go public while it raises capital. Should Anthropic raise $100 billion and debut at a valuation of around $2 trillion, it would surpass SpaceX’s IPO as the largest ever. SpaceX ultimately raised roughly $86 billion in its IPO and debuted at a $1.77 trillion valuation, partly due to visions for its own role in AI. The mega-sized SpaceX IPO trounced previous public offerings, with Saudi Aramco a distant No. 2, after it raised roughly $29 billion in 2019. “SpaceX was such an outlier — the world’s biggest IPO ever, by far. And it’s very possible that they’ll be in second place (roughly) a month from now,” said Jay Ritter, professor emeritus at the University of Florida. Is it a good time for Anthropic to go public? To be sure, the risk of AI taking over the world has been discussed for years. But scrutiny intensified in recent weeks after multiple incidents of AI agents going rogue and trying to hack into other systems. Reuters last week obtained a copy of Anthropic’s IPO prospectus, which has yet to be released, and reported that it includes warnings that the company’s AI model could potentially cause a “catastrophic or existential risk to humanity.” While tech leaders have agreed to self-police, Anthropic is still expected to grow its business and compete with rivals like OpenAI. Heightened safety concerns would exist whether the company went public or not, experts told CNN. Higher interest rates can also depress valuations for stocks and put a chill on the IPO market. But waiting to go public doesn’t guarantee interest rates will fall, and for a company that’s hungry for cash like Anthropic, going public can still make sense, said analysts and Ritter, the professor emeritus at the University of Florida. Delaying an IPO indefinitely also carries the risk that market conditions get worse, or other unforeseen challenges arise, and it becomes more difficult to get back on track toward an IPO. At the same time, the Nasdaq Composite is currently trading near a record high, which is a positive scenario for a tech IPO. “You can’t really ever time an IPO to eliminate all future uncertainty with respect to your company and your product,” Jill E. Fisch, professor of business law at the University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School, told CNN. “I don’t think there’s a magic line for any company in terms of, ‘Yes, now we’ve crossed the threshold, we’ve solved all of the safety issues, and now we can go forward with 100% confidence.’ I don’t think it really works that way,” Fisch said. Anthropic and OpenAI are in a heated race to produce advanced AI models, and the companies are burning billions in cash to advance research and development. Anthropic lost $42 billion in 2025 and plans to spend north of $500 billion on computing and infrastructure in the coming years, according to Reuters. However, the company reportedly told investors that it will be profitable for a second straight quarter this year, according to the Financial Times. Anthropic builds its revenue by renting out advanced models of its Claude bot to major businesses. Angelo Zino, tech analyst at CFRA Research, said that while the market conditions might not be conducive to every company’s plans to go public, he thinks Anthropic is in a league of its own. He cited strong signs of demand for its products and a path to profitability despite the company’s enormous capital spending. “I think there’s going to be a very strong appetite and demand for Anthropic,” Zino said. AI has been the central theme propelling the stock market to record highs in recent years. At its stratospheric valuation, Anthropic is asking investors to believe in its ability to continue monetizing its AI services and expand its market share. “If the company executes its business model, it’s going to do fine,” said Ritter, the professor emeritus at the University of Florida. “But you know, a lot of times things don’t work out.”

cnn.com.title: Supreme Court to hear arguments in one of the most important climate change cases to reach its docket in years
cnn.com.text: The Supreme Court will hear arguments Monday in one of the most important climate change cases to reach its docket in years, a multibillion-dollar effort to hold major oil companies like ExxonMobil liable for the damages caused by planet-warming pollution. The city and county of Boulder, Colorado, sued two energy companies in 2018, attempting to recover the cost of repairing infrastructure and providing access to public health services following fires and floods. Boulder argues the companies not only contributed to climate change but also misled the public about the role fossil fuels played in climate change. Dozens of cities and states have filed similar lawsuits against oil companies, which warn the litigation amounts to a carbon tax that could ultimately bankrupt the energy industry. It is the first case the court is hearing in a new term that begins Monday that features disputes over the AR-15 bans, religious schools and voting. A decision is expected by June. Boulder claims that it is exercising inherent state police powers to protect the health and safety of its residents, and that the practice is not novel. Dozens of states sued the largest tobacco companies in the 1990s seeking damages and alleging deceptive practices — litigation that led to a massive settlement. “This litigation is not an attempt to solve climate change,” Boulder told the court. “It merely asks that petitioners bear their fair share of local costs incurred in part because of their tortious conduct.” Exxon and Suncor Energy, the US subsidiary of a Canadian-based company, say it has long been understood that greenhouse gas emissions are inherently an interstate challenge and that those principles effectively preempt state tort laws. “As this court has consistently recognized, resorting to a single state’s law to resolve an inherently interstate dispute contradicts the basic scheme of the Constitution,” the energy companies said. In an unusual twist, conservative Justice Samuel Alito announced last week that he would recuse himself from the case. Though he did not state a reason at the time, he later told Bloomberg News that he felt it was “prudent” to step away given his holdings in energy stocks. The decision opens the possibility of a 4-4 split that would, by default, allow the litigation to continue. Exxon and Suncor filed the appeal at the Supreme Court last year after Colorado’s highest court sided with Boulder. If the US Supreme Court also backed Boulder, it wouldn’t be the end of the case; it would only permit the litigation to continue in state court. If the court can’t find an answer to the big questions raised by the appeal, it could deal with the case in a more limited way. It’s not clear whether the appeal is ripe for Supreme Court review. If the court concludes that it’s too soon, that will send the case back to state courts — at least for now.

cnn.com.title: ‘I’m here to save lives’: Inside the unlikely Biden-Trump partnership to secure a Gaza ceasefire
cnn.com.text: Secure rooms in the US Capitol are cavernous compared to the White House Situation Room. They are designed for full committees or larger gatherings, not intimate discussions. On Nov. 20, 2024, Jake Sullivan and I had gone to one of those rooms to brief our successors two weeks after Donald Trump resoundingly defeated Kamala Harris. Sullivan was Biden’s national security advisor. His named successor was Mike Waltz, a congressman from Florida. I was Biden’s lead on the Middle East and a chief negotiator on talks to free hostages held by Hamas in Gaza in exchange for a ceasefire with Israel. My named successor was Steve Witkoff — a real-estate tycoon and Trump’s best friend. Shortly after the election, I had called Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law and former Middle East hand. My message was that we had a chance to secure a Gaza deal so long as we could be seen as working together without any daylight between the incoming and outgoing teams. That was a tall order given the polarization in Washington, but it was the only chance we had — and for the first time in months, circumstances trended in our favor. The hostage talks had collapsed in August, when shortly after Biden, together with the leaders of Egypt and Qatar, presented a new proposal endorsed by Israel, Hamas terrorists murdered six hostages in a tunnel under Rafah, a city in southern Gaza. One of those hostages was Hersh Goldberg-Polin, an American who had been grievously wounded and lost an arm in Hamas’s attacks at the Nova music festival on Oct. 7, 2023, before being taken captive. Following the collapse of the negotiations, Israel had won a string of military victories. It started on Sept. 17, 2024, with an operation that exploded thousands of beepers carried by Hezbollah militants in Lebanon. I first heard about what became known as Operation Grim Beeper from a contact in Mossad, Israel’s external intelligence service, who told me, “We just blew the dicks off Hezbollah.” In many cases, that was not metaphorical. Hezbollah, like Hamas, a terrorist group backed by Iran, had made the fateful decision to join in the Hamas attack on Israel. On Oct. 8, 2023, it began firing daily rocket barrages into northern Israel, eventually displacing nearly 80,000 people. Israel had been prepared to forgo an operation against Hezbollah if there was a hostage deal. But with no deal in sight, Israel soon followed the beeper operation with a ground assault into the Hezbollah strongholds of southern Lebanon. By the end of September, Hezbollah’s leader, Hassan Nasrallah, was dead, together with most of his senior lieutenants, buried in an underground Beirut compound. On Oct. 1, following Nasrallah’s death, Iran made its own foolish — and fateful — decision to launch another massive ballistic missile attack against Israel, following on a failed attack it had launched months earlier. This time, Iran launched nearly two hundred missiles at once, exceeding its earlier salvo. In the Situation Room that afternoon, as interceptors destroyed incoming missiles at the edge of outer space, we received reports of a direct hit on a college dormitory in Tel Aviv. I was seated just across from Harris, less than five weeks from Election Day. She mouthed, “Oh, shit.” We knew that if Iran inflicted significant Israeli casualties, the Israelis were prepared to launch a massive counterattack into Iran. Fortunately, that report, like many first reports, was wrong. Only remnants of a destroyed missile struck the building, causing little damage. The attack was mostly defeated, dismaying the Iranians, who had believed their larger salvo of missiles would be successful. About two weeks later, on Oct. 16, Israeli forces killed Hamas’s leader, Yahya Sinwar. He was found in Rafah, not far from where Hersh and five other hostages had been shot to death in a tunnel. Sinwar’s death removed a major obstacle to a deal — him — and allowed the Israelis to be more flexible on some terms now that the mastermind of the Oct. 7 attacks could no longer reclaim power. For Israel, it was akin to the United States military killing Osama bin Laden after 9/11. Finally, on Oct. 26, Israel conducted stealth air attacks against Iran, targeting and destroying many of its strategic air defense systems. We worked closely with the Israelis on this counterattack, walking the Israelis back from a more aggressive response. Biden told Netanyahu that we would deploy more air defenses to Israel and received assurance from Netanyahu in return that Israel’s response would focus on Iran’s own air defense batteries. The aim was to change the balance of power without triggering a wider war. We messaged Iran’s leaders afterward that their country was now wide open to air attacks should Israel (or the United States) choose to launch them. With Russia bogged down in Ukraine, Iran could not soon replace the destroyed air defense batteries, most of which were Russian and had proved ineffective against Israel’s capabilities. Iran never responded to Israel’s counterattack. With the tables turned on Iran, Sinwar dead, and Hezbollah’s leadership decimated, we predicted that Hezbollah would soon accept a ceasefire deal with Israel. That would be the moment to return to the Gaza deal — picking up where we had left off in August. My case to Kushner was straightforward. If Israel and Hamas knew that Trump would implement the deal on the table, we had a chance to close it before he took office. But if not, we would lose the best chance we had had since the war began. It was time to seize the moment, and the only way to do that was by working together. Kushner fully agreed. He told me that he would not be joining the new administration but said my successor on the Middle East was someone close to Trump, a pragmatic problem-solver who would want to work with me to the extent appropriate. He did not mention Witkoff, whose name emerged days later as Trump’s likely Middle East envoy. Biden invited Trump to the Oval on Nov. 13, 2024, mostly for a one-on-one. When the cameras came in briefly, Biden promised a smooth transition. “Politics is tough,” Trump said. “And it’s in many cases not a very nice world, but it is a nice world today, and I appreciate very much a transition that is so smooth, it’ll be as smooth as it can get.” I saw Biden afterward. Unlike many Democrats at the time who saw the election as an existential disaster, Biden — at least with me — was focused on working with the incoming team wherever we could. That was especially so on the hostage crisis. According to Biden, the two presidents agreed to coordinate, setting the stage for my meeting with Sullivan, Waltz, and Witkoff seven days later. In the secure room at the Capitol, Sullivan snapped open a document pouch and arrayed briefing materials in front of him, including maps of the region and background on Iran’s nuclear program. We sat alone at a large table, waiting for Trump’s team to arrive. Waltz entered, followed by Witkoff. The former was a retired military officer with perfect hair and rod-straight posture. The latter was a brash real estate developer known for carrying a pistol in a sock through the alleys and streets of New York, where he built a multibillion-dollar empire. Both exhibited a lighthearted manner, something that I had lost handling the Gaza crisis, where tens of thousands had died, over one hundred hostages remained in tunnels underground and the region stood on the brink of an all-out war. The meeting began awkwardly, the four of us standing at the corner of the large table in the oversize room, introducing ourselves by titles. Waltz took his seat, and we followed. “Trump told us to solve everything, that’s our mission,” Witkoff said, laughing. “Solve it!” Waltz added. Senator JD Vance, the incoming vice president, popped in unexpectedly. We stood. He asked what we were talking about, and when we said the Middle East, he told us that was his cue to leave. (Run as fast as you can, I thought.) Vance, Waltz, and Witkoff discussed recent calls they’d each had with Trump, comparing notes on what they had heard — apparently different things. The calls had come at all hours, and Waltz asked both men whether Trump ever slept. Witkoff answered, “I’ve known him for forty years, the answer is — no, not very much.” “Force of nature,” Waltz remarked. Witkoff explained that he had been Trump’s real-estate attorney before branching out on his own. “I’ve had success, but there’s only one Trump,” he told us. Vance came around the table to shake my hand, and Sullivan’s. He said he wanted to work with us during the transition period, which seemed sincere, and then left the room. With a map on the table, Sullivan walked through what had changed in the Middle East since the hostage talks collapsed in August. It was head-spinning even for those of us who had been living and breathing the issues every day since then. For Witkoff, I recounted my difficult experience on the hostage talks, and explained why we might now, finally, have a shot. Of course, for that to happen we had to be seen — by both Hamas and Israel — as working together, as both parties would demand to know Trump’s views. “The only reason I’m here is to save lives,” Witkoff said. “It’s the most noble thing anyone can do with their life, to save another life. So, I’m all in, count on it.” He asked what we needed from him, and from Trump. I took out the text. Every detail of a carefully negotiated agreement — from the extent of Israel’s redeployment during a ceasefire, to the timing and sequence of hostages and prisoner exchanges, to the minute-by-minute details on delivery of humanitarian assistance with the guns silent — was reflected in a package of texts that had been hammered over months shuttling between Doha, Jerusalem, and Cairo. The outstanding issue was agreement from Hamas on the hostages to come out during the first stage of the ceasefire, a category that included women, the elderly, and the sick or wounded, something the group still had never seriously engaged on. There would not be a hostage deal, I explained, without an agreed list of the hostages to be released. Witkoff claimed that he knew most of the leaders in the Middle East from his real-estate business, and he asked whether we’d be comfortable with his traveling to the region to reengage and to preview his new role. Sullivan said that would be fine, so long as he was not negotiating, and kept in close contact with me before and afterward. Witkoff wrote down his number, and we agreed to speak regularly from that moment forward. For the remainder of the briefing, we discussed Iran. With Trump entering office and Iran now vulnerable to direct attack, the Israelis believed Tehran might race to enrich uranium to weapons grade — the precursor for a nuclear bomb. Throughout the crisis, since Oct. 7, Iran had been enriching uranium to 60% grade, a step away from the 90% required for a bomb. It was the only country in the world without a weapons program to do so. The previous week, Sullivan had convened the Principals Committee to war-game the scenario of Iran enriching to weapons grade. Participants were unanimous that if we saw such indications, we’d recommend a US military strike against Iran’s nuclear facilities, including its deeply buried facility at Fordow. The operation had been rehearsed over the past year should the president — or a future president — need it. We dispatched a message to Iran’s leaders warning them not to think about escalating their nuclear program. Witkoff raised his hands. “Trump says I’ve got Iran, but maybe I don’t want it. Are you f**king kidding with all of this?” Finally, Saudi Arabia. We reviewed a package of agreements that we had completed on a deal for normalization between Israel and Saudi Arabia, before the Oct. 7 crisis. I explained that the deal might be possible over Trump’s term, so long as Gaza could be settled. Netanyahu’s hard-right coalition government made everything more difficult, but it might not outlast Israel’s next election in 2026. (These elections are now scheduled for later this month.) Witkoff came around to my side of the table. He extended his hand: “I’m here to save lives. I don’t give one shit about politics. If we save one life, we save the world.” The table was now set for that, I assured him.

cnn.com.title: The 10 Senate seats most likely to flip in 2026
cnn.com.text: Nearly four weeks out from Election Day, the Senate battleground map is growing after signs of improvement for Democrats in several red-leaning states. For the first time this year, CNN’s list of 9 Senate seats most likely to flip expands to 10 to include Kansas, which hasn’t sent a Democrat to the Senate in 94 years. A new wave of polling also shows Democrats ahead or competitive in red states like Ohio, Alaska and Texas. All four states went for President Donald Trump by double digits in 2024. To win the Senate majority, Democrats will need to pick up four Republican-held seats while defending three of their own, including Michigan. Trump’s approval rating stands at 34%, according to CNN’s Poll of Polls, amid high frustration over the economy and the war he launched against Iran. Democrats have also seen surging enthusiasm in special elections since Trump returned to office and early signs of elevated turnout in early voting. But they have also expressed unease over the massive amount of spending coming from the GOP. From the start of October through Election Day, Republicans are poised to outspend Democrats on advertising in eight of the ten most competitive Senate races, according to ad-tracking firm AdImpact, even though that advantage will be blunted by GOP-aligned outside groups having to spend more for ratings points than Democratic campaigns will. Our ranking of the seats most likely to flip in November is based on CNN reporting, including conversations with strategists involved in Senate races, as well as our analysis of candidate fundraising, polling and the partisan environment in the states. The rankings are a snapshot of where the contests stand at this point and can shift as the midterm election season enters its final month. 1. North Carolina North Carolina remains the state most likely to flip this year. Democratic former Gov. Roy Cooper, who has made affordability issues a centerpiece of his campaign, has a strong position over GOP nominee Michael Whatley, the former Republican National Committee chairman and Trump ally vying to replace Sen. Thom Tillis. An Elon University/YouGov poll released last month showed Cooper up 11 points over Whatley among likely voters. The Senate Leadership Fund, a key Republican outside spending group, is pausing its ad campaign there. Over the weekend, Republican outside groups cut more than $15 million from their remaining ad bookings, according to AdImpact data. Still, Trump campaigned with Whatley in North Carolina last month in an effort to turn out his base in a state he won three times. 2. Ohio Ohio moves up two spots on this list, a reflection of the prime position of former Sen. Sherrod Brown. Brown, who lost reelection to a fourth term by less than four points two years ago, has led GOP Sen. Jon Husted in most polls. A New York Times/Siena University poll of likely voters conducted at the end of September showed a tight race, Brown at 49% and Husted at 46%, within the survey’s margin of error. A Marist poll of registered voters in Ohio showed Brown up eight points over Husted last month. In the NYT/Siena University poll, Husted’s favorability is at 37% while Brown is at 46%. That’s perhaps a reflection of Brown having a longer history with many Ohio voters than Husted, the former lieutenant governor appointed to take Vice President JD Vance’s seat last year. Brown’s attacks on Husted over data centers – calling him “the face of data centers in Ohio” – have proven particularly potent as Republicans’ campaign arm in Washington has warned the issue is an “anchor” on Husted’s campaign. Senate Democrats last week blocked a Husted-sponsored bill that would have recommended states take action on data center-related energy costs. And campaigning for Husted on Saturday, Trump defended data centers in southwestern Ohio, a reflection of the president’s longstanding opposition to pausing their construction. In one buzzy digital spot released last week, Brown’s campaign also featured voters using expletives as they reacted to Husted’s past comments suggesting people living in poverty are “not very experienced at navigating the real world.” (Brown’s campaign is running an expletive-free version of the ad on TV.) Republicans have pulled from a 2024 playbook to run ads attacking Brown on transgender politics, hoping that will move the needle in the state. Brown has responded with a TV spot of his own featuring voters talking about how Ohio already has laws addressing transgender policies and wanting candidates to focus on other issues. One big question heading into the final stretch is whether GOP spending could help tighten this race. Republican groups are set to spend more than $80 million there from the start of October through Election Day while Democrats have allotted more than $50 million. 3. Alaska Alaska moves up two spots. The enormous and sparsely populated state is notoriously hard to poll, but a NYT/Siena poll of likely voters released Saturday found Democrat Mary Peltola up seven points over GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan, 50 to 43%. November’s contest will be determined by ranked-choice voting, and two others join Sen. Sullivan and Peltola on the ballot, including another GOP candidate named Dan Sullivan, a former schoolteacher. The possibility of voters confusing the same-name candidates has been a point of concern for Republicans ahead of November. Democrats consider Peltola, a former congresswoman, as one of their strongest recruits, and she’s kept some national Democratic politicians like former Vice President Kamala Harris at arm’s length at a time when her opponent attempts to tie to her to “lower-48 liberals.” Sullivan stood beside Trump in the Oval Office to tout a $54 billion investment from South Korea for the Alaska LNG pipeline project just weeks before the election. Peltola also moved quickly to praise the president’s announcement, saying she looks forward to “continuing this bipartisan work” with Trump. Peltola’s demeanor towards aides and use of vulgar rhetoric came under scrutiny last month with a New York Times report detailing allegations of hostile behavior from some former aides. Her campaign denied any pattern of abusive pattern but acknowledged that Peltola has struggled at times to deal with the deaths of her mother and husband in 2023. Alaska’s other Republican senator, Sen. Lisa Murkowski, also came to her defense, noting Peltola’s personal struggles. 4. Maine Maine drops two spots on our list. But the race between Republican Sen. Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson remains extremely competitive as the two prepare to debate for the first time this week. A University of New Hampshire poll conducted last month found Jackson slightly ahead of Collins among Maine likely voters – 51% to 47% - marking the first public survey showing the Democrat with the advantage in the state. Other recent polls, including a CNN survey conducted by SSRS and a NYT/Siena poll, have shown no clear leader. Collins remains in a vulnerable position given Harris won her state by 7 points in 2024. Polling has indicated the contest hinges more on negative views of the Maine senator and Trump than it does on perceptions about her Democratic opponent. Democrats have hammered Collins for siding with Trump on consequential votes even as she’s struck out on her own on issues like tariffs and the Iran war. They have also seized on a ProPublica report alleging Collins’ office was involved in a pay-to-play scheme during her 2020 campaign. Collins has forcefully denied the allegations as a “political hit job.” Collins has survived tough reelection battles in the past, and Republicans are leaning hard on reminding constituents of what she’s accomplished for the state. GOP groups also have spent millions on corruption ads of their own against Jackson, a former Maine Senate president, along with TV spots hammering the Democrat on tax policy. Starting Tuesday, Collins and Jackson will have four debates over ten days. 5. Texas Texas jumps two spots with Democrat James Talarico in a stronger-than-expected position and Republicans in the middle of a nine-figure rescue mission to save Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton. Democrats believe Talarico’s broader appeal, coupled with unease with Paxton’s scandals and the leftward shift of Latino voters, are giving the party its most realistic chance of turning Texas blue in three decades. A NYT/Siena poll conducted over the final nine days of September found Talarico up six points over Paxton among likely voters – 51% to 45%. Meanwhile, a Fox News poll released last week showed no clear leader in the contest, with Talarico at 51% and Paxton at 49%. Paxton needs loyal Republicans, including those who sided with Cornyn in May, to turn out in November. Trump is doing his part to help with the base, arguing Paxton is a conservative fighter while mocking his personal appearance. After holding an event in Denton on Thursday, Trump will return to San Antonio for a rally on Wednesday – his second trip to the state in a week. Over the final month, Republicans currently have a nearly 8-to-1 spending advantage in remaining ad reservations – about $70 million to $9 million. But like North Carolina, Republicans are relying on outside groups here and have made much of their bookings late in the cycle when ad inventories are stretched, imposing a premium on their spending. 6. Michigan Michigan shifts down three spots. The race between Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers, a former congressman who lost to Sen. Elissa Slotkin in 2024 by 0.3%, remains one of the GOP’s few offensive opportunities this cycle. A Marist poll of registered voters released last week showed El-Sayed up seven points over Rogers – 51% to 44%. But all polls of likely voters in September painted a different picture. with no clear leader in the contest, including the most recent survey released by Fox News on Wednesday. The GOP spending advantage in this race is a major factor that could keep this race close up until Election Day. For the month of October, Republicans are set to spend more than $43 million while Democrats have reserved about $25 million. Republicans here have mounted a determined effort to paint El-Sayed as outside the mainstream, running in waves of ads calling the Democrat “dangerous” and “radical.” “He’s too extreme for Michigan, and your vote can stop him,” says an ad from a pro-Rogers group. But frustration with Trump and concerns about the economy make the environment tough for Rogers in a state hit hard by tariffs and gas prices driven up by the Iran war. According to the Fox News poll, 6 in 10 likely voters say they disapprove of the president’s performance, and 7 in 10 likely voters cite cost-of-living issues as extremely important. 39% are extremely concerned Rogers is too closely aligned to Trump while 36% said El-Sayed’s positions are too liberal, the same poll showed. The GOP nominee has sought to create some distance from the president on Iran, calling for the war’s swift end amid rising prices – even though he praised Trump’s decision to start the conflict mere months ago. Rogers’ strategy hinges on winning over disaffected Democrats and independents, while also turning out the president’s base supporters, who aren’t as reliable of voters in elections where Trump is not on the ballot. El-Sayed, meanwhile, recently appeared with Harris to drum up support from Black voters, including those who feel a protest movement against the Biden administration’s policy towards Israel and Gaza hurt her presidential run in 2024. Though he still faces some skepticism from Jewish Democrats, he also won the endorsement of Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel, one of the most prominent Jewish officials in the state. El-Sayed and Rogers will have their first debate on Thursday. 7. Iowa The competitive contest in Iowa moves up one spot. Two polls of likely voters released in the last week show Democratic nominee Josh Turek and GOP Rep. Ashley Hinson running neck-and-neck. A NYT/Siena poll of likely voters showed Hinson’s support at 48% and Turek at 47% while a Fox News poll found Turek at 49% and Hinson at 47%. The agriculture-heavy state has felt the impacts of Trump policies like tariffs and the war in Iran, which have created price shocks for farm equipment, fertilizer and diesel. Trump’s approval rating in Iowa is at 42%, according to the Fox News poll, and more likely voters expressed concern about Hinson aligning too closely to Trump (52%) than that Turek’s position is too liberal (43%). Turek has worked to link Hinson directly to Trump and recently ran an ad tying her votes to high gas prices in the state. Iowa is also home to three competitive House races and a gubernatorial contest where Democrats believe state auditor Rob Sand has a real chance of flipping the office blue and in turn helping Turek and others on the ballot. Like Rogers in Michigan, Hinson has put some distance between herself and the Iran war, calling for its immediate end to drive down prices, and she’s criticized Trump’s moves on beef imports. She also appeared alongside the president in the Oval Office as he announced plans for a $15 billion steel plant that could create 1,750 permanent jobs and thousands more temporary ones – though that promise has drawn some skepticism from Iowans from both parties. Republicans are deploying additional money to the state to try to get Hinson across the finish line. The Republican-aligned Senate Leadership Fund upped their advertising spend by $20 million for the month of October, and Republicans are already on track to outspend Democrats in the state for the final weeks of the campaign. 8. New Hampshire New Hampshire has dropped two spots, but the competitive contest between Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas and GOP former Sen. John Sununu is keeping Democrats on their toes. A University of New Hampshire poll conducted in September showed Pappas up 8 points over Sununu with likely voters while a New York Times/Siena poll over roughly the same period revealed no clear leader in the contest. Democrats ultimately believe their voters and independents will side with Pappas in a state Harris narrowly won in 2024, but Pappas has also warned that his party needs to prioritize the state more. Sununu is a very familiar name for voters in New Hampshire, where his brother and father both served as governor. Democrats are spending significant time trying to remind voters which Sununu is on the ballot and attacking his lobbying background. Republican strategists also feel Republican Gov. Kelly Ayotte, who is polling ahead in her reelection bid, could create a lift for Sununu in November. But New Hampshire voters are well-known for splitting their tickets, and the environment for Republicans is still tough. 9. Kansas Kansas appears on this list for the first time as it emerges as a new headache for the GOP in the midterms’ final stretch. Adam Hamilton, a Republican-turned-Democrat megachurch pastor, has put the state in play. A NYT/Siena poll of likely voters in Kansas showed a tied race between Hamilton and Republican Sen. Roger Marshall, who is seeking a second term. Marshall won his first Senate race in 2020 by double digits and Trump won Kansas by 16 points in 2024. Now, the GOP-aligned Senate Leadership Fund will dedicate millions of dollars in advertising to defend Marshall. Marshall, an OB-GYN, is facing blowback after reporting on his involvement in lawsuits over medical debt. Hamilton’s campaign has seized on the developments, drawing complaints from Marshall, who called the reporting a “hit job” during a debate last month and said he engaged in “common business practices.” Marshall is also contending with the same Trump-related headwinds pressuring Republicans across the country, tariffs and fuel costs hitting Kansas and Iowa farmers alike. He’s taken some steps to distance himself from the president – releasing a statement last month chiding US Immigration and Customs Enforcement for “mass disruptions to local communities and businesses.” Hamilton, meanwhile, is leaning into his partisan conversion to appeal to a broad set of voters, positioning himself apart from “dysfunction” in Washington. “We have to fix our broken politics by meeting in the middle,” he says in a top ad from last month. “It’s time for something different.” Just last week, Mike Hayden became the second Republican former governor from the state to back Hamilton over Marshall. “I supported Roger Marshall before. But he has spent his time in the Senate putting party and politics over the people of Kansas,” Hayden wrote in an opinion piece. “It’s time for a change.” 10. Georgia Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff looks well-positioned in his reelection bid against his GOP challenger, Rep. Mike Collins. Through the end of June, Ossoff had out-raised Collins, $77 million to $6.5 million, according to FEC records for their principal campaign committees. It’s also the only Senate race where Democrats are set to have a significant ad spending lead over the final month ($23 million to $16 million) as Republicans appear wary of committing major resources to the contest – a significant contrast to races in Ohio. Strategists on both sides are closely watching the governor’s race in the state as Republicans hope their candidate Rick Jackson can offer a boost to Collins. But Ossoff is also working hard to lift Democrats across Georgia, including gubernatorial nominee Keisha Lance Bottoms. States we’re still watching Many of these states seem like longshots but will still be on our radar until November. Nebraska is another midwestern state feeling the economic strains of Trump’s war with Iran. The contest remains an uphill climb for independent candidate Dan Osborn, who unsuccessfully ran for Senate in 2024, as he now challenges GOP Sen. Pete Ricketts. South Carolina Sen. Darline Graham is running against Democrat Annie Andrews, a pediatrician, for a full term after being appointed to her late brother Sen. Lindsey Graham’s seat. One thing to watch here is how much GOP spending comes into the state in the final stretch. A Democrat hasn’t won a South Carolina Senate seat in nearly three decades. Mississippi Democratic Senate nominee Scott Colom has attracted a lot of attention in his race against Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. But a Colom win is a longshot for Democrats in a state Trump won by nearly 23 points. Minnesota Democratic Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan is facing off against Michele Tafoya, a former sports broadcaster turned conservative activist. Republicans are excited about Tafoya’s candidacy, but Minnesota went for Harris by 4 points in 2024 and is affected by the same headwinds as other Midwestern states.

cnn.com.title: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor takes legal action against UK police over Epstein arrest
cnn.com.text: King Charles’ younger brother Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor has launched legal action against police in England over his arrest earlier this year on suspicion of misconduct in public office following revelations from the Epstein files in the United States. Mountbatten-Windsor, 66, has asked for a judge to determine if Thames Valley Police’s actions against him earlier this year were lawful. The development was first reported by Britain’s The Telegraph newspaper on Sunday. He has lodged a judicial review in relation to the search warrants that were executed at his home at the Sandringham Estate and his former home at Royal Lodge in Windsor. A court hearing will be held on Thursday, British media reported Monday. Thames Valley Police confirmed to CNN on Monday that it was “engaged in legal proceedings in relation to warrants previously obtained from the Central Criminal Court” and would not comment further with legal proceedings ongoing. CNN has also reached out to the UK Judicial Office for comment. The former Duke of York became the first senior royal in centuries to be arrested in February, the latest extraordinary development in a yearslong scandal over his ties to the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, which obliterated his reputation and has thrown the royal family into crisis. He was detained by police on his 66th birthday at his new home on his brother’s Sandringham estate in Norfolk, eastern England, on February 19. He was taken to Aylsham police station where he was questioned for almost 12 hours before being released under investigation. No charges were filed; police have said its investigation is still ongoing. Mountbatten-Windsor’s arrest came after the force previously said it was assessing whether the former prince had shared confidential information with Epstein during his decade as a UK trade envoy. Mountbatten-Windsor has vehemently denied any and all wrongdoing in his dealings with Epstein, and has denied any personal gain from his role as a trade envoy, according to British media reports. He stepped down from official royal duties in 2019 following a calamitous interview with the BBC over his friendship with Epstein. But headlines related to the late financier continued to plague the disgraced royal. In 2025, King Charles stripped his younger brother of his title as prince, following public outcry after the release of a posthumous memoir by Virginia Giuffre, a prominent accuser of Epstein who alleged that Mountbatten-Windsor had sexually assaulted her as a teenager. Giuffre – who the prince claims never to have met – died by suicide in April 2025 at the age of 41. In addition to denying all allegations against him, Mountbatten-Windsor has also previously insisted he never witnessed or suspected any of the behavior of which Epstein is accused.

cnn.com.title: Spanish PM Sánchez calls November election amid growing housing protests
cnn.com.text: Spanish Prime ⁠Minister Pedro Sánchez on Monday called ⁠an ​early ​election in an apparent effort to seize the initiative following nationwide protests over a housing crisis sparked by the eviction of a 87-year-old woman. The election, scheduled for ​November ⁠29, will bring the current parliamentary term to an end more than six months ahead of schedule. “After informing the head of state, I have decided to convene an extraordinary meeting of the Council of Ministers this morning to dissolve Parliament and call a general election,” Sánchez, leader of the Socialist Workers’ Party (PSOE), said in a televised address from Moncloa, his official residence in Madrid. The announcement came after Sánchez’s government last week failed to secure parliamentary backing for two propsoed laws aimed at tackling the country’s housing crisis. The measures were proposed following mounting public anger at the eviction of Maria del Carmen Abascal, known in Spain simply as Maricarmen, an 87-year-old resident of Madrid’s Retiro neighborhood, whose case has become a symbol of the country’s housing emergency. Maricarmen had been living in the same house for more than 70 years but was evicted after her rent increased from €500 ($560) to €2,650 ($2,970). Thousands of people took to the streets in fury, and she has become the face of the ruthlessness of Spain’s housing crisis. For more than a week, hundreds of people have camped out in Madrid’s central Puerta del Sol to protest the crisis, and rallies have taken place elsewhere in Spain. Madrid’s Tenants Union, one of the groups organizing the protests, claimed about 950,000 people took part in demonstrations across the country over the weekend. Sánchez, who has been prime minister for more than eight years, called the election three days after right-wing parties in parliament defeated proposed laws aimed to ease the hosuing crisis. Analysts expect Sánchez to focus on housing in an effort to win over popular support. The conservative Popular Party, which opposed the ptoposed housing reforms, is leading in opinion polls. “We need to renew people’s support,” Sánchez said on Monday. “We need to mobilise and win a much larger progressive majority in parliament, one that will allow us to overcome vested interests, deliver new social advances and continue transforming Spain.” Sánchez’s socialist PSOE party has suffered several setbacks in regional elections this year, and a series of corruption scandals involving close associates have also tarnished its reputation. The migration crisis in Ceuta - in which tens of thousands of migrants crossed into the Spainish terriority bordering Morocco - during the summer intensified that criticism. “I know that among part of that social majority there is dissatisfaction today,” he said. “You are outraged to see their interests being trampled on in Parliament for the benefit of a select few.” As he called for snap elections, he conceded his government had made some “mistakes” but argued it had been faced with unprecedented challenges from abroad. He cited the war in Ukraine and the conflicts in the Middle East, he also highlighted Spain becoming one of Europe’s strongest economies. Sánchez is one of few left-wing leaders in Europe, as the right surges Sánchez is one of the few center-left leaders in Europe amid a surge in right-wing populism, and he has taken a firm stand on issues such as Palestinian statehood, the responsibility of social media companies and the US campaign against Iran. Spain refused to allow US bombers to use bases on its territory. Sánchez has been outspoken in his criticism of US strikes, provoking anger and threats from the White House. But rather than back down, Sánchez and his government doubled down, winning public support for his opposition to the Trump administration. In March, Trump threatened to cut off trade with Spain. “We could use their base if we want, we could just fly in and use it, nobody’s going to tell us not to use it,” he said. In contrast to much of Europe, Sánchez has also said that immigration is essential to sustain economic growth and moved to regularize the status of hundreds of thousands of undocumented migrants in Spain earlier this year. “I trust my fellow citizens,” Sánchez went on to say. “I know that you are a courageous and compassionate people who rise to challenges, and that you have no qualms about being the first, and the last, to stand on the right side of history.” Sánchez has put together a series of coalitions with left-wing parties and small separatist parties over the past eight years but has struggled to get legislation through at times, often falling back on decrees. The government has been unable to pass a budget for three years. Opinion polls suggest a coalition led by the center-right People’s Party (PP) with the support of the far-right Vox party is the most likely outcome in the election. If Vox were to join an incoming government, it would be the first time the far-right would be part of a government in Spain since the return of democracy after the death of dictator Francisco Franco in 1975.

cnn.com.title: Key takeaways as Brazil heads to presidential runoff that could reshape Latin America
cnn.com.text: Brazil is heading for another Lula-Bolsonaro showdown. But this time it is Jair Bolsonaro’s eldest son Flávio who stands between leftist President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and another term in power. A Bolsonaro victory would push the region further towards the right, hand US President Donald Trump a powerful ideological ally in its largest country and potentially strengthen Washington’s hand as it seeks to counter China’s influence across the hemisphere. For Lula, 80, the runoff vote leaves one of Latin America’s most prominent left-wing leaders fighting for what is likely will be last term if he wins. Bolsonaro seems to be thriving without his father Together, Lula and Bolsonaro accounted for more than 92% of the votes, underscoring the strong grip of the Lula and Bolsonaro camps on Brazilian politics.
