But neither secured the 50% needed to avoid a runoff, now set for October 25. The situation now resembles that of 2022, but Bolsanaro performed better than his father did in the first round four years ago. The crucial battleground was the Southeast, where nearly 40% of the electorate lives. There, Flávio won São Paulo and Minas Gerais. His victory in Minas Gerais carries particular symbolic weight: the state has voted for the winner in every presidential election since 1989 when Brazil held its first direct presidential election after military rule. The result suggests Bolsonaro, who exceeded poll projections, has done more than simply inherit his father’s political movement. He may have expanded it. With a campaign focused on crime and the economy, he secured nearly four percentage points more than his father in the first round in 2022. He leaned heavily on his father’s image while also seeking to present himself as a more moderate figure. For Lula, the result raises an uncomfortable question. Can his political legacy and record in office still deliver an electoral majority? Minas Gerais helps explain his predicament. He received 43.21% there, well below the 48.3% won in the first round of 2022. Nor did he achieve the lead margin his campaign had hoped for in the Northeast, his main stronghold. The race is far from over The runoff will depend on who can capture voters who backed eliminated candidates and whether either side can mobilize Brazilians who stayed home on Sunday. The eliminated candidates collectively accounted for 7.82% of votes. Most of those votes went to candidates on the center-right or right, potentially giving Bolsonaro another advantage. But abstention is another potentially decisive reservoir of votes. About 21% of eligible voters did not cast a ballot, and mobilizing them could tip the scales in a tight election. Polls leading up to Sunday showed the two candidates tied in runoff scenarios. Lula must now overcome a first-round deficit amid voter concerns over purchasing power and crime, an issue Bolsonaro made central to his campaign, as well as controversies surrounding key figures in scandals seen as close to the president. Bolsonaro, meanwhile, enters the runoff with another advantage: political momentum beyond the presidential race. His party and allies won numerous Senate seats as well as governorships in key states, potentially giving a Bolsonaro presidency significant legislative and regional support. An even more polarized runoff is expected. Lula will likely frame the vote as a referendum on democracy and while Bolsanaro will focus on his tough-on-crime rhetoric and allegations of corruption against Lula and his party. Trump has plenty at stake Few outside Brazil have more riding on the runoff than Trump. The US president openly endorsed Bolsonaro earlier in the campaign and maintains a tense relationship with Lula’s government. He has been notably quieter in recent weeks but there is little ambiguity over which outcome would better suit Washington. Since Trump returned to the White House, no left-wing candidate has won a presidential election in Latin America. Now, Washington hopes to bring about an ideological shift in Brazil, the region’s biggest economy, that will help it fully impose its “Donroe Doctrine” and contain China’s influence. “Trump had already welcomed Bolsonaro to the Oval Office at the White House and has imposed punitive tariffs on Brazil, the sole motivation for which appears to be political,” international relations expert Farid Kahhat, a professor at the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, told CNN. “The fact that he hasn’t spoken out publicly again doesn’t change the fact that he already did so in the past and that he has made public policy decisions in favor of the Bolsonaros,” he added. For Kahhat, Trump’s recent restraint may itself be strategic. “They’ve already decided it was better to keep a lower profile,” he said. There is good reason for caution. Open intervention by Trump could have the opposite effect in the world’s tenth-largest economy, which is far less dependent on Washington than some of its neighbors. “They’ve noticed that in Brazil, [interference] might not work the same way as it does in Honduras or Colombia,” Kahhat said. Lula has also used the banner of national sovereignty as a campaign weapon. Political scientist Manuel Alcántara Sáez, director of the International Center for Political and Social Studies (CIEPS-AIP) in Panama, said another Trump intervention could end up helping Lula. “It would be more beneficial for Lula because there is a stronger sentiment against US interference,” he said. Trump isn’t the only regional ally to have backed Bolsonaro. Argentine President Javier Milei supported him and attended his campaign launch, where he hurled insults at Lula. “Since then, I haven’t noticed Milei getting so involved in the campaign,” Alexander Main, director of international policy at the Center for Economic and Policy Research, told CNN. “I think maybe they felt it wasn’t helping that much.” But Bolsonaro’s strong showing quickly drew celebration from the Latin American right. Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella who won in June with Trump’s backing said on X: “May God have mercy on our brother country as He did on Colombia. True change is defeating the left.” Milei followed by congratulating Bolsonaro, saying: “The American continent is made up of citizens who want to live in freedom.” Is Latin America really moving right or just voting governments out? Bolsonaro’s performance appears, at first glance, to fit neatly into Latin America’s broader rightward turn. But analysts caution that something more complicated may be happening. With strategies based on antagonism and the “cancellation” of the opponent, policy proposals and promises “matter very little” in convincing undecided voters, Alcántara Sáez said. Beyond the committed bases, “the rest of the electorate is driven by other kinds of impulses, including fatigue and despair at seeing, on one side, an 80-year-old candidate and, on the other, a candidate who is the son of someone in prison, convicted of leading an attempted coup,” he said. That fatigue echoes a broader pattern across Latin America: incumbent parties struggling to survive voter frustration. Kahhat said that although “this is a time of crisis for the left throughout the region,” the string of right-wing victories should not necessarily be read as a wholesale ideological conversion. “It depends on the context, but it is not necessarily a rejection of left-wing movements as such, but rather of those in power at a time of great economic instability,” he said. Brazil’s runoff will therefore test two competing explanations for the political transformation sweeping the region: whether Latin America is undergoing a durable shift to the right, or whether frustrated voters are simply punishing whoever happens to be in power. For Alcántara Sáez, there is another dividing line that may prove just as important: how Latin American governments position themselves toward Trump. “Lula would clearly represent someone who would never in his life go along with the ‘Shield of the Americas’ initiative, whereas Bolsonaro would,” he said, referring to a political and security initiative floated by Trump. “So, rather than a shift to the right, I think this pro-US or anti-US. dimension is what we should be looking at more closely.” That makes October 25 about considerably more than who governs Brazil. The result could help determine whether the region’s largest power acts as a counterweight to Trump’s vision for the hemisphere, or becomes one of its most important allies.

cnn.com.title: Samoan leader apologizes for ‘Heil Hitler’ salute at 2007 family reunion
cnn.com.text: Samoa’s prime minister has apologized after an old video of him surfaced performing the Nazi salute while leading a chorus of “Heil Hitler” at a family reunion in 2007. Prime Minister Laaulialemalietoa Leuatea Schmidt said his words were “not intended for the public” and apologized in a statement published by the government Monday. “Whatever the context or intention at that gathering twenty years ago, I recognise that those words and gesture were inappropriate and capable of causing offence and hurt and I apologise for using them,” said Laaulialemalietoa, who became PM of the Pacific Island nation last year. The antisemitic remarks were made during a “private family gathering” in Savai’i, the country’s largest island, in 2007, Laaulialemalietoa said, when he was serving as deputy speaker of Parliament. In the seven-second video clip, Laaulialemalietoa is seen leading about a dozen people in the Nazi-affiliated salute, saying “Raise your right hand, Heil Hitler,” while the group mimics his words and gesture, according to the Samoa Observer newspaper, which first reported on the video Sunday. Laaulialemalietoa banned the Samoa Observer from all government press conferences last year for what he’s called “unfair” reporting. Samoa is a tiny nation of about 221,000 people in the South Pacific, near Fiji. It sits to the west of American Samoa, the US territory in the eastern part of the Samoan island chain. Samoa was colonized by Germany in the early 20th century, and many Samoans have German heritage and surnames. New Zealand took what was then known as Western Samoa from the Germans in 1914 and retained control of Samoa until the country’s independence in 1962. In his statement Monday, Laaulialemalietoa said his behavior in the clip does not reflect his personal beliefs or the beliefs of the government or people of Samoa. “I reject Nazism, antisemitism, racism and all forms of political extremism,” he said, adding that he now considers “this matter addressed.”

cnn.com.title: Masha’s husband was fighting on the front line. But she was the one killed by a Russian drone
cnn.com.text: It was not meant to be Masha. Her husband, Danylo Yivzhenko, is the soldier in the family. As a combat medic with Ukraine’s Third Separate Assault Brigade, he made the decision to go to war, knowing the risk. Masha was a civilian, back home in Kyiv, worrying about her husband on the front line. But it was Masha, 29, who was killed by the Russians when a powerful drone struck her office building in the Ukrainian capital on September 25. It’s an injustice that Yivzhenko cannot comprehend. “I am a soldier and I am fighting against Russia. If a Russian military drone or a ballistic missile, or whatever else, kills me – that is fair. We kill Russians. Russians kill us. We are servicemen; we understand what we are doing,” he told CNN. “Killing a soldier is horrible, but it is normal. But Masha was a civilian. She did not assemble drones, she did not hold a weapon in her hands, she did not wear a military uniform. She was a civilian in a civilian city who was simply doing her civilian job that day.” Daily life as it was known in Kyiv stopped on August 27, when Russia began pounding the city with near non-stop aerial assaults. Since then, not a single day has passed without an air raid warning in the city. On average, there have been seven air raid alerts a day. Some days, there have been as many as 13. The Ukrainian military is increasingly unable to defend Kyiv from these assaults because of critical shortages of air defense weapons to bring down Russia’s missiles and its newest jet-powered drones. Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelensky, has been begging allies to help, and the Ukrainian military is racing to develop effective interceptors domestically – but neither has yet led to a meaningful shift. In just over a month – between August 27 and Oct 4 – at least 98 people have been killed and 435 injured in Kyiv and the wider Kyiv region, a number that is significantly higher than in previous months. Several high-profile buildings at the heart of the capital have been struck by Russian drones during this period, including the headquarters of the Security Service of Ukraine, the National Academy of Sciences, High Council of Justice and a TV and internet provider’s data center. Russia consistently claims it only strikes military targets, despite ample evidence of civilian sites being struck on a regular basis. Russia used to launch its aerial attacks overnight under the cover of darkness, to minimize Kyiv’s chances of intercepting them. This meant people were often exhausted after a sleepless night in a shelter, but their lives could go on relatively as normal during the day. But Russia’s newest jet-powered drones have made it possible for Moscow to terrorize Ukraine at any time of the day. And each time Russia fires at Kyiv, an air raid alarm is triggered and life in the capital stops. Many businesses and services, including some public transit operations, shut down, and everyone is meant to head to a shelter. The Ukrainian capital is split in half by the Dnipro river. The right bank is home to the majority of Kyiv’s business centers, offices and government institutions, whereas the left bank is mostly residential. The bridges connecting the two sides are crucial – some 600,000 vehicles cross them every day. And these vital links have become the most recent target for Russia. Kyiv’s Southern Bridge, which serves ground transportation as well as the city’s subway system, was hit five times within two days on Thursday and Friday. The city’s Northern Bridge was hit twice on Saturday and Sunday. The disruption has forced Kyiv authorities to start work on creating a new pontoon bridge. Schoolchildren suffer Russia’s shift toward this new strategy coincided with the start of a new school year in Ukraine – and children are among those hit hardest by the constant interruptions. According to Kyiv authorities, roughly half of the city’s 250,000 children are attending schools in person full time, while most of the rest alternate between remote and in-person learning. A handful of schools are operating fully online. Some schools have gone as far as moving all of their classes underground. Others spend precious learning time moving children to shelters. The enormous risks of bringing children into classrooms were made clear on Thursday, when a Russian drone struck one of Kyiv’s schools while more than 100 children were inside. The school’s headteacher, Olena Chorna, said an earlier air raid alert had only just ended when the sirens started blaring again. “We all hurried down to the shelter and stayed there … 104 children were in the shelter. We could hear things being destroyed; the school was filled with smoke, but in the shelter all the doors were closed and we couldn’t feel a thing.” No one was injured but extensive damage was caused to the building. But with alerts now much more common, many find it hard to keep following the official guidance. “I can’t stay in shelters all the time, because I have to keep living, keep studying,” university student Sophia Zaremba told CNN. Zaremba, who is 20, said the day-to-day reality of living under fire was catching up with her. She witnessed a Russian drone strike next to her university building the day before speaking to CNN. She knew an air raid alert was in place, but she had urgent errands to take care of, she explained. “It was unexpected. You get used to the fact that drones are flying around and that there are various places nearby where they might hit… but this was loud, and it caught us off guard,” she said. She told CNN that all she could think of in the moment was that another explosion might be imminent. “I just thought the alarm was still going off and, God forbid, the next strike might be nearby.” All her remaining sense of security has been shattered, she added. “I haven’t been able to get out of bed for half the day today because I just don’t have the mental strength to do anything.” Russia’s current weapon of choice against Kyiv is its new wave of jet-powered drones, known as the Geran-4 and Geran-5. These killer machines resemble tiny cruise missiles, flying at speeds of up to 600 kilometers per hour (310 miles per hour) and often carrying powerful warheads. They often travel too fast and too high for Kyiv’s mobile fire groups to shoot down, so ground-to-air missiles, fighter jets or interceptors must be deployed – all of which are in extremely limited supply in Ukraine. At the same time, these drones cost as little as one-tenth as much as a traditional cruise missile to produce than traditional cruise missiles, which means Russia can afford to launch dozens of them at the same time. According to Yurii Ihnat, spokesman for the Ukrainian Air Force, Russia launched 2,850 jet-powered drones in August and 3,177 in September. Masha Yivzhenko was killed when her office building in central Kyiv was hit by a Geran-5 drone on September 25. According to Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to Zelensky, another jet-powered drone was circling the site of the strike at high altitude, providing a radio signal for the device. Once the building was struck, the second drone flew off to attack a McDonald’s warehouse in the suburbs of Kyiv, Beskrestnov said. Yivzhenko told CNN that one of the things he loved most about Masha was the fact the two of them — both former journalists – always had something interesting to talk about. “She was my best friend and my whole life was built around the fact that we had each other,” he said. When Yivzhenko enlisted in 2024, after working as a volunteer medic since the beginning of the war, the couple got a dog, Jessie, so that Masha wouldn’t be completely alone. They took out a mortgage to buy an apartment and were planning their future, despite the war. “We bought Masha a car because we were planning to have children,” he said. Yivzhenko was in Kyiv for a few days last week. On the day of the attack, he drove Masha to her office to pick up her laptop so she could work from home. She popped in for a few minutes and he walked Jessie while waiting for her to come back. And then the drone struck. First responders at the scene told Yivzhenko that his wife had died on impact. Her body was found under the stairs on the first floor of the office building. “She didn’t burn, she didn’t bleed to death. She died instantly. The blast wave threw her down from the fifth floor,” he told CNN. “I identified her, and they let me go. I have buried my brothers-in-arms and I am mentally prepared for the fact that I will bury my parents when they get old. And all of that is normal. That is life. But by killing Masha, they killed me.”

cnn.com.title: Trump fights on home turf as Democratic midterm hopes rise
cnn.com.text: Republicans are defending territory they never expected to be at risk four weeks before Election Day, as President Donald Trump implores voters not to desert his party with the promise of more cash giveaways. A top White House adviser, meanwhile, argued Sunday on CNN that “partisan pollsters” are wrong that voters are hurting financially — a message that suggests a disconnect between the country and a president who boasts of an economic “golden age.” And polling released over the weekend pointed to growing peril for the GOP, with Democrats leading or in tight races in states Trump won easily two years ago, amid signs that Latino voters, who helped power him back to the White House, are drifting away. The Iran war remains an anvil for Republicans heading into the final stretch of the midterms, with few signs that high gasoline and diesel prices will return to cheaper levels soon — at least in time for voters to feel the difference by November 2. Still, polls four weeks away do not forecast directly how the election will turn out, and there is palpable nervousness among Democrats with painful memories of their past defeats by a president who is now throwing everything at the final weeks. The intensifying political combat underscores the critical stakes of the election, as Democrats aim for House and Senate majorities they’d likely use to probe deep into Trump’s White House and his family’s finances during the final years of his term. Democrats need only a few pickups to win back control of the House, where they currently have 214 seats, compared with 219 Republicans (including one independent who caucuses with the majority). They need a net gain of four seats to win the Senate in a duel that carries the tantalizing possibility of a Supreme Court nominating fight after conservative Justice Samuel Alito told CBS News that he now considers retirement every term. Trump, seeking to defy approval ratings in the 30s, campaigned in deep-red Alabama on Friday; on Saturday he spoke at a rally in Ohio, which he won by 11 points in 2024 but where a critical Senate race this year is too close to call. His travel schedule is another sign his party is on the defensive a month out. He pleaded with Republican voters in the Deep South to “pretend I’m on the ballot” and waxed about the unprecedented “golden age” he says he’s conjured. In an apparent attempt to sweeten his message, the White House announced a $90 payment to around 20 million seniors who are on Medicare Part B. Last month, Trump promised every American adult $5,000 if Republicans win the midterms. In Ohio on Saturday night, the president crudely promised his voters victory against the Democrats, if only they’d turn out in huge numbers to vote. “We’re going to win big, and we’re going to shove it up their ass,” he said. Trump aide tells CNN tales of ‘depressed’ voters are false The White House is pushing back hard on a narrative of economic pain. “Ahead of an election cycle, the fact that there’s possibly partisan pollsters telling us that the people are really, really depressed, it’s a classic Democrat move,” Kevin Hassett, director of the National Economic Council, told CNN’s Jake Tapper on “State of the Union” Sunday. Hassett blamed high prices for groceries and food on former President Joe Biden and argued that fresh government data Friday showing only 29,000 jobs were created in September was an outlier. Democrats claim that such characterizations reflect denial in the White House. “People can’t afford their lives,” Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly said on CBS’ “Face the Nation,” dismissing Trump’s promised payouts as “trying to buy votes.” GOP Sen. John Kennedy of Louisiana warned that the biggest election issue was the cost of living. “We have to tell the American people the truth,” Kennedy said. He added on NBC’s “Meet the Press” that “we (keep) telling them not to believe their own lying checkbooks.” “The American people, both sides, feel anger,” Kennedy said. “If they don’t feel anger, they feel deep melancholy.” Multiple polls back up Kennedy’s assertions on the economy. In the latest, for CBS News this weekend, 70% of voters said Trump’s policies were pushing prices up. And 56% said Trump’s policies were responsible for today’s economy, while only 20% blamed Biden. In an AP/NORC poll last week, 69% of adults said that Trump’s handling of the cost of living had been worse than expected. Democrats have offered scant details about what they’d do to cut the cost of living. But in a midterm election that is shaping up as a referendum on an unpopular president, that may not matter. Trump has complained that “nobody’s selling” the fact that “there’s no economy like this economy.” But he’s hardly sticking to one single message himself. He appeared to share Republican Arkansas Sen. Tom Cotton’s cell phone number on social media Saturday amid a dispute over daylight saving time; on Sunday, he lashed out at Fox News for not sufficiently covering his Ohio rally and filled Truth Social with photos of himself with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and AI illustrations staking claims to Greenland. A map once thought problematic brims with possibility for Democrats A Senate map once thought to favor Republicans now looks challenging for the party that currently holds both the House and the Senate as part of a monopoly on Washington power. On Friday, a top GOP super PAC paused spending on a Republican-held seat in North Carolina, where Michael Whatley trails in the polls. Fresh New York Times/Siena polls published Saturday showed Democrats leading in the races for Republican-held Senate seats in Alaska and Texas. The surveys also found no clear leader in races in Ohio, Kansas and Iowa — results that will also cheer Democrats because the seats are currently held by Republicans and Trump romped to victory in each state in 2024. Trump’s approval rating on the economy languishes at or below 40% in each of the states. And roughly half of voters surveyed want a candidate who will provide a check on Trump. Other tight races are raging in Michigan, where progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed is trying to keep retiring Sen. Gary Peters’ seat for Democrats; and in Maine, where Democrats finally hope to pick off longtime GOP Sen. Susan Collins. In another danger sign for the GOP, a new NBC/Telemundo poll released Sunday found Latino voters saying by a 24-point margin that they’d prefer to see the Democrats win Congress. Just 27% of Latino voters approve of Trump’s job performance overall, with 20% approving of his handling of the cost of living. In 2024, Trump forged historic breakthroughs in virtually every segment of the Latino community, leading to hopes among some GOP strategists of a permanent realignment. But there’s been a backlash to the White House’s intensive deportation campaign. In knife-edge states including Texas, where Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico is conjuring hopes of a first statewide victory for his party in more than 30 years, Latino defections could prove hugely significant. Voter sentiment can change in the final weeks before an election, and Trump insists pollsters always underplay MAGA support. It would not be a surprise if key races tighten, especially if the base rallies for the president one last time. Trump beseeched Americans during his rally in Alabama to recognize he’d made “unbelievable progress” and promised “new levels of greatness.” But the evidence of nationwide angst over the cost of living is compelling. And since Trump promised to fix the issue in 2024, the election may come down to this simple question: Do voters believe his invocations of a “golden age”?

cnn.com.title: Britain’s Green Party votes to class Zionism as a form of racism
cnn.com.text: Britain’s Green Party voted on Sunday to class Zionism as a form of racism, drawing criticism from British Jews and from the Israeli government which said it now viewed the party as “a body that gives legitimacy to terrorism.” The party – which received 6% of the vote in national elections in 2024 – said it regarded Zionism as “an ethnonationalist political project” and repeated its call for Britain’s Labour government to end all arms trade with Israel. “The motion also restates the Green Party’s backing for the right to self-determination and calls for the establishment of a single democratic state throughout historic Palestine,” the party said in a statement. The definition of Zionism – which inspired the foundation of the modern state of Israel in the 20th century – and what it implies for the rights of non-Jews in Israel and neighbouring territory, is contentious. Jewish groups sometimes define it as a right to Jewish self-determination. The Green Party motion passed by a majority of 1,022 to 813 despite opposition from many senior figures. Party leader Zack Polanski, who is seeking election to Parliament on Thursday in former Prime Minister Keir Starmer’s now-vacant London constituency, did not vote. The result was condemned by British Jewish groups. “The Green Party has made antisemitism party policy and become a racist party,” the Movement for Progressive Judaism said, adding that the support of some Jews for the motion did not mean it would not be used to discriminate against others. Israeli foreign minister Gideon Sa’ar has decided to declare Polanski barred from entering Israel, the foreign ministry said in a post on X Sunday. It said the Green Party motion “constitutes a clear antisemitic text according to the IHRA (International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance) definition, as it denies the Jewish people’s right to self-determination,” the ministry said. Mothin Ali, deputy leader of the Green Party and a supporter of the motion, told Sky News on Saturday that the heavy Palestinian death toll in Israel’s conflict with Hamas – which followed the Palestinian militant group’s deadly 2023 attack on an Israeli music festival – was the key context for the vote. “The motion defines Zionism quite clearly. It defines it as an ethnonationalist movement. It defines it as ethnic cleansing. It defines it as genocide,” Ali said. Britain’s government views Israeli settlers’ actions in the West Bank as amounting to ethnic cleansing but has said courts must decide if other Israeli actions qualify as genocide. Israel – which rejects claims of ethnic cleansing and genocide – called on Sunday for other British political parties to condemn the Green Party vote. “The Greens have adopted not only the green of Hamas, but also its ideology: the elimination of the State of Israel through armed struggle,” it said. Polanski and other senior Green Party figures said they would “continue to call out the heinous crimes of the Netanyahu government,” and that “there is no conflict between supporting the rights of Palestinians and the rights of Jewish people.”

cnn.com.title: US removes all Air Force bombers from UK base following new threat
cnn.com.text: The United States has moved long-range bombers back to their American home stations after an unspecified new threat, according to a US official, days after the British government arrested a number of individuals in connection with an alleged Iranian plot to target the UK airbase where the planes had been stationed. “We can acknowledge now that all U.S. bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have re-deployed to their home stations in the United States,” the official told CNN. The statement did not include details on why the planes were moved. The source familiar called the latest threat a “real world incident.” It is unusual that the US military would move the bombers back to their home stations instead of deploying them to another base in the region, the official said. The UK Ministry of Defense declined to comment. The Royal Air Force base at Fairford has been used to deploy US B-1 bombers involved in the war against Iran and is an operating location for US Global Strike Command, which is tasked with managing long-distance strikes. CNN national security analyst Alex Plitsas said it was likely several dozen bombers were stationed at Fairford, adding that it was unusual to move all the aircraft. “It speaks to the credibility and the seriousness of the threat overall to the base that we’re talking about,” he told Ben Hunte on CNN Newsroom. The relocation of the bombers comes amid the investigation into the alleged plot. British police on September 27 arrested five men on suspicion of terror and explosives offenses close to the airbase. The men – identified only as British nationals between the ages of 23 and 25 and from the London area – were quickly released on bail, with police confirming no explosives were found in three vans at the scene. Their release sparked criticism from President Donald Trump, who said “I wouldn’t have done that.” A 25-year-old British-Iranian dual national was also arrested on Thursday in connection with the alleged plot. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said last week there are “strong indications” Iran was involved in the incident. “We will say more in due course, but we can confirm our belief that we believe Iran to have played a part,” he told the BBC on Sept 30. Burnham’s remarks appeared to support the US’ assessment that the incident involved a foreign actor. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said “the hands of a foreign actor” were involved in the alleged plot but declined to provide details in an interview with Fox News last week. “I think it ties us to the reality here. We are dealing with elements in the world, and in the case of Iran for example, who have openly threatened to attack American interests globally,” he said. Meanwhile, Iran has denied any involvement in the incident, described the accusations as baseless and summoned the British ambassador in Tehran, Iranian state media reported Thursday. During the meeting, Iran’s Deputy Foreign Minister Majid Takht-Ravanchi reportedly urged London to revise what he called its “inappropriate approach” toward Tehran. This has been updated with additional details.

cnn.com.title: Flydubai hijacking attempt exposes worrying gaps in aviation security
cnn.com.text: The quick-thinking actions of the captain of last week’s Flydubai flight bound for Israel prevented what could have been an unmitigated hijacking disaster. But aviation safety experts say the incident raises serious concerns about the security failures before the flight and how it happened in the first place. The suspected attacker, named as co-pilot Hamam al-Hammami, was removed from Oman’s national airline last year following concerns about his extremist views, sources told CNN. Both the United Arab Emirates and Israel have strict aviation security regulations – yet al-Hammami was allowed to fly. “A lot of the post 9/11 security measures that were adopted were meant to prevent an external threat – loading bombs or things onto an aircraft, you know, preventing a threat from amongst the passenger base from getting access to cockpits,” said CNN national security analyst Alex Plitsas. “It wasn’t really designed with the theory that a pilot would do something like that.” There is no international standard for background checks. Experts said pilots’ licenses and security passes are handled at the national level, and the rules vary depending on the country. Questions about background checks in aviation industry The allegations of extremist views and the suspected attacker’s dismissal from a previous job have raised concerns about the reliability of background checks in the aviation industry. CNN has reached out to Oman Air, the Dubai government’s media office and Dubai Airports Company for comment. Flydubai said it could not provide comment while the incident remained under investigation. All flight crew members require an “airside” pass, which allows them to go to the non-passenger side of airports and aircraft, according to aviation expert Alastair Rosenschein, who worked as a pilot in the United Kingdom for four decades. Those passes typically require police checks and background checks to obtain, but experts say the process comes down to each country’s regulations. The Israeli Ministry of Transport told reporters on Saturday that it relies on foreign air carriers’ commitment to international regulations, as well as signed declarations that each carrier’s pilots and crews have been vetted. Rosenschein said that he doesn’t have insight into the specific process in the UAE, but “I do know where the responsibility lies, and that is with the government, with the airlines, and with security services – because no one else has the authority to investigate or pass on this information.” “There’s not really anything cast in stone as to how people are vetted – and there should be,” Rosenschein said, and questioned: “Why did the Omanis not suspend his pilot’s license?” Aviation expert and British pilot Gideon Ewers noted that a pilot’s license is essentially just a technical qualification that shows someone knows how to fly a plane. The license itself doesn’t come with a record of previous employment issues or infractions. Questions about hiring practices and ongoing checks Hiring practices also vary greatly by each airline, but most involve some sort of psychological evaluation, flight simulation tests and references from previous employers or trainers, Rosenschein said. Pilots must also pass regular medical exams. It’s unclear how the attacking pilot would have passed a referencing process if he was dismissed from the Omani airline for concerns about his extremist views. “The hiring process at company ‘A’ can be quite different from the process at company ‘B,’ even though it’s a similar role,” Ewers told CNN. “Any pilot who’s involved in the recruitment will say their primary question is asking themselves, ‘Would I want to sit in a cockpit with this guy for 12 hours?’” Rosenschein added that the main way airlines know if somebody is unfit to work is through internal company reporting. He said that “if somebody is acting strangely – maybe they started drinking heavily on night stops, etc. – they should be reported by their colleagues.” He argued that this attempted hijacking, as well as previous cases of pilot suicide-murders, show that much more needs to be done in terms of industry staff checks, including information sharing between airlines and countries, social media checks, random staff checks for substances like alcohol and regular psychological exams. None of that is standard across the industry. “I think that we have to move to a far more serious regulation in the industry because so many lives are at stake in an aircraft,” Rosenschein said, although he noted that flying today is far safer than when he began working as a pilot in the 1970s. CNN reached out to the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO), the UN agency that helps countries cooperate on aviation matters, which said standards are “under continuous review by ICAO and are enhanced as ICAO identifies emerging priorities and new best practices.” A weapon on the flight deck On Saturday the UAE cleared up suggestions the suspect smuggled in a knife by confirming he used the cockpit’s crash ax, something found on most passenger planes in case an emergency requires breaking out of a damaged aircraft or breaking open panels to reach a fire. “You have a weapon on the flight deck. Should that remain there? I don’t think it should,” Rosenschein said, adding that the ax also presents security issues related to those outside the cockpit, as the door is sometimes opened during flights for bathroom breaks. It’s a difficult balance for airlines, which are tasked with preventing both accidental and malicious emergencies, as well as internal and external threats. For security, cockpit doors are locked from the inside, and experts say most planes are fitted with a switch on the control panel that can open that hard door. It’s unclear in the Flydubai incident if that’s how the injured Indian pilot opened the door to allow passengers to help. Some planes are also outfitted with emergency entry door codes, to allow access to the flight deck in the event of incapacitation of the crew, such as a pilot having a heart attack or stroke. But that would be unlikely to help in the event of any pilot-intended incident, such as an attack or pilot suicide. Investigations ongoing The United Arab Emirates and Israel are both investigating the incident, according to officials. There will also be an investigation conducted in Saudi Arabia, where the flight was diverted for its emergency landing. Saudi Arabia has no formal diplomatic ties with Israel. In the coming days, investigators will likely explore the flight data recorder and cockpit voice recorder first, said Marco Chan, a senior lecturer in aviation operations at London’s Kingston University. They will likely be digging further into the attacker’s medical history and training history, Chan told CNN. Investigators will also likely interview the other crew members, passengers and the off-duty pilots who managed to safely land the plane, he said. One Israeli official told CNN it is not yet clear how the Omani pilot would have obtained clearance to fly to Israel, given that Oman and Israel do not have formal diplomatic relations. Israel’s Tax Authority confirmed the names of all passengers and crew were in the hands of Israeli authorities before the flight had taken off, but it said questions about the vetting of crew members should be referred to the Ministry of Transport. Shin Bet, Israel’s internal security agency, also referred CNN to the Ministry of Transport, which it said is “responsible for all security matters concerning foreign airlines.” The Ministry of Transport said that its procedures do not include checking the names of flight crew members, although those names are submitted to the Israel Tax Authority, which collects them in case of requests by security services. The ministry added that all flight crew members are required to have a travel visa to enter the country, and an Omani passport should have been flagged at check-in. But the ministry also said its “procedures do not address the threat from a pilot.” On Sunday evening, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu instructed the head of the country’s National Security Council to carry out a “thorough examination” of all aspects of the security of foreign civil aviation coming into Israel. When it comes to broader aviation hiring practices and background checks, security experts said those checks should theoretically be applied to everybody, regardless of nationality.

cnn.com.title: Latino voters, souring on Trump, swing toward Democrats, new poll finds
cnn.com.text: Latino voters have deeply soured on President Donald Trump and his party, particularly on crucial economic issues, a new NBC/Telemundo poll released Sunday finds. In the survey, Latino voters say by a 24-point margin, 59% to 35%, that they’d prefer to see the Democrats win control of Congress over the Republicans in November. That’s considerably broader than the 12-point Democratic margin among Latino voters at this point in 2024, although not as robust as the preference for Democratic victory ahead of the 2018 midterms. The nation’s roughly 36 million Latino voters played a critical role in Trump’s 2024 victory, veering away from a history of overwhelmingly supporting Democratic candidates. Exit polls that year showed he garnered 46% of the Latino vote, compared with 51% for Democrat Kamala Harris. In the NBC/Telemundo poll, just 27% of Latino voters approve of Trump’s job performance overall, with an even smaller 20% approving of his handling of the cost of living. Although Latino voters give Trump a marginally higher 30% approval rating on immigration, two-thirds say that his administration has gone too far in its approach to immigration enforcement. Roughly one-quarter say they know someone who has been deported or detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement in the past two years. A 62% majority of Latino voters rate the Republican Party as a whole negatively, up from 46% in September 2024. And they say, 48% to 27%, that they believe the Democratic Party would do a better job than the GOP of dealing with the economy. Those findings track with a new CBS/YouGov poll, also released Sunday, in which Latino likely voters say, 60% to 39%, that they’d favor a Democratic candidate over a Republican in their House district. Among the full electorate, that poll finds, likely voters favor the Democrats by a 9-point margin – similar to the results of ​other recent generic ballot polling​. In the CBS poll, a 56% majority of registered voters say they think Trump is doing a worse job in his second term than he did in his first term, and 70% say they believe his policies have led to higher prices for food and groceries.

cnn.com.title: Researcher at Russian plague laboratory dies of ‘unknown’ infection
cnn.com.text: Dozens of people were reported to be in isolation after a Russian laboratory worker at an institute dedicated to studying the plague and other infectious diseases died of an undisclosed illness. The researcher, a 28-year-old female laboratory technician at the Irkutsk Research Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia, in the town of Shelekhov, died after being diagnosed with a pneumonia of “unknown” origin, according to Rospotrebnadzor, the Russian agency that handles infectious disease. The agency played down the link between the researcher’s death and her work. “No micro-organisms associated with the employee’s professional duties were detected in samples taken from the patient,” it asserted, adding that the “epidemiological situation” in the region was stable. Nevertheless, the agency’s head, Anna Yuryevna Popova, traveled to Irkutsk on Friday, according to the local governor, Igor Kobzev, for what he described as an extraordinary meeting of the regional anti-epidemic commission. The meeting was in connection with a “suspected case of a particularly dangerous infection affecting a resident of the region”, Kobzev said on Telegram. Reached by phone on Monday, the institute where the researcher worked told CNN it was not commenting on the incident. Anti-epidemic measures Regional authorities are implementing a “comprehensive set of anti-epidemic measures,” according to Maxim Modin, the mayor of the Shelekhovsky district in eastern Russia, near the Mongolian border. The inpatient facility at the hospital where the worker was treated has been placed under quarantine, and several departments have stopped discharging or admitting patients, Modin said. Other hospitals in the region have also been closed, according to local media reports. The woman’s death was confirmed by officials last week. Ekaterina, a resident of Shekelov, told CNN on Monday that there were no visible changes in the city, but locals were anxious. “My acquaintances are slightly panicking,” she said. Another resident, who wished to remain anonymous, said he was “shocked” by the news. Unofficial reports, including by the independent regional news outlet Liudi Baikala, have said that nearly 200 people are under observation. There have been no cases of infectious diseases reported among institute staff over the past 10 days, and all of the employee’s recent contacts are being tested and examined, Modin said. In its only comment on the incident, the Kremlin said people should only trust updates coming from the official agency. “One should rely on official statements from Rospotrebnadzor rather than listening to various rumors and speculation,”  Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Monday. Deadly but not easily transmitted Angela Rassmussen, a virologist at the Vaccine and Infectious Disease Organization, told CNN that while pneumonic plague is deadly, it is not very transmissible and one would have to be exposed to a high viral load to become sick. In that sense, it is unlike respiratory illnesses such as COVID, she said. There is endemic plague among wildlife in parts of Siberia, Rassmussen added. According to its website, the Anti-Plague Institute employs around 95 researchers and is a major public health facility responsible for monitoring and preventing outbreaks of high-risk bacterial and viral infections across Siberia and Russia’s Far East. The head of the neighboring republic of Buryatia, Alexei Tsydenov, said earlier that the employee died “possibly from the plague.” He also noted that “there are no plague outbreaks” in Buryatia. Pneumonic plague is one of three types of plagues that are caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis. The other two types typically spread from contact with infected fleas, animals or infected tissues. An aluminum plant near the laboratory instructed staff to wear masks as a precautionary measure. The director of Irkutsk Aluminum Plant, Artem Fominikh, noted “conflicting reports” were circulating and called for calm. The infection in the Irkutsk region is “most likely not the plague, but even if confirmed, there will be no spread of this disease,” a former head of Rospotrebnadzor, Gennady Onishchenko, said on Friday. Onishchenko told state news agency TASS that the onset of cold weather would likely prevent transmission. A US State Department spokesperson told CNN Sunday that it was aware of the possible death due to pneumonic plague in Russia. “We are monitoring the situation closely with the CDC and our other interagency partners,” the spokesperson said. “Many details have not been confirmed. We encourage Russian authorities to share accurate information quickly and openly.” Patients with pneumonic plague develop fever, headache, weakness and and “a rapidly developing pneumonia with shortness of breath, chest pain, cough, and sometimes bloody or watery mucous,” according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). The World Health Organization notes that the plague has a high fatality rate, but is also easily treated with antibiotics.

cnn.com.title: Supreme Court heads into new term with one eye on President Trump
cnn.com.text: When the Supreme Court kicks off a new, nine-month term on Monday, one key player will be noticeably absent: President Donald Trump. After months of near-constant confrontation with the White House, the nine justices will retake their seats behind the court’s mahogany bench without a docket full of Trump-driven, separation-of-powers blockbusters that defined the last term — from tariffs to birthright citizenship to the firing of once-independent government officials. The respite is unlikely to last. In the coming weeks, the justices will decide whether to wade into Trump’s messy defamation brawl with magazine columnist E. Jean Carroll, his mass cancellation of federal research grants, whether the Department of Government Efficiency must provide records detailing its slashing of federal agencies last year, and the administration’s ban on transgender Americans serving in the military. Those and other cases could be added to a term that already includes an important Second Amendment challenge to bans on AR-15 rifles, the most significant case dealing with climate change to reach the justices in nearly two decades, and a fight over whether religious preschools receiving taxpayer money may decline to enroll the children of same-sex couples. So far this next term, the court has granted 28 cases, less than half of what the justices will likely decide by June. “There’s a very good chance that the 35 or so that the court is likely to grant in the remainder of the year will be the ones that are really the highlights,” Masha Hansford, an attorney at Davis Polk & Wardwell and a former assistant to the solicitor general, said at a recent event organized by the National Constitution Center. One area where the court is already delving into Trump’s policies this term is immigration. The court has announced in recent days that it will hear arguments over the president’s mandatory detention policy and his push to deport migrants to countries other than their homeland. While important, neither of those cases has drawn the same level of attention as last year’s birthright citizenship case. Dance with Trump After Trump and his allies launched a rhetorical war against lower courts in early 2025, the president and the Supreme Court seemed to slide into a détente by the middle of the year — a delicate dance in which Trump has abided by the losses handed to him by the high court even as he has occasionally lashed out against the justices who supported them. The court overwhelmingly sided with Trump on its emergency docket — the fast-track cases that are usually decided without argument. And it also backed the president in major regular cases that were argued during the last term and resulted in full opinions. One of those included the blockbuster decision allowing him to fire the leaders of agencies like the Federal Trade Commission. But the court was also willing to push back against Trump in some of those cases, such as by rejecting his emergency global tariffs and his push to undo birthright citizenship as it had been understood for more than a century. Still, Trump has not shied away from railing against the 6-3 conservative court this past summer, including the three justices — Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett — whom he named to the bench during his first term. Trump told Time Magazine last week that he regretted nominated them. “I gave them ​the position of a lifetime,” the president lamented, “and they vote against me often.” The justices themselves have largely demurred when asked about Trump’s unusually personal attacks on the court. Justice Samuel Alito, a conservative who spoke to CBS as he prepares to publish a new book this week, said there has been a “great change in what presidents have said about the court when they are unhappy about our decisions.” But, Alito said, that “very harsh” criticism has been “bipartisan.” Pressed on Trump’s harsher statements, Alito said, “he has his own way of saying things.” Girding for an election Before the court decides any of the regular — or merits — cases it has granted, there’s a chance it will have to deal with a flood of litigation tied to next month’s midterm election. Whether that is a deluge or a trickle may be in voters’ hands. Derek Muller, a law professor and election law expert at Notre Dame, said he believes the likelihood of post-election litigation will be low “because there probably won’t be enough decisively close cases where litigation would really matter.” But, he said, “if it does happen, it could significantly transform the upcoming Supreme Court term.” The court has already juggled a series of redistricting disputes spun off from the president’s push for a mid-decade redrawing of House district boundaries. And last month it shut down Trump’s controversial proposal to give the US Postal Service a role in screening — and potentially rejecting — mail ballots sent to voters across the country. Also waiting in the wings are several important non-Trump merits cases that could define the 2026-2027 term. It seems almost inevitable that the court will review state laws requiring the Ten Commandments to be posted in public school classrooms. Moreover, a legal battle raging between prediction sites like Kalshi and Polymarket and state governments has already reached the high court and could make its way to an oral argument sometime next year. Banning AR-15 rifles The court’s conservative majority has been steadily expanding gun rights under the Second Amendment for years. It have a huge opportunity to do so again this term. In December, the court will hear arguments in cases challenging bans on AR-15 rifles enacted in Connecticut and Cook County, Illinois. Gun rights groups say the semi-automatic rifles are widely owned by Americans and are permitted in the vast majority of states. Gun control advocates counter that the weapons have been frequently used in mass shootings and should not receive Second Amendment protection because they are more “dangerous” and “unusual” than other types of guns. The case draws heavily on a landmark 2008 decision from the Supreme Court, District of Columbia v. Heller, which stood for the prospect that arms “in common use” are protected under the Second Amendment. “I think we know how this case is going to come out,” Deepak Gupta, a veteran appellate attorney, said at a recent event hosted by the Georgetown Law Center, suggesting that the court would likely strike down the AR-15 bans. “We know the outcome, but we don’t know how it’s going to be decided.” Suing Exxon for climate change On the very first day of the term, the justices will confront a long-running dispute about whether cities and states may sue fossil fuel companies for billions of dollars in damages caused by climate change. The appeal before the court deals with one such suit from Boulder, Colorado, but the decision will almost certainly play into dozens of other pending cases filed by cities and states attempting to hold oil companies accountable. ExxonMobil and Suncor, the two companies that brought the case to the high court, argue that climate pollution is inherently a federal issue, in part because emissions waft across state lines. That understanding of federal control, they say, should effectively supersede state law. But Boulder says that there’s nothing in the Constitution or in federal law that backs up ExxonMobil’s position, and that the Supreme Court should let the lawsuit proceed. Particularly notable is Alito’s decision to recuse himself from the case because of stock he owns in fossil fuel companies such as ConocoPhillips and Phillips 66. That opens the possibility of a 4-4 split, a rare outcome that would uphold the decision by Colorado’s Supreme Court that allowed Boulder’s lawsuit to proceed without setting a precedent. Immigration emerges as a theme One important Trump-related case that has reached the docket deals with the administration’s policy of imposing mandatory detention without bond hearings for people who entered the country illegally and who are targeted for deportation. Though the cases are lower profile than birthright citizenship, the court’s decision in the detention case could have enormous consequences for the president’s push to round up migrants living in the United States. Trump broke with decades of past practice – including that of his first administration – and reinterpreted an immigration law Congress enacted in the 1990s to find that people in the country illegally should be subject to mandatory detention without bond hearings. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has recorded a massive increase in the number of migrants held in detention, from just under 38,000 at the end of the Biden administration to more than 65,000 this past summer. The detention case is one of several dealing with immigration this term. Late last month, the court granted another important immigration case dealing with the Trump administration’s policy of removing certain people to countries other than their homeland – despite human rights concerns raised about some of those countries. Religious schools v. LGBTQ rights The Supreme Court in recent years has repeatedly sided with religious schools seeking public funding. Now it will answer a question it has largely avoided in those earlier cases: How to handle a religious school that declines to work with LGBTQ families. The case comes out of Colorado, which enacted a ballot provision in 2020 that provides state funding for a universal preschool program. While the program allows religious preschools to take part, it also includes a nondiscrimination provision that requires each school receiving public money to provide eligible children an equal opportunity to enroll, regardless of race, religious affiliation, sexual orientation, gender identity and other factors. Two Catholic parishes in Colorado that operate preschools sued over the policy and brought the case to the Supreme Court in November. They argue that honoring that anti-discrimination provision in the program would require them to violate their faith. “The tea leaves are pretty good for the challengers generally,” Roman Martinez, a Latham & Watkins partner who regularly appears before the Supreme Court, said at the Georgetown event. “What’s driving the court is a commitment to a type of pluralism,” he said. “The court, I think, is very concerned about religious groups sort of having equal access and being treated equally as a matter of practice, not just as a matter of formalism.”

cnn.com.title: Saudi-led coalition pledges support for Yemeni offensive against Iran-backed Houthis
cnn.com.text: The Saudi-led “Coalition to Support Legitimacy in Yemen” pledged full support on Sunday as Yemen’s internationally recognized government announced the start of a major military offensive aimed at rolling back recent gains by the Iran-backed Houthi movement. Last month, the Iran-backed Houthis carried out a lightning offensive down the Red Sea coast, successfully seizing control of a key port and further putting pressure on the safety of international shipping. Rashad al-Alimi, head of Yemen’s presidential council, said in a televised speech on Sunday that the ‌military ⁠operations aimed to reclaim the ​remaining ​territory held ‌by Houthis ⁠and restore ​state ​authority across the ⁠country. An offensive had been widely expected amid dozens of Saudi airstrikes against Houthi positions and further Houthi gains in southern Yemen. The renewed fighting has already forced tens of thousands of people from their homes, and what happens next could shift the balance of power in Yemen and further exacerbate an already bleak humanitarian crisis. Three out of every four families in parts of Yemen are going hungry because of the surge in fighting, the World Food Program said last week. Al-Alimi said the decision to launch operations followed “the Houthi militias’ continued mobilization, escalation and attacks, as well as their threats against civilians, facilities, neighboring countries, and international shipping lanes.” In a separate statement, military spokesperson Majid Al-Nuzaili said government forces had begun a “battle for liberation” aimed at ending Houthi control over remaining territory and restoring state institutions. Al-Nuzaili also called on fighters aligned with the Houthis to lay down their arms and return to their homes, saying the government remained committed to protecting civilians during the offensive. The Saudi-led coalition spokesperson Turki al-Maliki said they will continue providing “full operational support” to Yemeni government forces in what he described as efforts to restore state institutions and end “the Houthi coup.” Al-Maliki also accused the Houthis of continuing attacks against Saudi Arabia and international shipping in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandeb Strait. “Such threats undermine regional and international security, jeopardize freedom of navigation and international trade, the lifeblood of the global economy,” he added. Yemen’s Houthi-controlled armed forces said on Sunday that Saudi Arabia had carried out 106 air and missile strikes over the previous 24 hours targeting the capital Sanaa and other areas of the country. The Houthi statement did not provide details on casualties or damage resulting from the reported attacks. In retaliation for airstrikes against Sanaa and other locations, the Houthis claimed Sunday that they had struck vital Saudi energy facilities. “The first targeted Aramco company in the Saudi capital, Riyadh, and the second targeted Aramco company in the Khurais area,” causing large fires at the targeted sites, a Houthi military statement said. There has been no word from the Saudis on the claimed strikes. Early in September, the Houthis took a swath of Yemen’s Red Sea coast as far south as the critical Bab al Mandeb waterway, a chokepoint for commercial shipping crossing into the Indian Ocean. They announced that Saudi shipping trying to use the strait would be targeted, threatening additional pressure on global trade and energy routes. The Houthis have fired ballistic missiles and drones at multiple targets in Saudi Arabia since late July, including industrial and energy infrastructure. Much of the recent fighting has been in the southern region of Taiz, as the Houthis have sought to cut off government forces in the regional capital. The Houthis claimed on Sunday to have taken a critical highway linking Taiz with the seat of the Yemeni government in Aden. Taiz is the third largest city in Yemen, with a population of several hundred thousands. It is also home to thousands of government troops. Further east, in the al-Jawf region, the Houthis on Sunday claimed to have inflicted heavy casualties on government forces with a barrage of missiles and drones as they redeployed for the new offensive. Yemeni government forces, backed by Saudi airstrikes and a blockade of Houthi areas, started fighting the Houthis more than a decade ago. On Monday, officials from Saudi Arabia will convene with Turkish and Pakistani officials in Riyadh to discuss regional developments. The meeting is part of the Strategic and Political Defense Committee, a NATO-style defense pact established in August, which is committed to organizing security and military cooperation in the region. The Saudi foreign ministry has said that it “does not represent an effort to establish a military axis or a sectarian bloc.” The war in Yemen, which began in March 2015, had killed 377,000 people by the end of 2021, including those killed by direct and indirect causes, according to the United Nations. Over 150,000 of these deaths were the direct result of the armed conflict, it said, while more have died as a result of hunger and disease due to the humanitarian crisis caused by the war. A 2022 UN-brokered truce brought a period of relatively low levels of hostilities between the two sides until violence surged again in August. This story has been updated.

cnn.com.title: Trump announces leadership of AI task force
cnn.com.text: President Donald Trump on Sunday announced the leadership and duties of a “Super Intelligence Force,” which he said will “ensure that America continues to lead the world” when it comes to artificial intelligence. The president said in his announcement on Truth Social that the task force will “protect the interests” and “improve the lives” of Americans. He said it will coordinate the government’s engagement with consumers, public interest groups, religious organizations, infrastructure providers and AI companies. The group will be led by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, Chairman of the Federal Trade Commission Andrew Ferguson, Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering Emil Michael, and Director of the Office of Personnel Management Scott Kupor. The task force will report to Trump and White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, the president said. Trump announced last month that he was planning to create an “AI Force” and name an AI czar as the government faces growing calls to impose guardrails on the technology’s rapid development. CNN reported Friday that Trump was expected to tap Clayton to lead the group. The announcement detailing the task force comes in the wake of episodes that have raised widespread safety concerns tied to AI, including AI agents going rogue and attempting to hack into federal databases. The president has made clear that he considers outpacing China and preserving AI-driven economic gains a higher priority than addressing growing public concerns, and previously referred to fears over AI as being a “hoax.” His support for the technology comes amid widespread frustrations over the data centers used to support it, which are shaking up midterm races. The president hosted top AI executives at the White House last week. The group signed a new commitment aimed at better “self-policing” their companies’ AI models, arguing that the light-touch approach represents the best way to balance safety concerns with the president’s desire to accelerate a technology he’s dubbed “Super Intelligence.” “I’m seeing tremendous self-policing, and they understand that they have to self-police,” Trump told reporters. “These models are very complex and, again, I believe they’re going to be used for the good.” When asked about AI during his confirmation hearing to lead the US intelligence community, Clayton said the technology is a “game changer.” “When something’s both an opportunity and a threat, you better get your arms around it,” Clayton said. Kupor said Sunday on X that “the U.S. will continue to lead in SI to enhance the well-being of all Americans.” Michael wrote on X that the Pentagon “has seen what is possible when red tape is removed and America’s best technology is rapidly put into action.” “Working alongside America’s leading technology companies, we are putting the most advanced SI capabilities into the hands of our warfighters at speed and scale,” he said. This story has been updated with additional information.

cnn.com.title: Co-pilot accused of trying to hijack Flydubai plane probably acted alone, Israeli sources say
cnn.com.text: The co-pilot accused of attacking his colleague on board the Flydubai flight to Israel and trying to seize the controls probably acted alone, Israeli sources told CNN. International investigators are still working to determine a motive but an Israeli official said information from the inquiry suggested the suspect acted alone. Another Israeli source said that, at the moment, Israel does not know of any link to a group or government. Both stressed this was their understanding so far. The United Arab Emirates and Israel are both investigating the incident. The Interior Ministry of Saudi Arabia, where the plane made an emergency landing, is also conducting investigations. The attorney general of the UAE, Hamad Saif Al Shamsi, said the co-pilot on board the flight had attempted to seize control of the plane by attacking his colleague with a crash ax – a piece of equipment required on most aircraft. The attorney general called the attempted hijacking a “terrorist act.” Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told Fox News on Thursday that Israel understands the suspect “underwent Islamist radical indoctrination,” based on “personal information” collected during the suspect’s ongoing questioning. Netanyahu did not give any further details. In the immediate aftermath of the attack, US President Donald Trump said that the suspect could be linked to Iran “based on what I’m hearing.” But he gave no other details. Flydubai flight FZ1073 narrowly avoided disaster on its journey from Dubai, plummeting thousands of feet in a matter of minutes amid the attack on the plane’s captain. Despite being wounded, pilot Captain Smit Machchhar managed to unlock the cockpit door and signal his distress to passengers and crew, who bravely rushed into the cockpit to regain control of the aircraft. Sources told CNN the suspect, named as Hamam al-Hammami, is an Omani national who had been removed from a previous job at Oman’s national airline last year following concerns about his extremist views. A LinkedIn profile bearing the name Hamam al-Hammami said he worked at Oman Air for seven years, leaving in February 2025, before joining the Moroccan airline Royal Air Maroc in June 2025 and departing in January 2026. One source told CNN that the profile belongs to the Flydubai pilot in Wednesday’s incident. The profile has since been deleted and CNN has reached out to LinkedIn for comment. A post made to the LinkedIn profile on Wednesday, about nine hours after the incident, included a photo of the former leader of al Qaeda. It is unclear who published the posts or whether they were scheduled in advance. An Israeli official told CNN that al-Hammami had worked for Flydubai for only eight months. Another source said the alleged assailant had previously worked for Royal Air Maroc. In a statement to the Associated Press, Air Maroc said the suspect trained with the airline for three months in 2025 as part of the pre-employment process but he was not selected. The Australian Federal Police (AFP) also told CNN that it is investigating al-Hammami’s links to the country, and said an update will be provided when appropriate. New Zealand Police confirmed to CNN on Monday that the co-pilot spent time in the country, and that authorities there are also now investigating. Questions remain over how a citizen of Oman, a country which does not have formal diplomatic relations with Israel, was authorized to co-pilot a plane bound for Tel Aviv, despite Israel’s strict security regulations. The names of all passengers and crew were provided to Israeli authorities before the flight had taken off, Israel’s Tax Authority confirmed, adding that it is the Transportation Ministry’s responsibility to give answers on the matter of vetting. But a Transportation Ministry spokesperson told reporters on Saturday that its protocols do not include checking the names of flight crew members. The incident has triggered criticism of the Israeli government, particularly Transport Minister Miri Regev, and some opposition figures have called for her removal from office.

bbc.com.title: Teenager's hand blown off during confrontation between France school protesters and police
bbc.com.text:
- Published
A 15-year-old boy's hand was blown off during unrest near a school in France, an official has said, as student protests continue across the country.
The "very serious incident" happened in the north-eastern city of Lens on Monday morning, according to the prefect of Pas-de-Calais, François-Xavier Lauch.
"The student's life is not in danger," he said, adding that the teenager was transferred "very quickly" to a hospital in nearby.
Around 500 schools were partially or totally closed across the country on Monday amid student protests over the condition of school buildings and staffing which have led to clashes with police in recent days.
There are mixed reports in French media about how the boy came to sustain the injury.
Regional newspaper La Voix Du Nord reported that they lost their hand after picking up a police stun grenade.
Officials have not yet provided details.
A regional prosecutor said an investigation would be carried out by the French police watchdog, the General Inspection of the National Police (IGPN), "so all light can be shed on what happened".
The incident took place close to the Auguste Béhal high school, the prefect said.
Lauch said a "larger gathering" of students than on previous days had assembled outside the school.
"At the start of the morning, they threw various projectiles at the local police officers who were on site initially. When I say projectiles, I mean stones, fireworks, and mortars," he told French media.
"Instructions were given by the interdepartmental director of the National Police, naturally with my approval, to deploy a company of riot police (CRS) here to maintain order, and it was in this context that this event occurred."
The school issued a statement on Monday morning, saying: "In light of the events that took place this morning and in order to ensure the safety of the entire school community, the institution is switching to distance learning from now on.
"In addition, to support everyone during this period, a listening and support unit has also been set up at the establishment."

bbc.com.title: No10 insists UK military base RAF Fairford is safe after US withdraws bombers
bbc.com.text:
- Published
Downing Street has insisted RAF Fairford is safe, after the US withdrew all of its bombers from the military base.
The Pentagon confirmed on Sunday it had removed its bombers - thought to be about a dozen B-1s - from the base back to their home stations in America.
US media reported a new threat led to the bombers being removed, which follows a major incident on 27 September when police were alerted to three "suspicious vehicles" near the airbase.
A Number 10 spokesperson said he would not comment on "foreign nations' military operations", but said the base was safe, and pointed to US President Donald Trump's comments last week, where he "praised our police, defence and security services" in relation to the base.
He added that Defence Secretary Wes Streeting had said last week, "we have tried and tested approaches to defend our bases around the country and throughout the world".
RAF Fairford - in the Cotswolds in Gloucestershire - is at the centre of an incident being investigated by counter-terror police.
Five men were initially arrested on suspicion of terror offences and subsequently released on bail. A sixth man, a UK-Iranian national, was also later arrested and released on bail.
Whitehall sources have not disputed that the decision from Washington to remove the bombers was in response to the incident at the airbase in Gloucestershire.
The BBC has also been told it was a military rather than a political decision - taken at an operational level - and communicated from the US military to its British counterparts.
Earlier on Monday, the New York Times reported US commanders had received new threats about an Iran-backed plot against RAF Fairford according to two US officials.
The newspaper wrote the new information was part of the same threat warnings from three weeks ago, but officials acted quickly after specific details emerged in the past 24 hours.
Days after the incident at RAF Fairford, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said there were "strong indications" that Iran had played a part in the incident but did not provide further details, while US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Fox News that it "clearly involve[d] the hands of a foreign actor" without going into further details.
Tehran has strongly denied any involvement.
In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces".
RAF Fairford, near the village of Whelford in the Cotswolds, has been used as a forward operating location by the USAF for decades.
In recent months, the US has flown B-1 and B-52 bombers from the base for the Middle East, after the UK approved a US request to use it for defensive strikes on Iran.

bbc.com.title: Georgia officials hunt for suspect in shooting that killed two and injured 35
bbc.com.text:
- Published
Investigators in the US state of Georgia are on the hunt for a suspect in a mass shooting that erupted in the early hours of Sunday, killing two people and injuring 35 more.
A crowd of roughly 1,000 people had gathered for a block party in the southern rural community of Vienna when, according to officials, more than 50 shots were fired.
Two of the victims were pronounced dead at the scene, while another 25 were transported to multiple nearby hospitals, some in critical condition.
No known arrests have been made and authorities have not given a possible motive for the violence. Victims ranged in age from 14 to 51.
The incident occurred on Sunday morning around 01:30 local time (05:30 GMT), during a Dooly High School homecoming celebration, though it was not a school-sponsored event.
"Our hearts are with the families grieving the loss of loved ones, those who were injured, and everyone affected by this tragedy," the school said in a statement.
Anticipating a large gathering, authorities from the Dooly County Sheriff's Office were already positioned at both ends of the crowd as gunfire rang out.
"Some people were reporting fireworks and then someone said somebody been shot," Dooly County Sheriff Craig Peavy told local media.
Peavy said officials then worked their way through the crowd, as people ran scrambling in different directions, while authorities made their way towards victims.
Ashley Gee, who was there, told the Atlanta Journal-Constitution news outlet that the barrage of gunfire sounded "like a machine gun".
Authorities arrived and found several people injured. The two deceased victims were found several blocks away from the scene of the shooting on Pine Street.
Dooly County Coroner Brett Walls told the BBC's US media partner, CBS News, the two killed were both men, ages 20 and 23.
The Georgia Bureau of Investigations Medical Examiner's Office said it would conduct an autopsy in each case.
The bureau also said it would join the investigation at the request of the Dooly County Sheriff's Office, describing operations as "active and ongoing".

bbc.com.title: Flydubai co-pilot planned to crash plane into Tel Aviv airport or building, reports say
bbc.com.text:
- Published
The co-pilot accused of trying to hijack a flydubai plane planned to crash the aircraft into Tel Aviv's Ben Gurion airport or a tower block in the Israeli city, US and Israeli reports suggest.
The Omani national was a "lone wolf" extremist, according to the reports.
The United Arab Emirates' attorney-general has said the co-pilot attempted to carry out a "terrorist act" on flight FZ1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv last Wednesday.
