Pneumonic plague is caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, usually found in small mammals and their fleas. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), the plague is highly infectious and can be fatal if not treated early.
Local media named the woman who died as 28-year-old laboratory technician Darya Shipilova.

aljazeera.com.title: Singapore turns matchmaker amid rock-bottom birthrate
aljazeera.com.text:
Singapore – Nur Aisyah, a 30-year-old civil servant, has spent the past couple of years looking for a partner, with little to show for it.
Nur rarely meets men through work or her hobbies and finds dating apps such as Tinder and Bumble “terrible”, with potential suitors either putting scant effort into their profile or struggling to hold a conversation over text.
Nur is open to having children but also struggles to imagine raising them in a city where housing and childcare costs are high, and where the burden of childcare typically falls hardest on women.
“I feel slightly pessimistic about the future as a whole,” Nur, who asked to use a pseudonym, told Al Jazeera.
So when Singapore’s technology agency GovTech recently rolled out FirstDate, a dating platform for public servants that uses a Nobel-winning algorithm, Nur signed up out of curiosity
“It’s more of the mindset of ‘Why not?’” she said. “It makes quite a funny story if something did come out of this.”
Born out of GovTech’s annual hackathon, where staff develop and test new ideas, FirstDate is being piloted among single government employees aged 21 to 35.
Participants log in using their national digital ID and answer a survey about their interests, habits and values before being matched with one prospective partner at a time.
Sign-ups for the pilot closed on Monday.
GovTech has told local media that no decision has been made on whether to expand the service beyond employees at government agencies.
Singapore’s decision to get into the matchmaking game is its latest attempt to lift a birthrate that has sunk to historic lows.
Fewer than 30,000 babies were born in the Southeast Asian city-state in 2025, bringing the fertility rate to a record low of 0.87.
In August, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong announced a series of new measures to support families, including almost 70,000 Singapore dollars ($55,000) worth of financial benefits for every child from birth until age 17.
For Singapore, whose six million citizens are practically the city-state’s only resource, the prospect of a shrinking, fast-ageing population is existential.
In February, Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong warned that without intervention, the citizen population could begin to shrink by the early 2040s, leaving fewer workers to care for the elderly.
Singapore already leans heavily on immigration to meet its workforce needs, with the government expecting to take in 25,000 to 30,000 new citizens annually over the next five years, a politically sensitive influx in a country whose 6.2 million inhabitants fill an area less than half the size of London.
Yet even as Singapore’s bureaucrats urge people to have babies, many Singaporeans have enthusiastically embraced a child-free lifestyle, preferring to reap the benefits of living in a double-income household with fewer bills or to lavish their attention on pets.
Singapore has never been shy about meddling in matters of the heart.
In a 1983 speech that sparked what became known as the “Great Marriage Debate”, Lee Kuan Yew, Singapore’s founding father and longest-serving prime minister, warned that graduates, especially women, were marrying late and having fewer children than the less educated.
The following year, Lee’s government introduced the controversial Graduate Mothers’ Scheme, which prioritised the children of university-educated mothers in school admissions.
Around the same time, the government established the Social Development Unit (SDU) to organise events where graduate singles could mingle, prompting some Singaporeans to joke that the body’s initials should stand for “Single, Desperate and Ugly”.
Critics called the agency elitist, and a separate body for those with only secondary school qualifications followed in 1985.
“We have a highly interventionist government, even in a private sphere of love and marriage,” Tan Ern Ser, adjunct principal research fellow at the Institute of Policy Studies in Singapore, told Al Jazeera.
Tan said that although past governments’ attempts to play matchmaker were neither “significant nor cost effective”, Singapore’s current generation of bureaucrats is no less eager to involve themselves in the dating game, using the power of technology.
Still, Tan said, a government-backed platform does not mark a return to the era of arranged marriages, and “couples who are identified as compatible could still have a love match.”
FirstDate relies on the Gale-Shapley algorithm, devised by mathematicians David Gale and Lloyd Shapley in 1962, which pairs people according to the ranked preferences of each side.
Shapley shared the 2012 Nobel memorial prize in economics for discovering the algorithm, versions of which are used in school admissions and medical residency placements.
“This is a fundamentally different approach from most dating apps,” Jean Liu, an associate professor of psychology at the Singapore Institute of Technology, told Al Jazeera.
“It is more akin to offline matchmaking, with endless profile swiping replaced by a single match.”
That FirstDate grew out of a hackathon, Liu said, reflects “an appetite to innovate on the nation’s ‘hard problems'”.
Whether it will help people find love any better than mainstream dating apps is another matter.
Questionnaires have limited value in predicting whether two people will hit it off, and the matches are only as good as the pool of people who join, Liu said.
“The process may break down if too few people sign up.”
The app’s greatest value, Liu said, may be in giving the government an opportunity to evaluate and publish dating data, something app companies, which treat their algorithms as sensitive company information, rarely do.
Singapore is not alone in trying to pair up singles.
Tokyo’s metropolitan government launched Tokyo Enmusubi, an AI-powered dating app, in 2024, while the Seoul government’s “Seoulting” programme hosts curated blind dates at landmarks such as the Han River.
Online, Singaporeans’ reactions to their government’s latest bid to play cupid have ranged from scorn to amusement.
Some commentators have dismissed FirstDate as a waste of public money, while others have joked about “state-assigned spouses” and whether finding love will now be included among their work targets.
Jamie, a government employee who works in education, received the email inviting her to join the platform but has no plans to sign up.
“I think it’s quite cringe. It just sounds like someone is trying too hard,” Jamie, who declined to give her last name, told Al Jazeera.
“Our social skills have atrophied. I am so exhausted after work that I just want to go home and lie down,” Jamie said.
She said she does make an effort through community groups, but has yet to meet anyone who shares her values or is emotionally ready for a relationship, so “nothing happens”.
Jamie said she also wonders about privacy.
“What kind of data are they collecting in order for a match, and what are they doing with said data?” she said.
According to FirstDate’s website, profiles are visible only to a person’s match, contact details are shared only when both parties agree, and data will not be monetised or shared with third parties except where the law requires or permits.
For Teo Kai Xiang, a PhD student and former Straits Times journalist, dating reduced to a list of preferences reflects “a deeply transactional and instrumentalist view of love”, in which partners become “co-owners of a financial venture” and “breeders of sought-after children”.
That mindset, Teo said, is sharpened by Singapore’s public housing system, where the rational move for couples chasing subsidies is to apply for an apartment before marriage.
This algorithm “does not fix or challenge this HR interviewer mindset”, said Teo, who also questions why those aged 36 and above are excluded.
Though he welcomes the experiment, Teo would like to see the government do more to revive the city-state’s third spaces and nightlife instead of “ramming pro-fertility rhetoric down our throats”.
The bigger barrier to dating, he said, is cost – from pricey late-night transport to high rents that keep many singletons living with their parents into their 30s.
Singles cannot buy public housing, home to about 80 percent of residents in Singapore, on their own until they turn 35.
“The truth is that we don’t really know what exactly makes love work, such that we can articulate and implement it on a societal scale,” Teo said. “It’s too messy, too complex, too idiosyncratic, and too human.”

npr.org.title: Drones buzz overhead, troops hunker underground in Ukraine's hellish Kill Zone
npr.org.text:
Drones buzz overhead, troops hunker underground in Ukraine's hellish Kill Zone
KYIV, Ukraine — The frontline in the Russia-Ukraine war stretches the entire length of this country, from north to south. It has barely budged in four years and is sometimes compared to the static, deadlocked, trench warfare of World War I.
Yet straddling this frontline is the Kill Zone, dominated by constantly evolving drone technology that's defining this conflict — and the future of warfare.
"This Kill Zone is a belt of territory which is full of Russian drones, Russian mines, and also artillery. It's nonstop reconnaissance and surveillance," said Ukraine's Sr. Lt. Taras Myshak, the spokesman for Ukraine's 59th Separate Assault Brigade. He spoke with NPR on Zoom, just a few miles from the frontline in eastern Ukraine.
Ukraine has a similar arsenal threatening the Russian forces that are dug in on the other side of the line.
The most important thing to know about the Kill Zone is that any sign of movement — just sticking your head out of a foxhole for fresh air — can get you noticed, and attacked, by the drones constantly buzzing overhead.
Myshak says even routine movements, like rotating troops in and out of this zone, is a nightmare.
"Not far from where we are talking today, we have a group that moved through the Kill Zone and they will they walk four hours just to go one kilometer," he said. "Because all the time they hear the drone and they have to hide and wait. Then the drone passes, and they can move."
Nightfall doesn't make it any safer to move because the drones have thermal cameras that detect body heat and make it even harder to hide.
"In the night, it's even more dangerous," he said.
A frontline that barely budges
When Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, it advanced rapidly in conventional fashion with large columns of troops in armored vehicles. Later that fall, Ukraine's counteroffensive drove the Russians back in some places.
Since then, the two armies settled in and the frontline has moved only incrementally, mostly with limited gains by Russia. This line now stretches more than 700 miles. On either side of the line, the Kill Zone is a band roughly 10 to 20 miles miles wide, and dominated by drones.
"The Kill Zone is basically a product of drone warfare," said Rob Lee, a U.S. Marine veteran who now lives in Ukraine and monitors the war for the Foreign Policy Research Institute of Philadelphia.
Because Ukraine has far fewer troops, and relies heavily on drones, it has a remarkably small presence on the frontline.
Lee said that in many places, Ukraine has fewer than 10 soldiers per mile, in small groups, spaced out hundreds of yards apart.
"Those infantrymen are maybe two positions where it's two to four people," said Lee. "They're underground for the most part. They're trying to remain hidden."
These troops are not really trying to hold back advancing Russian soldiers, he added. They act more as spotters, relaying Russian movements to Ukrainian drone operators behind the front lines, who then track down the Russian intruders from the air.
Lee says the frontline is so saturated with drones that it's virtually impossible for either side to pull together a large ground force without being detected and drawing fire.
Military vehicles like tanks and armored personnel carriers are even easier to spot and attack.
"Because of such a high density of drones, it became very difficult to bring vehicles near the frontline at all," he said.
Neither army planned to fight this way.
Ukraine had no real drone industry at the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says the country will make 10 million this year.
Russia has ramped up its own drone production. It's expected to make more than 7 million this year, including jet-powered aircraft that are often evading Ukraine's defenses.
Starting from scratch
When Dima Putiata joined Ukraine's military four years ago, he knew nothing about drones and didn't think this was a manly way to wage war.
"When I saw that we have drones, I was not smart enough. I said, 'No, we don't need to have it. Let's fight like men.' I was a little bit maybe romantic in this way," said Putiata.
In addition to skeptics like Putiata, few Ukrainian troops were trained to use these new weapons.
"No one had drone operators," he recalled. "It's just, 'Oh, you're a driver? You can use it.' Or, 'Oh, can I use a drone? You can try.'"
By the time he left the military in May, Putiata, a sergeant, was commanding 26 drone crews in and around the Kill Zone in northeastern Ukraine.
Both sides have rapidly embraced the technology even if they don't know where it's headed next, he said.
"They understand how to use it here and right now, maybe not really understanding how to use it in the future," he noted. "My point is, you just need to keep going and adapting."
Recognizing the role of drones
Two years ago, Ukraine became the first country to establish drones as an independent branch of its military.
This innovation now includes the widespread use of ground drones, which look like trollies and perform a wide range of tasks that have become too dangerous for troops.
The robots deliver food, medicine and ammunition to frontline. The robots can be loaded with machine guns that now carry out regular attacks.
The ground robots are also being used to evacuate wounded soldiers from the Kill Zone. But drone operators and combat medics have separate skills, and it turns out you need both.
"The drone operator doesn't know how to properly evacuate a wounded soldier, and the medic doesn't know how to operate a ground robot," said Lyuba Shipovich, a Ukrainian-American, who heads a private group, Dignitas, that trains troops on drones.
"So now we're trying to create combined program that will train both the medic and the robot operator," she said.
Media coverage tends to focus on long-range air strikes Russia and Ukraine are inflicting deep inside each other's territory.
But the vast majority of the fighting is in the Kill Zone, with drones now responsible for 80 percent of all casualties, according to Rob Lee and other military analysts.
Dima Putiata, the former Ukrainian soldier, says what started in this war has already spread to other conflicts.
"With drones, this is the cheapest flying munition that can be massively produced. You can destroy a lot of stuff," he said. "It's much cheaper than it used to be to have a war, unfortunately."
A kind of war, he predicts, that the world will see more often.
NPR's Hanna Palamarenko contributed to this story.

npr.org.title: FBI arrests a woman accused of spying on Taiwan leader's family for China
npr.org.text:
FBI arrests a woman accused of spying on Taiwan leader's family for China
BANGKOK — The FBI arrested a woman at Los Angeles International Airport as she was leaving the country and accused her of spying on the Taiwan president's family for China.
Wanying Zhang, also know as Heather, surveilled the Taiwanese president's son and his family for the Chinese government while in the United States, according to the FBI.
Zhang, 34, was arrested on charges for working for China as an unregistered agent, Assistant U.S. State Attorney Bill Essayli announced on social media. Zhang took photos and videos of her targets and sent license plate information to Chinese officials, he said.
Zhang was arrested as she was departing for a flight to China. Her nationality was not clear, and an attorney who represents her could not be determined. She was due to appear Monday in federal court in Los Angeles.
Taiwan's Presidential Office confirmed President Lai Ching-te's relatives were the targets, without specifying if it was the president's son, saying that "this is a classic case of transnational repression."
"Taiwan condemns in the strongest terms such barbaric acts — which disregard human rights and national sovereignty and aim to suppress, threaten, or even harm individuals advocating for freedom and democracy or their families — as such behavior should not be tolerated in the civilized world," spokesperson Karen Kuo said in a statement.
The Chinese Embassy in the U.S. did not immediately respond to a request for comment Monday and the Foreign Ministry in Beijing was closed for holidays.
Taiwan and China split after a civil war in 1949, but Beijing claims the island as part of its own territory. Lai, who was voted into office in 2024, has said that Taiwan and Beijing do not belong to each other and that the "People's Republic of China has no right to represent Taiwan."
China considers him a separatist and has called him a "destroyer of peace."
While in office, Lai has stepped up spending on defense for Taiwan, notably pledging to increase defense spending from 3% to 5% of the GDP, and pushing through a special budget for the construction of a T-Dome air defense system.

npr.org.title: Imran Khan supporters march in Pakistan to demand his release after talks failed
npr.org.text:
Imran Khan supporters march in Pakistan to demand his release after talks failed
ISLAMABAD — More than 5,000 supporters of imprisoned former Pakistani Prime Minister Imran Khan began a dayslong march toward Islamabad on Sunday to demand his release, after talks between the government and the opposition fell through.
The looming showdown threatens to deepen Pakistan's political uncertainty at a time when the country is also grappling with a surge in militant attacks.
Khan is current Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif's main political rival and has been imprisoned since 2023 on corruption and other charges that he and his party say are politically motivated. Despite his imprisonment, he retains a substantial and passionate support base, keeping him at the center of Pakistan's turbulent political landscape.
The demonstrators, traveling in a convoy of trucks, buses and cars, departed from Lakki Marwat district in the northwestern province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, where Khan's party holds power. Organizers have planned overnight stops along the route as the caravan makes its way toward the capital. Sohail Afridi, the province's chief minister, and a staunch Khan supporter is leading the march.
Speaking from a specially designed container truck emblazoned with a large portrait of Khan, he expressed confidence in the movement's ability to press its demands and bring the political standoff into the heart of the capital.
Authorities have erected roadblocks, using containers, at the entrance to Islamabad and inside the city.
Khan's Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf party, or PTI, and the federal government were in talks to postpone the march but failed to reach a resolution. Gohar Khan, the party's chairman, said negotiations remained deadlocked after two rounds.
Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi blamed Afridi for the failure of the talks, warning that he would be held responsible for any loss of life during the planned march.
Sharif's government urged postponement of the march, citing a surge in militant attacks by the Pakistani Taliban in the northwest. His government has accused PTI of sympathizing with the Pakistani Taliban, also known as Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan.
The organizers now vow to reach the capital after rallying with hundreds of thousands of Khan supporters.
Besides Khan's release, protesters are demanding his transfer to a hospital and permission for his family to visit him. Officials say he is in good health and receives regular family visits but maintain that meetings with the imprisoned former leader cannot be used for political purposes.
The march was originally scheduled for Sept. 27 but was postponed after party leaders said authorities blocked key approaches to Islamabad, including Attock Bridge, a major crossing for convoys from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
Previous protests by Khan's supporters have turned violent, including one in 2024 in which security personnel and civilians were killed.
Khan, a former cricket star, was ousted in a parliamentary no-confidence vote in April 2022. Sharif returned to office after the February 2024 election, which Khan's party says was rigged to deny it victory. The government denies the allegation.
____
Riaz reported from Peshawar, Pakistan. Associated Press writers Ishtiaq Mahsud in Dera Ismail Khan and Rasool Dawar in Peshawar contributed to this report.

npr.org.title: SCOTUS hears major climate change case. And, Brazil's presidential race goes to runoff
npr.org.text:
SCOTUS hears major climate change case. And, Brazil's presidential race goes to runoff
Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.
Today's top stories
Investigators have found that the co-pilot who attempted to take control of a flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv last week aimed to crash it into Israel's Ben Gurion airport, according to a person familiar with the matter but not authorized to speak publicly. Authorities in the United Arab Emirates who are leading the investigation say the incident has been classified as a terrorist attack. They have not identified a clear motive, and the investigation is ongoing.
- 🎧 The co-pilot likely acted alone, according to the source. He carried out the attack with a crash axe, which is an emergency tool meant for breaking through panels or doors in the event of a crash. Israeli officials report that the co-pilot is from Oman. NPR's Kat Lonsdorf tells Up First that the co-pilot's origins have raised concerns about how he was allowed to fly in Israel, as the country prohibits pilots from nations with which it doesn't have diplomatic relations to fly in its airspace. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu says Israel checks the backgrounds of pilots flying into the country, and this pilot must have gotten through a "loophole." While people in Israel are praising the passengers and the captain as heroes for averting disaster, a broader debate is emerging over government failures that allowed something like this to happen, Lonsdorf says.
A new Supreme Court term starts today with arguments in a significant climate change case. Boulder, Colo., is suing Suncor and Exxon Mobil, arguing that the companies misled the public about the harms of fossil fuels and caused costly disasters that cost the city time and money. This case could impact other states seeking to hold companies accountable for allegedly harming local communities.
- 🎧 The energy companies argue that this case should not be in state court, saying climate change is a global issue best addressed by the federal government, according to NPR's Carrie Johnson. Only eight justices will hear the case after Justice Sam Alito's surprising recusal last week, Johnson says. Alito has no stock in the two companies involved, but he has investments in other energy companies that could be impacted by the court's ruling. His recusal raises the risk of a tie, which would uphold the Colorado Supreme Court's ruling allowing the case to continue in state court.
Brazil's presidential race will go to a runoff later this month between left-wing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and right-wing Senator Flávio Bolsonaro. In the tight first round, Bolsonaro, the son of Brazil's former far-right president, led with about 47% of the vote, while Lula followed closely with 45%.
- 🎧 Lula must close the runoff gap by attracting new voters, particularly among the millions who sat out yesterday's election, NPR's Carrie Kahn says. Winning over the 8% who supported other candidates will be challenging, as the people they backed are right and far-right candidates who will align with Bolsonaro. Disillusioned with politics, many Brazilians wanted new, younger candidates. Yasmin Soares, a Lula supporter, told Kahn that Bolsonaro's strong performance is scary and that the right brings hatred. Kahn says she heard similar sentiments from many Lula voters who fear a Bolsonaro conservative back in power.
Life advice
Tech companies are "reinventing the rip-off," according to Lindsay Owens, head of the consumer advocacy group Groundwork Collaborative. She says corporations try to hide pricing schemes, such as using browsing data or a customer's geo-location to determine the cost of goods and services. In her book Gouged: The End of a Fair Price — And What That Means for Your Wallet, she uncovers these schemes and offers advice on how to protect yourself from being overcharged. In an interview with Life Kit, Owens explained steps you can take to get the best possible deal.
- 💸 Avoid shopping through retailer apps. When signed in, they might experiment with your data, potentially manipulating prices against you.
- 💸 Comparison shop by checking the product's price across multiple devices while logged in, logged out and with and without incognito mode.
- 💸 Try shopping the old-fashioned way in person, but keep in mind that big-box retailers and grocery stores are increasingly using electronic shelf labels to change prices at any time.
For more advice on how to avoid being ripped off, listen to this episode of NPR's Life Kit. Subscribe to the Life Kit newsletter for expert advice on love, money, relationships and more.
Behind the story
by Andrew Limbong, Society & Culture Reporter
In a town not far from Barbara Kingsolver's house in southwestern Virginia is a historic marker noting Marion, Va., as "the birthplace of modern Mountain Dew." I came across it on the drive down I-81 to interview the Pulitzer-Prize winning author. It took me by surprise — I didn't expect such a momentous event here, in Appalachia. After all, isn't this the middle of nowhere?
There's some quibbling — the drink's roots trace back to Knoxville, Tennessee, which is why the word "modern" is in the designation. But it's here, in Marion, where the Dew truly realized both its potential and its propensity for change.
When I first encountered Kingsolver's work (The Poisonwood Bible, in high school AP English class), I was more partial to Mountain Dew Code Red — the version most associated with hardcore gamers. That didn't end up being my life, though.
Contested memories, an overlooked and condescended-to town, expectations of the future that go awry, how things change (but do they, really?) — we get into all of that in my interview with Kingsolver about her new novel, Partita. It's about a young classical pianist from Appalachia who has the chops to really make it, until her life gets upended. Kingsolver grew up loving classical music, and even went to college on a music scholarship. But that didn't end up being her life, either.
Give the full interview a listen in NPR's Book of the Day podcast feed.
3 things to know before you go
- Contemporary art world titan Theaster Gates is taking his career in a new direction by acquiring Pickard China, the last remaining manufacturer of fine china in the United States.
- Philadelphia's historic Academy of Natural Sciences closed just short of its 200th birthday last week amid an intense effort by local residents, politicians and scientists to save it.
- The U.S. Coast Guard says searchers have found debris off Nantucket, Mass., from a Canadian air ambulance that disappeared Saturday while carrying six people from Bermuda to Boston.
This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen. Majd Al-Waheidi contributed.

npr.org.title: Nobel medicine prize goes to 3 scientists for research into brain activity
npr.org.text:
Nobel medicine prize goes to 3 scientists for research into brain activity
STOCKHOLM — The Nobel Prize in medicine was awarded Monday to three scientists working on the mechanisms the brain uses to switch on, or off, the activity of individual nerve cells.
Karl Deisseroth, 54, Peter Hegemann, 71, and Georg Nagel, 73, have carried out research into light-gated ion channels and optogenetics. They are based at universities in Germany and the United States.
The Nobel committee lauded their work, writing on X that the method "is now being used in laboratories around the world to reveal the brain's mysteries."
The Nobel Assembly said Deisseroth is based at Stanford University in California, while Hegemann is at Humboldt University in Berlin and Nagel at the University of Würzburg in Germany.
Thomas Perlmann, the secretary of the medicine committee, said he was able to reach all three winners by phone Monday.
The prize was announced at the Karolinska Institute in Stockholm, kicking off Nobels week.
The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million).
Last year, the prize went to three scientists researching the immune system.
Monday's medicine prize is followed by the physics prize on Tuesday, chemistry on Wednesday and literature on Thursday.
After Friday's peace prize is awarded, the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences will be announced on Oct. 12.
The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million), whether for an individual, small group of laureates or organization.

npr.org.title: Former Prince Andrew files legal action to quash warrants that led to residence searches
npr.org.text:
Former Prince Andrew files legal action to quash warrants that led to residence searches
LONDON — The former Prince Andrew has filed a legal action challenging the warrants that authorized searches at two of his homes earlier this year as British police investigated allegations related to his links to the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
A judicial spokesperson confirmed that Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor had filed a claim with the High Court in London and a hearing is scheduled for Thursday.
The Daily Telegraph previously reported that Mountbatten-Windsor had asked the court to determine whether Thames Valley Police acted lawfully in searching the former prince's homes near Windsor Castle and on King Charles III's Sandringham estate.
The searches were conducted in February when Mountbatten-Windsor was arrested on suspicion of misconduct in public office following allegations that the former prince shared sensitive information with Epstein during his time as the U.K.'s trade envoy.
Police questioned Mountbatten-Windsor for 11 hours before he was released under investigation, meaning he was neither charged nor exonerated.
It was the first time in nearly four centuries that a senior British royal was placed under arrest, underscoring how deference to the monarchy has eroded in recent years.
Thames Valley Police said Monday that its investigation was continuing, even as it confirmed that the department was involved in legal proceedings about the search warrants. A department spokesman declined further comment while those proceedings are underway.
The allegations against Mountbatten-Windsor came to light when the U.S. Justice Department released millions of pages of documents from its investigation into sex trafficking by Epstein and his connections to a network of wealthy, powerful men around the world.
Mountbatten-Windsor's relationship with Epstein has been a source of embarrassment to the royal family for more than a decade and forced him to give up royal duties in 2019.
But as further revelations began to leak out of the U.S. investigation last year, the king moved to insulate the monarchy from the fallout by stripping his younger brother of his princely title.
After Mountbatten-Windsor was arrested, Charles departed from the "never complain, never explain" approach of his late mother, Queen Elizabeth, and took the unusual step of issuing a statement on the investigation.
"Let me state clearly: the law must take its course,'' he said at the time. "As this process continues, it would not be right for me to comment further on this matter.''

npr.org.title: Spain's prime minister calls early elections as pressure mounts over housing crisis
npr.org.text:
Spain's prime minister calls early elections as pressure mounts over housing crisis
MADRID — Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez announced early elections Monday after his government suffered a bruising legislative defeat last week on emergency measures related to the country's housing crisis.
The vote will be held Nov. 29.
In recent weeks, Spaniards have demanded solutions from the government over housing affordability, holding protests in cities across the country after public outrage grew over the televised eviction of an 87-year-old woman in Madrid last month.
Right-wing opposition parties joined forces to scuttle two emergency decrees in Parliament that included measures to reduce evictions and real estate speculation. The setback sparked wide speculation that Sánchez could consider moving up a national election that would have otherwise taken place next year.
In a televised address, Sánchez argued that a broader progressive coalition in Parliament would allow Spaniards to tackle the biggest issues facing the country today.
"The time has come, therefore, for the Spanish people to decide what future you want for yourselves and for your country," Sánchez said.
Sánchez, 54, has been Spain's prime minister since 2018, making him one of Europe's longest-standing leaders.
He has become one of the leading international progressive heads of government thanks to his defense of migration, his diplomatic efforts to defend Palestinians and his criticism of the American and Israeli war against Iran.
He has also enjoyed one of the fastest growing economies in the developed world in recent years.
But back home, the Spanish leader has been hemmed in by a series of legal cases involving his Socialist party as well as his wife and brother, who both deny wrongdoing.
He has also struggled to account for this summer's border crossing by tens of thousands of mostly Moroccans into Spain's North African territory of Ceuta, where a humanitarian crisis remains two months after the initial crisis.
He has led a coalition minority government along with the left-wing junior partner Sumar since 2023. But his reliance on several smaller parties to get anything done has hamstrung his legislative ability.
Throughout his political career, Sánchez has earned a reputation as a political escape artist capable of winning elections he looked set to lose.
Speculation around whether he would call snap elections centered on the momentum that his party may now have around issues of affordability, while the opposition Popular Party — which holds the most seats in Parliament already — is likely to define the contest around corruption.
"Sánchez is choosing this moment because it is arguably the best time to do so, given that the issue of housing frames the electoral conflict or debate in terms that are highly favorable to (his party's) position," said Oriol Bartomeus, a professor of political science at the Autonomous University of Barcelona.
"Sánchez can frame the election — or has realized he can frame it — in very classic left-versus-right terms," Bartomeus said."
The Socialist leader will face Popular Party leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo, who aims to take control of the government.
"At last, the Spanish people will decide," Feijóo said Monday after the announcement of the the snap election. "These aren't elections like the previous ones. This is about Spain beating Sánchez," he said.
The formal dissolution of parliament will need to be approved by the Cabinet, which Sánchez has convened for later Monday.

npr.org.title: Super El Niño is here. What's so super about it?
npr.org.text:
Super El Niño is here. What's so super about it?
Federal forecasters say this year the planet could see the strongest El Niño event on record. It's already being called "Super El Niño" and even "Godzilla El Niño." El Niño is a natural climate pattern that has far-reaching impacts across the planet, potentially affecting hundreds of millions of people.
Where those impacts happen can vary drastically from one El Niño to the next. Here are the basics of what this historic event could bring.
What is El Niño?
El Niño occurs every two to seven years. It develops when a vast amount of water in the eastern Pacific Ocean warms up around the equator. That water releases massive heat, redistributing warmth from the ocean to the atmosphere. That shifts weather patterns around the world.
The flip side of El Niño is a La Niña, which is marked by relatively cool water in the tropical Pacific around the equator. These events are responsible for some of the biggest weather variability the planet experiences.
Loading...
El Niño is like dropping a rock in a pond, says Daniel Vimont, professor of atmospheric and oceanic sciences at the University of Wisconsin-Madison. "Even though you're not where the rock hit, you still may feel the effects of those waves," he says. "El Niño is the same thing, except it's an enormous rock in our entire Earth's system, and we feel the response."
How strong is it?
Sure, "Godzilla El Niño" is catchy, but technically, NOAA forecasters say this year's El Niño will fall into the "very strong" category. It's measured by the temperature of the ocean in a particular region off South America. The warmer the water, the stronger the El Niño. When that water is more than 2 degrees Celsius warmer than average, it qualifies as a "very strong" El Niño.
The last strong events were in 2015-16, 1997-8 and 1982-83. El Niños typically peak in November and December, but already, this El Niño is the strongest ever measured for this time of year. NOAA forecasters expect it to last through early 2027.
What will the impacts be globally?
All that added heat in the atmosphere raises temperatures globally. El Niño years tend to be the hottest on record. Forecasters say this year may get close to taking the top spot, but it's very likely that temperature records could fall in 2027. The planet is already warmer due to climate change, because emissions from burning fossil fuels are trapping more heat in the atmosphere.
El Niño also shifts rainfall patterns globally, raising the chances for destructive flooding in some parts of the world. Other regions get drier, exacerbating droughts. Both impacts can be catastrophic to agriculture around the world. The United Nations World Food Programme estimates that El Niño could push at least 49 million more people into acute food insecurity by the end of 2027.
Loading...
What will the impacts be in the U.S.?
In El Niño years, the southern U.S. tends to see more intense rainfall because the jet stream shifts to the south. That raises the risk of floods along rivers and in cities. Still, in the Southwest, more rain could alleviate drought and recharge underground aquifers.
"El Niño tends to juice up those storms so that you get more really strong rain events," says Martin Hoerling, meteorologist and adjunct lecturer at the University of Colorado Boulder. "So if you were running a deficit in your water supply, a big El Niño, especially like the one we're having, can really get you into recovery mode that otherwise might have taken you years."
The northern half of the country gets warmer and drier, something that could exacerbate the current drought in the Intermountain West. Some states experience mixed effects during El Niños, like California. The state saw historic flooding in the 1997-98 El Niño, but was drier than average during the 2015-16 one. Climate experts say the current El Niño is so strong, it's more likely California will experience extreme rain.
El Niños can also lead to fewer hurricanes in the Atlantic Ocean, since it's more difficult for the storms to form. In the Pacific Ocean, hurricanes can get more frequent, fueled by warmer ocean water. Already this year, hurricanes have intensified rapidly in the Pacific, and Hawaii has had close calls with several hurricanes that brought destructive rain and wind.
Loading...
Can we blame it all on El Niño?
Certain weather changes are common during El Niños, but there are no guarantees that extreme weather events this winter will match those predictions for every region.
"El Niño is like loading the dice," Vimont says. "While we're loading the dice for a certain type of response from El Niño, we still know that in any given year, there are still natural fluctuations that may mask that or cause the response to be slightly different than what we might expect."
In addition to that natural variability, weather events are also being affected by climate change. The most intense storms are already producing more rainfall in most of the U.S., since a warmer atmosphere can hold more water vapor. Heat waves and droughts are also getting more intense due to rising temperatures. Climate experts say El Niño and climate change impacts will both play out this winter, but while El Niño will fade, the effects of climate change will continue.

npr.org.title: Republicans and Democrats find a unifying target: Pharmacy benefit managers
npr.org.text:
Republicans and Democrats find a unifying target: Pharmacy benefit managers
Amye Joseph says America's political polarization has made it an "interesting time" in her Tennessee household.
She and her husband, Charlie, have been married for 35 years. She's a Republican. He's a Democrat. But their shared disenchantment with profit-driven healthcare has provided a unifying target: pharmacy benefit managers, known as PBMs.
The Josephs' frustration is focused on CVS Health. The conglomerate, which reported $400 billion in revenue last year, includes a major health insurer (Aetna), one of the country's dominant PBMs (CVS Caremark), and America's largest retail pharmacy chain (CVS Pharmacy).
"We hate CVS. I'm going to be straight-up," Amye Joseph said.
She laments the lack of face-to-face interaction with pharmacists, prices that seem to rise without explanation, and pressure from the couple's CVS Caremark drug plan to use CVS stores instead of their local pharmacy.
"They're not even a middleman," she said. "They're a money grab for CVS."
PBMs were conceived as a way to manage prescriptions and hold down costs. But these middlemen have become bipartisan punching bags, accused of sucking up profits at the expense of employers, governments, and patients.
And while healthcare debates still divide Democrats and Republicans in Washington, D.C., taking on PBMs has become a unifying cause in an era of widespread frustration over rising healthcare costs.
In recent years, every state has imposed restrictions on PBMs. The Josephs' home state of Tennessee, where the GOP has a lock on state government, is among a growing number looking to outlaw companies that own PBMs from also owning brick-and-mortar pharmacies, as CVS does.
That's aligned conservative, business-friendly Republicans with Democrats, who are traditionally more open to government regulation.
This legislative push reflects a feeling even in the GOP that the market for prescription drugs is being gamed, said Antonio Ciaccia, CEO of 46brooklyn Research, a nonprofit think tank that tracks drug pricing.
"Republicans are looking at this issue, saying, We know what competition is supposed to do, and it isn't happening," said Ciaccia, a critic of the PBM industry. "This is not a free market."
Charlie Joseph, a retired fire captain who now works as a custodian, was miffed when he realized he could save money on his blood pressure medication if he paid cash at his local pharmacy rather than using his CVS Caremark drug plan.
He now buys a 90-day supply for the same price he would have paid for a 30-day supply through the CVS plan.
"Right now, it's more of an inconvenience than anything else as far as it goes, but there's no consistency," he said. "The whole healthcare thing is just frustrating, on a good day."
CVS spokesperson Phil Blando said the price of individual drugs can vary.
"Looking at the price of a single prescription does not reflect the value of a comprehensive pharmacy benefit," he said in a statement. "Our focus remains delivering the lowest possible total cost and the greatest overall value for members and plan sponsors."
Unified opposition
PBM officials say their industry has been unfairly maligned. "PBMs are the only part of the prescription drug supply chain working to lower drug costs, which makes PBMs the target of powerful groups, Big Pharma and pharmacists," said Greg Lopes, a spokesperson for the Pharmaceutical Care Management Association, which represents PBMs across the nation.
"Drug manufacturers attempt to shift blame for high drug costs to PBMs in order to retain their profit margins and weaken PBMs' ability to lower costs," he said.
Drugmakers have worked for years to cast PBMs as unnecessary go-betweens, said Barak Richman, a lawyer and economist who studies healthcare competition at George Washington University. He called the fight between Big Pharma and PBMs a corporate "cage match."
"We have wildly passionate partisan divides on a lot of healthcare," he said. "But there's a lot of healthcare policy that I don't think is obviously partisan."
PBMs haven't won over many Democrats or Republicans. Attorneys general from nearly 40 states and U.S. territories last year wrote a letter to congressional leaders arguing that "horizontal consolidation and vertical integration have transformed PBMs from useful administrative service providers into market-dominating behemoths."
In state legislatures like Tennessee's, shared ownership of PBMs and pharmacies has drawn particular fire. Independent pharmacies have little choice but to contract with major PBMs while also competing with the conglomerate-owned pharmacies. Many lawmakers have said they want to protect small businesses.
"If a corporation argues that its pharmacy cannot survive unless it is owned by the same entity that sets the reimbursement rate, then we're not talking about a free market. We're talking about control," Tennessee state Sen. Bobby Harshbarger said in a February legislative hearing.
Harshbarger, a Republican who led the legislative push, is a pharmacist in a small city in northeastern Tennessee.
His mother, U.S. Rep. Diana Harshbarger, R-Tenn., is also a pharmacist and has sponsored a similar PBM ownership ban at the federal level. The Senate version has brought together some unlikely bedfellows, such as Sens. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass. and Josh Hawley, R-Mo.
State lawmakers vs. CVS
CVS officials argued that the Tennessee legislation was misguided. "Any proposed reform should be evaluated based on whether it improves access to care, simplifies the patient experience, and enhances affordability," Blando said in a statement.
It's unclear whether the PBM ownership ban will do that in Tennessee. An analysis by the state legislature's researchers concluded that the bill could drive up healthcare costs in the short term.
To fight the bill, CVS launched a $7 million TV advertising campaign, claiming it would have to close all its 134 pharmacies in the state, similar to its threat in neighboring Arkansas when state lawmakers there passed a similar measure in 2025.
CVS also sent text messages to Tennessee customers, asking them to contact their lawmakers to keep pharmacies open.
Ominous texts from CVS helped kill another PBM ownership ban in Louisiana last year.
Sponsors of the legislation said closure wasn't the only option: CVS could also divest either its stores or its PBM.
Tennessee lawmakers moved forward. State Sen. Rusty Crowe, a Republican from northeastern Tennessee, where the Josephs live, told his colleagues before the vote that they should consider the fierce resistance a sign that they were onto something.
"I learned when I was in the Vietnam War, when you start taking on flak, you know you're over the damn target," he said.
As with most votes in Tennessee's legislature, Republicans didn't need support from Democrats. But they got it anyway.
State Rep. Antonio Parkinson, a Democrat from Memphis, said he felt like he was voting in favor of lower drug prices and supporting "ma and pa" pharmacies. "If there's a benefit to my people, I'm supporting it."
CVS has not divested or closed its pharmacies in states that have passed ownership bans — the laws have yet to take effect. The Arkansas ban is being held up in court after CVS challenged the constitutionality of the law. CVS also sued in Tennessee, though the ownership ban doesn't take effect until 2028.
This story comes from NPR's health reporting partnership with Nashville Public Radio and KFF Health News.

npr.org.title: Supreme Court's new term kicks off with blockbuster climate change case
npr.org.text:
Supreme Court's new term kicks off with blockbuster climate change case
A new Supreme Court term begins Monday with arguments in a blockbuster case about the reach of state power.
Boulder, Colo., is suing two big energy companies, arguing they deceived people about the harms of fossil fuels and contributed to disasters that cost Boulder a lot of time and money.
The dispute could have ramifications far beyond the climate, to other areas where states are trying to hold companies accountable for their alleged harms to local communities.
In 2018, Boulder County slapped the giant energy companies Suncor Energy and Exxon Mobil with a lawsuit. Boulder argued the companies and a trade group knew decades ago that fossil fuels would hurt the environment, raising the risk of floods, extreme heat and wildfires.
Three years later, in late December 2021, the Marshall Fire swept across the county.
Daryl McCool left her home southeast of Boulder so fast she couldn't remember whether she locked the front door.
As it turned out, that didn't matter.
"There's basically nothing left," McCool said. "A 2,000-degree fire burns everything, like coins were melted, bicycles melted."
The historic 1901 house where she raised her son had turned to ash. McCool spent years helping her neighbors file insurance papers and apply for grants to rebuild their homes. Now, she tries to educate people about the human costs of climate change.
Who has power to grapple with climate change
Corey Riday-White is legal director at the Center for Climate Integrity. It supports communities trying to hold oil companies responsible for environmental harms.
"This case represents whether or not we believe as a society that corporations should be held to the same standards that all of us are, right?" Riday-White said. "If you know you are going to cause harm, and you don't tell someone, then you should help clean up that harm."
Boulder's lawsuit has not gone to trial; it's still in the early stages in the Colorado court system. But the energy companies are asking the U.S. Supreme Court to throw out the case now. The companies say only the federal government has the power and expertise to grapple with something as big as climate change. To let Boulder's case proceed, they say, would have huge implications.
Todd Zywicki is a professor at the Antonin Scalia Law School at George Mason University.
"This is about whether a bunch of rich hippies in Boulder County are allowed to dictate environment and energy policy to the entire rest of the world," Zywicki said in a recent webinar about the case.
Exxon referred NPR to the company's court filings. Suncor didn't respond to an email requesting comment.
The Trump administration is siding with the energy companies, arguing global warming is a global issue.
"Essentially Boulder claims that Colorado can reach around the United States, the entirety of the United States, and to my mind, regulate production everywhere by attaching liability to it," said Sai Prakash, a law professor at the University of Virginia who filed a friend of the court brief backing Suncor and Exxon.
"It Boulder can attach liability to these two companies … I think it can attach liability to thousands of others as well," Prakash said.
Seeking to recover past and future costs
Boulder argues it's not suing to regulate greenhouse gas emissions. Rather, it says, it wants to recover past and future costs of repairs, emergency services, and property damage.
Dozens of similar cases where states and municipalities are suing energy giants have been moving through the courts at early stages. Any Supreme Court ruling could have repercussions for many of them.
Jonathan Adler, a law professor at the College of William and Mary, points out in court papers that Congress has the authority to override state laws here, but federal lawmakers haven't done anything.
Corey Riday-White, of the Center for Climate Integrity, said for the justices interested in ruling based on the text of the Constitution or federal statutes, there is not much to support Suncor and Exxon.
"They want the court to say, you can't bring any of these cases in court because this is the purview of the federal government," Riday-White said. "The problem is the big oil companies can't point to any legal doctrine, any statute, any part of the Constitution that backs up that finding."
How the court decides to draw the lines on state power could influence a lot more than climate litigation, according to Deepak Gupta, who regularly argues before the high court.
"Pollution by forever chemicals, nuisance suits over AI data centers, opioids litigation, all of these are about the local effects of conduct that runs across borders," Gupta said at a recent briefing sponsored by Georgetown's Supreme Court Institute.
The conservative supermajority on the Supreme Court may be uncomfortable letting state juries decide some of these pressing issues. But legal experts say they're not sure quite how the justices might shape a decision in the Boulder case.
Louie Delaware, who lost his Boulder-area home in the Marshall fire, said he plans to be at the Supreme Court Monday as it hears arguments in the case. Delaware said he tried to fight off the fire with a garden hose, but he lacked the appropriate protective gear, so he realized that he needed to drive away quickly.
"You know it's our responsibility to leave things better for the next generation," Delaware said. "And the way we're going right now is counter to what that's been in the past."
Last-minute Alito recusal
In a surprise move, the court notified lawyers in the case just one week before argument that Justice Samuel Alito had decided not to participate. The court clerk provided no explanation in his letter. But environmental organizations and watchdog groups had been calling for Alito's recusal because of his investments in Phillips 66 and ConocoPhillips.
Justin Kloczko of the group Consumer Watchdog said the decision is "the right decision, and one he should have made from the start."
"The public should not have to wonder whether a justice's personal investments could benefit from a ruling that shields the fossil-fuel industry from liability," Kloczko said in a written statement.
Alito's decision to step aside means eight justices will hear the case. In the matter of a 4-4 tie, that means the decision of the Colorado Supreme Court—allowing Boulder's lawsuit to proceed—will prevail.
But the high court may have left itself another option: among the questions the justices said they'll consider is whether they have jurisdiction to hear the Suncor case now, because it's still at an early stage in Colorado state courts.

theguardian.com.title: 15-year-old loses hand in clash with French police during school protest – Europe live
theguardian.com.text:
A 15-year-old boy lost his hand as clashes with police around French schools continue
We are also getting some dramatic news from France, where the school protests continue for another day and hundred of schools are closed today.
A 15-year-old student reportedly had his hand blown off on Monday during a protest in Lens, as reported by AFP.
A police union source said the student in the northern town of Lens appeared to have picked up a teargas grenade fired by riot police, hoping to fling it back, but the device exploded in his hand.
Elsewhere, a 17-year-old was arrested after allegedly throwing a piece of stone at police officers, striking a passerby in the face and making him lose sight in one eye, Le Figaro reported.
French education minister condemns 'acts of extreme violence,' but defends democratic right to protest
Today’s violent clashes raise concern about tomorrow’s big “day of protests” in France, as several groups mobilise to show their discontent with the state of the education system.
But education minister Édouard Geffray insisted that the protests represent “a freedom that must be respected and protected,” Le Figaro reported.
But he strongly criticised “acts of extreme violence” including, in some cases, direct attacks on schools principals.

A 15-year-old student reportedly had his hand blown off on Monday during a protest in Lens, as reported by AFP.
A police union source said the student in the northern town of Lens appeared to have picked up a teargas grenade fired by riot police, hoping to fling it back, but the device exploded in his hand.
Elsewhere, a 17-year-old was arrested after allegedly throwing a piece of stone at police officers, striking a passerby in the face and making him lose sight in one eye, Le Figaro reported.
Germany at risk of conflict with Russia as it steps up its 'shadow war' activities, intelligence chief warns
In other news, Germany is at risk of entering a violent conflict as Moscow steps up an increasingly aggressive “shadow war” against European democracies, its head of foreign intelligence warned, as reported by Reuters.
“The confrontation we are facing with Russia has taken on a new, more dangerous dimension,”Martin Jäger, head of the Bundesnachrichtendienst (BND), told the annual public hearing of intelligence chiefs in parliament.
“Germany is in danger of becoming embroiled in a violent conflict with Russia – the attempted attack in Leipzig is just one example,” he said, describing Russia as “waging a shadow war” with the threat of attacks against targets in Germany remaining “real and imminent“.
German authorities have warned repeatedly that Russia is conducting a hybrid campaign of drone and cyber-attacks, and have blamed it for an attempted drone attack on Leipzig airport in August.
Jäger, however, said Moscow was prepared to use force to achieve its goals, and that Russian intelligence services’ operations in and against Germany were “increasingly aggressive“.
“Russia is putting us to the test and closely watching how we handle this situation. From the perspective of the Kremlin leadership, any sign of wavering invites them to further increase the pressure on Germany.“
Jäger said there was no indication of an imminent large-scale Russian attack on Nato territory.
“However, Russia could engage in low-intensity military activities, particularly in the Baltic states.“
Germany must prepare for more meddling and attempts at intimidation, including threats of nuclear attack, he said.
“Moscow is betting on our weakness”, he added. “We have to stand up to that.“
Jäger said Moscow was trying to compel Germany, Ukraine’s largest donor, to drop its support.
“Russia is determined to bring Ukraine to its knees this coming winter,” he said. “We must expect Russian attacks of a severity and brutality that we have not yet seen.“
Sánchez’s minority coalition government with the smaller, leftwing Sumar alliance, has struggled to get legislation through a fraught congress and has not passed a budget since 2023. Junts, which offered him its conditional support three years ago, has attempted to extract maximum benefits from the government, only to abandon it when it feels so inclined, as it did with the emergency housing measures.
Faced with all that, it’s not hard to see why the prime minister may have decided that an early election was preferable to several more months of legislative deadlock, mud-slinging and uncomfortable headlines.
Sánchez, a politician with an almost feline allocation of lives, will be hoping that his efforts to tackle the housing crisis will contrast sharply with those of his rightwing opponents and thereby mobilise disenchanted voters.
Perhaps unsurprisingly given what’s at stake, the prime minister is once again pushing to characterise this latest election as a simple choice between progressive and reactionary politics.
“You, the men and women of Spain, must decide whether you want to join the far-right wave that drives regression wherever it governs, or to ensure that Spain remains a bastion of openness, social justice, and environmental responsibility.”
His opponents, meanwhile, will be hoping that, after eight long years, the public has grown tired and disillusioned, and that the great survivor of Spanish politics has finally lost his lustre.
Latvian PM Kulbergs on track to hold on to power after elections
Jon Henley
Europe correspondent
Meanwhile in Latvia, prime minister Andris Kulbergs is on track to hold on to power in Riga and will today set about forming a pro-Ukrainian coalition after his centre-right United List party scored an unprecedented victory in last weekend’s elections.
United List won 42 seats in the 100-seat assembly, the biggest parliamentary election victory since Latvia regained independence in 1991, a result Kulbergs put down to “the people truly wanting change”, meaning mainly “economic growth”.
A former businessman and amateur rally driver, Kulbergs, 47, came to power in May after the previous coalition government collapsed amid uproar over its handling of incidents in which stray Ukrainian military drones flew into Latvia undetected.
He will be forced to change coalition partners since one of the outgoing government’s members failed to clear the 5% parliamentary hurdle and looks able to secure a majority with either the nationalist National Alliance or the liberal Progressives.
Populist parties fared well, with United List followed by the Maga-style Latvia First, which finished second after courting the country’s substantial ethnic Russian minority, with the pro-Russian Sovereign Power third. National Alliance was fourth.
Kulbergs pledged continued support for Ukraine and a hard line towards Moscow. “Any economic ties with Russia makes us weak. Yes, it can bring some extra money, but it’s a weakness Russia might exploit,” he told reporters on Sunday night.
He also promised more anti-drone capability for Latvia and to maintain defence spending at 5% of GDP, one of the highest levels in Nato. His pro-Kremlin rivals said Latvia should stop any aid to Ukraine and instead focus on cost-of-living issues.
Four years after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine security remains central to political debate in Latvia, which is sandwiched between the Baltic Sea and Russia and Belarus to the east, with EU and Nato allies Estonia and Lithuania to the north and south.
Kulbergs said Russia was its principal security threat. “Because we are the external border of Europe, we must have a strong economy ... a strong border region,” Kulbergs said. “That is the main task.”
However, soaring living costs, low wages, an ailing healthcare system and long-term population decline also featured prominently. No Latvian government has survived a full term and analysts say Kulbergs could face an uphill battle even holding together his United List, itself a loose alliance of small parties and independents.
Members of Sánchez’s administration, his party and his inner circle have also been battling a series of corruption allegations over the past two years.
Meanwhile Sánchez’s wife, Begoña Gomez, is due to face trial after a judge charged her with embezzlement, influence peddling, corruption in business dealings and misappropriation of funds at the end of a two-year investigation.
David Sánchez and Begoña Gómez have both denied any wrongdoing, and the prime minister has previously accused his political and media enemies of launching a “harassment and bullying operation” against his family.
How an 87-year-old Spanish woman became the face of the fight for affordable housing – explainer
Ashifa Kassam
María del Carmen Abascal, 87, was evicted from her home, on a stretcher, after being given 30 minutes to gather her belongings.
The Guardian’s European community affairs correspondent, Ashifa Kassam, explains how her eviction sparked protests across Madrid, which led to ‘Maricarmen’ becoming the symbol of a long-running housing rights movement – which now is likely to be a central issue of the upcoming election campaign.
Spain 'will find its voice again,' opposition leader as he blasts Sánchez's record in government
The People’s Party’s Alberto Núñez Feijóo is speaking now, and he begins with what looks to be his party’s top reaction line today: “At last.”
He says Spain “will speak its mind, and will find its voice again.”
“At last, we can close this chapter and open a better one. At last, the person who should never have made it this far can go.”
He says “these are not like any previous elections in our democracy,” as he frames it as a battle for “defeating Sánchez and what he represents.”
“It is a choice between corruption and decency, between decline and prosperity, between a government that aspires only to survive and a country that looks to its future. The question … is whether they want four more years of what we are currently experiencing or whether they want to give change a chance.”
He talks about “corruption” in public institution and funds, “disregard” to social harmony, and “unbearable” cost of living and housing issues.
He says immigration is “out of control” as he draws on the recent migration crisis in Ceuta, while public infrastructure is “deteriorating,” with “power outages and increase insecurity.”
He says it’s all “not a question of money, but of mismanagement.”
“The truth also requires acknowledging that those who created these problems are incapable of solving them. If eight years were not enough, why do they want four more?”
He says Sánchez’s move to call early elections is about damage control and to get ahead of possible other crises.
He then moves on to what looks like to be the key framing of his campaign, as he promises “a government with the authority to lead” and to “rally the nation’s collective energy once again.”
“We must reclaim the pride of belonging to a country that refuses to resign itself to defeat. We must reject the formulas that have already devastated other nations and instead embrace a path where decisions are made by the majority of Spaniards. It comes down to this: decline or change, lies or change, incompetence or change, division or change, corruption or change.”
He then says:
“I am fully aware of the scale of the work that lies ahead. My hand will not tremble; if the Spanish people place their trust in me, I will not betray it.”
And he finishes where he started, saying the vote is coming “at last.”
In terms of technical process behind the snap election, it is now emerging that Sánchez told King Felipe VI about his plans by phone yesterday afternoon, Spanish news agency EFE reported.
The formal decision to dissolve the parliament will be approved at the government’s meeting later this morning.
There was a telling part in Sánchez’s address where he acknowledged some of the voters’ frustrations with his government.
“I know that we have made mistakes and have failed to do everything we had set out to do.
It is also true that there are still many injustices to correct, many social goals to conquer and many problems to solve, especially in the areas of inequality in public services and access to housing.”
To be fair, Sánchez’s has been running a minority government, and that’s not making his life any easier. Hence the direct call that “to do more, we need to renew and expand public support.”
Expect to hear more messaging along these lines: yes, we are not perfect, but we are moving in the right direction trying to secure more of your rights, and not to roll them back.
Can he make another comeback given the state of the polls, though? It would be quite a feat.
Sánchez calls snap election after housing legislation fails to pass
Sam JonesandAshifa Kassam in Madrid
The government’s efforts to address the housing crisis were set out in two decrees that contained a range of measures aimed at improving access to housing, from a ban on evictions until 2030 to the regulation of temporary lettings and lettings by room.
But the decrees were voted down in congress on Friday by the conservative People’s party (PP), the far-right Vox party, and the rightwing Catalan pro-independence party Junts.
The PP, which is leading the polls but which may need to rely on Vox’s support to form a government, said it had rejected the government’s plans as it believed that construction, and not regulation, was the best way to tackle the crisis.
The rejection of the decrees met with an angry response from the crowds who had gathered outside congress, eliciting boos and cries of “shame” and “Your profits; our misery”.
Long-brewing fury over the high cost of renting and the precarious nature of many tenancies exploded late last month following the eviction of Maricarmen Abascal, an 87-year-old woman who was removed from the home in Madrid where she had lived for 70 years. Abascal said she could not possibly afford the 230% rent hike demanded by the investment fund that bought her apartment.
Over the weekend, large demonstrations were held across the country as protesters stepped up their demands for urgent action on the housing crisis. Authorities said 70,000 people had taken part in a protest in Madrid on Saturday, while organisers put the figure at 500,000.
Although polls consistently place the PP well ahead of Sánchez’s Spanish Socialist Workers’ party – and show that support for Vox is growing – the prime minister may be hoping that the focus on housing, and the right’s rejection of his government’s plans to address the crisis, will mobilise leftwing voters.
Sánchez bets on anger over housing, defence of progressive values as he trails behind opposition in polls - snap analysis
Jakub Krupa
Pedro Sánchez is clearly hoping to mobilise voters around the housing crisis and the broader message of home, with opinion polls suggesting his left-wing government might otherwise struggle to retain power.
The conservative People’s Party (PP) looks most likely to take first place and could be take power alongside the far-right Vox party. Polling currently puts the PP on roughly 32-34%, well clear of Sánchez’s Socialists (PSOE) on 26-27%. Vox sits in third place on 18-19%, comfortably ahead of smaller left-wing rivals Sumar (5-6%) and Podemos (2-3%).
Vox’s potential entry into a governing coalition would mark the first time a far-right party has held power in Spain since the end of the Franco dictatorship in 1975.
A defeat for Sánchez would bring down one of western Europe’s few remaining left-leaning administrations at a time when populist and conservative parties are making gains across the continent.
Sánchez’s decision also brings forward one of Europe’s most closely watched electoral contests – originally slated for 2027 alongside major votes in France, Italy, and Poland.

theguardian.com.title: Accept ‘bad things’ in return for benefits of AI, says Sam Altman
theguardian.com.text:
Sam Altman says he believes the world should accept “bad things” happening with AI in exchange for the benefits of the technology.
The chief executive of OpenAI cited hacks, scams and “other bad things that will happen” in an interview that sparked an instant backlash from critics of the major AI companies. His comments came after one of his company’s safety experts resigned, saying at the weekend that its “culture is broken”.
In an interview released on Monday, Altman was asked about how OpenAI’s approach to safety differed from that of Anthropic, which has called for the industry to slow down after one of its researchers quit, warning that AI experts believed “it could kill us all by the end of the decade”.
“I think there’s a lot of daylight,” Altman said. “One of the differences between us and some of the stricter AI safety people is that we believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency [to use AI widely].
“I do think the lighter touch regulatory stance we advocate for comes with an accepting of the fact that some bad things are going to happen as society figures out the resilience.
“I wouldn’t take a trade of saying we will make sure there’s no major hacks, there’s no misuse of this technology, there’s zero scams or all the other bad things that will happen because I think that people will do tremendously – orders of magnitude – more good stuff than bad stuff.”
The interview for Politico’s Decoded podcast drew a strong response from Ron DeSantis, the governor of Florida. He said he had “no dice” with the idea “a handful of tech oligarchs get to make that decision [on safety] for the rest of us”.
His state last week asked a judge to bar OpenAI from developing new AI models without third-party approved guardrails.
Gary Marcus, a prominent AI sceptic and professor emeritus at New York University, said Altman was “saying the quiet part out loud: suck it up, so you can make us rich and powerful”.
OpenAI was hit by multiple safety crises over the summer, including when a swarm of its AI agents escaped their training “sandbox”, cheated, deceived and conspired to hack into the Hugging Face website. Other agents accessed Australian government data.
The company has scrapped the release of a cutting-edge model but Altman’s comments reflect a more bullish mood ahead of a stock market flotation.
The wave of public and political concern last month about the potentially catastrophic consequences of fast-progressing AI agents that act beyond human intent had led to hopes of US-wide or even international safety agreements.
However, Donald Trump and AI bosses including Altman and Dario Amodei of Anthropic signed a far more laissez-faire pact at the White House last week. The US president said he wanted the companies to “self-police” to limit the risks from AI-enabled cyber-attacks and bioweapons.
Geoffrey Irving, who worked at OpenAI and Google DeepMind and as chief scientist at the UK’s AI Safety Institute, said warnings about AI risks understated the dangers.
“There’s about a 50% chance we all die because of the development of smarter-than-human AI systems,” he said, adding that actions taken over the next two to 10 years would be decisive.
OpenAI’s David Robinson announced his departure at the weekend, saying “the companies building this technology aren’t being nearly careful enough” as they sprint from one product launch to the next.
His view was endorsed by Miles Brundage, an AI policy researcher who worked at OpenAI for six years. He said he regretted helping “spread the idea of iterative deployment”, which may have made sense when AI was less powerful “but makes no sense at all after many deaths have been tied to AI and as we’re careening towards extinction-level risks”.

theguardian.com.title: Shadow chancellor to address Tory conference as he claims slashing red tape could cut cost of new houses by £50,000 – UK politics live
theguardian.com.text:
No 10 insists RAF Fairford is safe after US withdraws its bombers
Downing Street has insisted RAF Fairford is safe after the US withdrew its bombers from the base over new security concerns, the Press Association reports. PA says:
The Pentagon confirmed yesterday that aircraft which were being stationed at the Gloucestershire base had been “redeployed to their home stations in the United States”.
The move follows the arrest of six individuals over the past week in connection with a suspected terror plot targeting the base.
US officials told the New York Times the redeployment of the bombers, which have been involved in carrying out strikes on Iran, had been ordered after more specific details about threats to the base emerged over the weekend.
Asked at at lobby briefing this morning whether RAF Fairford was safe, the PM’s spokesperson said: “Yes.”
He pointed to comments by defence secretary Wes Streeting saying there were “tried and tested approaches to defend our bases around the country and throughout the world”, but he declined to comment further on “foreign nations’ military operations”.
He added: “I would just point you to the president’s words last week, where he praised our police, defence and security services in relation to RAF Fairford.”
The five British nationals, all in their mid-20s, arrested near the base on September 27 have since been released on bail.
A sixth man, a 25-year-old dual UK-Iranian national, arrested on October 1, has also been released on bail.
Investors criticise Tories for proposing to get rid of regulations making new homes environmentally resilient
The UK Sustainable Investment and Finance Association (UKSIF), which represents fund managers committed to sustainable investment, has issued a statement criticising the Conservatives for proprosing to get rid of regulations that make new buildings environmentally resilient. (See 8.08am.)
In a statement, James Alexander, the UKSIF CEO, said:
The UK’s ageing, inefficient housing stock poses a risk to families’ well-being and the long-term financial stability of the property market.
That’s why investors have backed both strong standards for new homes and plans to upgrade existing properties, which can help to tackle this looming crisis.
Rolling out technologies like solar panels and efficient heating systems can cut energy bills while creating high-quality jobs in supply chains across the country.
Suddenly ripping up regulation designed to enhance property resilience could weaken the financing environment for housebuilding and the industries that support it.

Downing Street has insisted RAF Fairford is safe after the US withdrew its bombers from the base over new security concerns, the Press Association reports. PA says:
