A sixth man, a 25-year-old dual UK-Iranian national, arrested on October 1, has also been released on bail.
'There can be no economic growth on dead planet' - Greens accuse Tories of ignoring reality of climate crisis
The Green party has accused the Tories of ignoring the reality of the climate crisis. In a response to the measures announced by Andrew Griffith (see 8.08am), the Green MP Ellie Chowns said:
It is completely outrageous that, as evidence of climate breakdown and environmental collapse becomes ever-more impossible to ignore, the Conservatives would prefer to tear up environmental standards, weaken climate protection, and abolish organisations charged with protecting nature, rather than tackle the genuine issues affecting building in Britain.
There can be no economic growth on a dead planet. There is no success story in homes that overheat in summer, flood in winter, or leave families paying sky-high energy bills because we failed to build them properly in the first place.
Reform UK says Tories 'treating people like fools' by planning to scrap red tape they introduced
Here is Reform UK’s considered response to the Tory proposals announced by Andrew Griffith to boost building by getting rid of red tape. (See 8.08am.) It is from Richard Tice, the party’s deputy leader and business spokesperson.
Kemi Badenoch has forgotten that it was the Tories who introduced the policies which stifled growth and housebuilding in the first place.
They introduced the energy profits levy which gutted the North Sea, committed to the ‘Grocery Tax’ and laid the groundwork for its introduction, and imposed crushing net zero costs through heat pumps, nutrient neutrality and biodiversity net gain requirements.
And to show how far back the rot goes, they created the Environment Agency in the first place.
Now they’re copying policies Reform announced months ago and expect the public to hand the matches back to the arsonist. They’re treating the British people like fools.
This is not a party that has changed. The Tories spent 14 years creating problems and ignoring their devastating impacts.
Head of Jewish Greens says she may leave party over ‘Zionism is racism’ vote
Vivien Lichtenstein, the head of the Jewish Greens, has said she may leave the party after it voted to adopt a policy that equates Zionism with racism and calls for Israel to be replaced by a single Palestinian state, Peter Walker reports.
On Thursday voters in Holborn and St Pancras in London will vote in a byelection to replace Keir Starmer. It has been a safe Labour seat for years, and Sagal Abdi-Wali, who came to the UK as a child refugee from Somalia and who is now leader of Camden council is the party’s candidate to replace the ex-PM. But she is facing a tough challenge from Zack Polanski, the Green party leader.
It is hard to find a better guide to a byelection than Rob Ford, the politics professor and elections specialist, and he has written a long piece about the contest on his Substack blog. It is well worth reading, and here is his conclusion.
Burnham’s extended honeymoon with the electorate, and the Greens’ decline in the polls mean Labour go into this contest as heavy favourites. After all, if the Greens could not take Camden when Labour were hitting rock bottom with Starmer, what chance do they have now? But by-elections have a track record of delivering surprises, particularly when high profile figures are on the ballot. If Zack Polanski and his army of Green activists can convince local voters that the contest represents a low risk opportunity to send a warning shot across the bows of the new Labour leadership, they may yet be able to mobilise lingering distrust of Labour among voters still angry at being marginalised during the Starmer years.
It is rumoured that Dominic Cummings wanted to use the slogan “Tell Them Again” in the event of a second EU referendum. A similar message could yet reignite the smouldering resentment of young progressives still sore at the perceived betrayals of the Starmer years, and help Zack Polanski win against the odds next week. Burnham’s rise changed the political weather this summer. But the weather could yet change again next week.
Although Ford published his article today, it does not refer to yesterday’s Green party vote saying “Zionism is racism”, which will probably be bad for Polanski’s chances. Ford’s analysis is in part based on the fact that the constituency has unusual demographics. “The seat has exceptionally high shares of twentysomethings, single person households, full time students, graduates, middle class professionals, social renters, private renters, residents born abroad,” he says.
And this is fromPhilip Stephens, the former chief political commentator at the Financial Times, on the Tory plans announced today.
Of course we Tories are not climate change deniers …it’s just that we want to abandon the net zero target, scrap environmental controls, and expand Heathrow ….
This is from Vicky Spratt, the journalist and housing specialist, on the Tory proposals to cut building regulations. (See 8.08am.)
Shadow Chancellor Andrew Griffith has told the Tory conference that he would “scrap unnecessary net-zero housing red tape” and cut the cost of “delivering and therefore buying a new home by up to £50,000.”
How would the Tories guarantee that developers pass on these supposed savings to homebuyers?
And what about those new-build buyers who want solar panels and heat pumps and lower energy bills? Could cutting the requirement for building them in mean any savings just translated into higher bills for the homeowner?
Andy Burnham has been urged to back compulsory voting as a means of helping to overcome opposition to his proposal to make the pensions triple lock less generous.
The argument is made in a report published by the Fairness Foundation that has been written by Charles White, who runs the Campaign for Compulsory Voting.
In her foreword to the report, Polly Neate, a crossbench peer and former CEO of Shelter, said:
The pensions triple lock is protected by voter power. That’s how politics works, but it isn’t how democracy should work, and it certainly doesn’t give fairness a chance.
Now the prime minister has touched the third rail of British politics by daring to fix this unfairness, he needs voters on side. Compulsory voting would give Burnham the political cover and popular support to deliver. The people most likely to back reform, including younger voters, would be at the ballot box to reward a government that took on intergenerational inequality. Compulsory voting brings everyone into the decision, those directly affected and those who aren’t, encouraging a more considered response to major policy choices.
Burnham has said that he will set up a commission on electoral reform. He has not explicitly said that he wants it to look at compulsory voting, but there is increasing interest in the idea in progressive circles.
Scottish government on course to miss its child poverty targets 'by miles', thinktank says
John Swinney has been warned of the “increasing disconnect” between his words and his actions on child poverty, as the government looks set to miss legally-binding targets on the issue “by miles”, the Press Association reports. PA says:
In a highly critical report, the Joseph Rowntree Foundation (JRF) said a “shocking” 21% of children are growing up in poverty despite the first minister’s defining promise to eradicate it.
The Poverty in Scotland 2026 report warned that without “radical change”, Scotland will miss its legally binding target to cut relative child poverty to below 10% by 2030/31 by a “wide margin”.
The Scottish government previously missed its legal targets for 2023-2024, although the child poverty rate did fall.
The JRF said ministers need a much bolder plan to tackle poverty.
It said the government’s plan to review its targets “risks delaying action and lowering ambitions” as it called for new, stretching ones to be created.
The report said: “We have consistently heard the first minister describe eradicating poverty as his defining mission.
This commitment is welcome, but there is an increasing disconnect between the Scottish government’s rhetoric and the reality of life for families in poverty across Scotland.”
It called for ministers to bring forward a “new, much bolder and properly funded plan to reduce poverty in Scotland”, and reform local government funding to ensure that “services are best where they are needed the most”.
Chris Birt, associate director for Scotland at the JRF, said: “We are on course to miss the legally binding targets by miles, but parliament can choose to up the ante and provide challenging new targets that re-energise government efforts.”
Tories will abolish Climate Change Committee, shadow energy secretary Andrew Bowie says
Andrew Bowie, the shadow energy secretary, has said that the Tory plan to dismantled the net zero legislation will include gettting rid of the Climate Change Committee.
In his speech to the conference this morning, he said:
What is the difference between a grid that prioritises cheap power for Britain over a grid nearly entirely reliant on renewables?
Well we’ve done the work: it’s £320bn.
Conference, cheap power is crucial. For industry, for the British people.
At conference last year we announced the measures we would take to cut bills right now.
Removing VAT from energy bills – saving £94
Axing the Carbon Tax on electricity generation. A cut of £75.
Ditching Ed Miliband’s renewable subsidies - £22.
A total package to slash bills by £200 per year.
And we’ll go further.
We’ll scrap GB Energy.
We’ll scrap the auction rounds for offshore wind that tie us to higher and higher prices.
We’ll abolish the climate change committee that instructs the British public how often they should go on holiday, farmers what they should plant, commuters what they should drive and the government what they should tax.
And we’ll repeal Ed Miliband’s Climate Change Act and net zero 2050.

theguardian.com.title: Trump heads to Nebraska in attempt to shore up GOP’s midterm vote – US politics live
theguardian.com.text:
Trump heads to Nebraska in attempt to shore up the GOP's midterm vote
Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.
Donald Trump will be in Nebraska later today, campaigning alongside Republican senator Pete Ricketts, in an attempt to salvage the GOP’s dwindling midterms campaign.
The president is headed to Grand Island, located in the solidly conservative south-central part of the state. It’s part of what Trump says is a 32-day blitz of rallies ahead of 3 November that so far has taken him to ruby-red territory such as Oklahoma and Alabama.
On Wednesday, he will make his second stop in two weeks in Texas with a rally in San Antonio.
“The president’s coming to Nebraska to help me campaign, so I can get reelected,” Ricketts, who is running against an independent candidate backed by national Democrats, told the Associated Press last week on Capitol Hill.
The administration’s plan to allow more imports of foreign beef has particularly roiled the agriculture-rich state of Nebraska. Trump wants to lower beef prices for consumers but ranchers have rebelled against the import proposal, arguing it would undercut them.
“The plan to import low-quality foreign beef is not helping Nebraska ranchers,” Ricketts told the AP. “I would advise the White House to change that policy and look for longer-term things that will help us build the size of the herd and ultimately bring the price of beef down for consumers.”
This campaign is set against the president’s plummeting approval ratings, the unravelling of his Maga movement and an affordability crisis escalated by his unpopular war on Iran. But Trump supporters are also among the most motivated to vote and Republicans have far deeper coffers to mobilise their base.
Meanwhile, vice-president JD Vance will rally in Alaska for senator Dan Sullivan, a Republican locked in a tight reelection campaign.
In other developments:
The White House has defended a newly hired press aide who posed for a holiday photograph in 2021 wearing a “Fuck Joe Biden” T-shirt and holding a rifle. Beni Rae Harmony, the new assistant White House press secretary, revealed on Friday that she was going to work for Donald Trump just days after covering him as a correspondent for Real America’s Voice, a partisan rightwing outlet originally created as a video podcast platform for the president’s former adviser Steve Bannon.
The United States has removed its B-1 bombers from a British air base one week after five men were arrested nearby on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts, a suspected plot that British prime minister Andy Burnham said was likely backed by Iran. The planes had been stationed at RAF Fairford, the preferred European base for US bombers 90 miles west of London, which had recently been used for US strikes on Iran.
Donald Trump will begin his day in Washington in closed-door meetings, before he heads to Nebraska to campaign with Pete Ricketts. A reminder that Ricketts is rhetorical the incumbent Republican senator who is facing a competitive re-election race against the independent nominee, Dan Osborn, in November. The state – which Trump won by more than 20 points in 2024 – is the latest stop on the president’s midterms blitz in the final month until the election. He’s set to deliver remarks at 7pm ET.
And while Trump is in the Midwest, his vice-president, JD Vance, will campaign in Fairbanks, Alaska where he’ll stump on behalf of Dan Sullivan, the Republican senator who is fighting for re-election against Mary Peltola, the state’s Democratic congresswoman.
JD Vance, widely considered to be the Republican frontrunner for the presidential election in 2028, is aligning himself with the Make America Healthy Again (Maha) movement as some say it is shedding its grassroots supporters in favor of political and corporate interests.
The US vice-president has positioned himself as the inheritor of Make America Great Again (Maga), and attaching himself to Maha, which many in the Trump administration believe helped to win the 2024 election, signals a greater overlap between the two movements as the administration’s popularity plummets amid the war in Iran and rising prices.
More than two-thirds (68%) of rural Maha supporters said that Trump’s health policies have “had a negative effect or no impact on the health of people where they live”, according in a new AP-KFF survey that highlights the disconnect between the sprawling political project and its grassroots support, especially in rural areas that overwhelmingly supported Trump in the 2024 election. More Americans view the president and vice-president unfavorably than favorably, according to a January survey by Pew Research.
At the Maha summit in Washington DC on Tuesday, Vance traded jokes about memes and the “carnivore” diet of meat and fermented foods with Robert F Kennedy Jr, the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and the leader of Maha.
But Vance also highlighted his role in identifying what he says is fraud in Medicaid, Medicare and the Affordable Care Act marketplace – blaming it on immigrants, especially undocumented immigrants.
“We’ve found close to $250bn in fraud just since I’ve been leading the anti-fraud task force,” Vance claimed, though the administration has released scant details on who has been unenrolled from these programs and why the activity was considered fraudulent.
US bombers pulled from UK's RAF Fairford base after suspected terror plot
Dan Sabbagh
The US Air Force has pulled its bombers from RAF Fairford following an investigation into an alleged planned terror attack at the base.
The bombers were redeployed back to their home bases in the US, according to a Pentagon official who was not authorised to discuss sensitive military movements and spoke on Sunday on condition of anonymity.
A Pentagon spokesperson said:
While operational security precluded us from confirming the movement of our assets and forces in real time, we can acknowledge now that all US bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have redeployed to their home stations in the United States.
At least 10 B-1 bombers of 12 flew out of Fairford on Sunday, including some that arrived on rotation less than a week ago, underlining the haste of the departure and the apparent significance given by the US to the threat.
There was no immediate comment from the UK Ministry of Defence, though the rapid pace of the withdrawal will heighten concerns in the area around the RAF base in Gloucestershire.
Clayton, who leads the US’s 18 intelligence agencies, previously served as the top federal prosecutor in Manhattan and led the Securities and Exchange Commission during Trump’s first term.
In a social media post on Sunday, Trump announced that Clayton would lead what the US president called “the Super Intelligence Force (SIF)”.
Trump’s post also said the SIF would “coordinate the federal government’s engagement with consumers, public interest groups, religious organizations, critical infrastructure providers, and super intelligence companies”.

Beni Rae Harmony, the new assistant White House press secretary, revealed on Friday that she was going to work for Donald Trump just days after covering him as a correspondent for Real America’s Voice, a partisan rightwing outlet originally created as a video podcast platform for the president’s former adviser Steve Bannon.
According to a LinkedIn profile, Harmony, 24, previously worked as a producer for the far-right Turning Point USA host Jack Posobiec – and as a press aide “focusing on crisis management” for two far-right Republicans: congressman Paul Gosar of Arizona and former congressman Matt Gaetz of Florida.
In 2021, when Gosar was censured by the US House for posting an animated video that depicted him killing Democratic congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and attacking Joe Biden, Harmony recorded an outraged defense of her boss for his YouTube channel.
The photograph of Harmony and an older man posing with rifles in matching anti-Biden shirts, in front of Christmas decorations, was reportedly posted on Instagram in November 2021 by a far-right Republican House candidate, Jarome Bell, who mounted a failed campaign for Congress in 2022.

theguardian.com.title: Guardian readers fund life-changing surgery for Somali boy injured in US airstrike
theguardian.com.text:
On the rickshaw ride to the hospital, Marian Haji Abdi Guled felt a mixture of joy and apprehension: the day they had been waiting for had finally arrived.
Almost a year earlier, her then seven-year-old son, Abdiqadir Salah, had been seriously injured, alongside his two siblings, in what a Guardian investigation found was a US drone strike on the village of Jamaame in Somalia that killed at least 12 civilians, including eight children.
Abdiqadir’s small body had been impaled by shrapnel in the attack, and several chunks remained embedded in his back.
Doctors feared that without an operation to remove them, the boy would lose his ability to walk, but Guled had no money for an operation. For 10 months, the family had languished in Mogadishu with growing expenses and no income – unable to afford surgery, but unwilling to let the boy return to the village without it.
After the investigation, which told the story of Guled and other civilians affected by the attack, a group of Guardian readers from across the globe fundraised for Abdiqadir’s surgery and recovery.
Within a few hours, enough money was raised to cover his treatment and rehabilitation, as well as any medical expenses and treatment for her other two children, who sustained less extensive injuries.
“I was so happy when I found out that Guardian readers raised the money needed for my son’s surgery. I didn’t know people like this existed,” Guled said.
“The people who contributed to the surgery – I really appreciate their support and how they stood by our family when we needed it the most.”
On a Saturday morning in September, Guled waited anxiously as Abdiqadir was finally taken for surgery at Kaafi hospital in Mogadishu.
“Other patients were taken into surgery after him and came out before him – so I worried maybe something went wrong,” she said. “I got to a point where I knocked on the operating room door asking if my son was still alive, then was held back by other patients.”
Finally, her son emerged. Doctors told Guled the surgery had been successful, but complex. While the first two pieces of shrapnel from the missile had been successfully removed, taking out the final piece was considered too risky, possibly resulting in paralysis, so they concluded that it was safer to leave it and monitor his condition.
When the Guardian visited Abdiqadir a few weeks later, he appeared bright, energised and visibly happy. “I have one piece of metal still in me, and if they touch it, I might become paralysed,” the seven-year-old said. “[But] I don’t have any problem with the last piece of metal in my body, because I’m no longer in pain.”
The Guardian investigation into the US airstrikes that injured Abduqadir raised myriad questions about US military intelligence, such as how the targets were selected and why children were hit while they were clearly visible and out in the open. The US has not responded to any questions about the Jamaame attack.
In the months since then, US attacks on the area have continued: from December 2025 to July 2026, it carried out at least three airstrikes around Jamaame, according to research by New America, a security thinktank that documents US military operations abroad. Residents say drones continue to fly above the town.
“We cannot return to Jamaame because what caused my children to be hurt is still there,” Guled said. “I fled Jamaame with my wounded children because of the drones, and the drones are still [flying].”
With the remaining financial support she received from Guardian readers, Guled plans to relocate with her children to the government-controlled port city of Kismayo, which has not been the target of drone strikes, and where Abdiqadir can receive further surgery if needed.
She still wants answers from the US government, nearly a year after they were bombed. “My son has been left scarred for life,” she said.
“I want the US government be held accountable for what they did to my family and for the US to stop bombing our community.”

theguardian.com.title: Senate-approved bills aim to ease burden on pilots amid mental health ‘stigma’
theguardian.com.text:
Pilots and air traffic controllers in the US could soon have an easier time achieving a healthy mental altitude – a move with implications for the safety of air travel in America.
The US Senate recently approved bills aimed at encouraging aviation professionals struggling with a mental health condition get treatment.
The House and president must still approve the legislation, but if that happens, the law could help those with depression and anxiety who are reluctant to seek medical care because they worry it will hurt their high-pressure career.
“It starts breaking down the stigma and showing that when you raise your hand asking for help, it is no longer a third rail,” said Chris Finlayson, a pilot and executive director of the Pilot Mental Health Campaign.
A 2016 survey of more than 1,800 pilots found that almost 13% met the criteria for a depression diagnosis and 4% reported having suicidal thoughts, according to a study published in the journal Environmental Health. Among European airline pilots, a quarter suffered from anxiety and 40% displayed alcohol misuse, according to a 2025 report in the Frontiers in Public Health journal.
Among US air traffic controllers, 19% struggled with moderate to severe anxiety, a 2025 Collegiate Aviation Review International report states.
While many adults struggle with those issues, pilots and air traffic controllers are less likely to seek care because of the stigma and concerns that it could disqualify them from flying, according to people in the industry.
In 2015, a Germanwings airline pilot, who had suffered from suicidal tendencies, deliberately flew a plane into the French Alps, causing 150 deaths. Afterwards, US senator Dianne Feinstein commissioned a report which found that the Federal Aviation Administration’s “ability to mitigate safety risks is limited by pilots’ reluctance to disclose mental health conditions”.
“You put a bunch of type A people that enjoy being in control [with] frankly archaic mental health standards for those type of people, and then you add in a little touch of federal bureaucracy and you have a perfect storm for people who just do not want to admit or say they have they have issues,” said Finlayson, who in 2021 developed long Covid and started to experience depression and anxiety attacks.
The Federal Aviation Administration has guidelines concerning which health conditions prohibit pilots from flying because, of course, they control the fate of thousands of people.
As such, pilots must disclose their medical history and medications to an aviation medical examiner approved by Federal Aviation Administration.
Until recently, the United States had much stricter rules than other countries concerning how long pilots with depression had to remain grounded.
For example, if pilots disclosed that they had started taking an antidepressant, they could not fly for a minimum of six months. In the United Kingdom, they can return to flying in as little as one month. The FAA also requires pilots to get approval from more doctors than other countries and to undergo neurocognitive testing, which other countries also do not require.
“Reporting these conditions has created an extra regulatory step to keep working,” said Dr Gregory Kirk, a psychiatrist who evaluates pilots to determine if they can safely fly.
Finlayson started taking an antidepressant, which provided relief, but he could not fly for six months. He then tried to stop the drug because he thought the depression was just tied to long Covid and temporary but realized he needed it, which meant he had to wait another six months to work. The FAA also kept asking him to do more testing, he said. He ultimately did not return to the cockpit for almost five years.
“It’s a death by 1,000 paper cuts,” Finalyson said. “There is this expectation that if you have even a mild to moderate treatable mental health issue, that you are a detriment to safety, even though that is not what modern science shows.”
In December 2025, the FAA changed its protocol to allow pilots to potentially return to the sky three months after starting an antidepressant. The legislation would shorten it to two months, which is still longer than most other countries. Antidepressants typically achieve their full therapeutic effect within four to eight weeks.
“If science has proven that a two-month period of waiting is appropriate, then that is what we should go to,” said Dennis Tajer, a spokesperson for Allied Pilots Association, the union for American Airlines pilots. “The longer the waiting period, if it’s not based in science, the more likely a pilot is to say, ‘Nah, I got this. I don’t want to put my career on hold that long.’”
The legislation also directs the FAA to follow its mental health aviation rule-making committee’s recommendations, including that it “minimize the requirement for neurocognitive testing”.
One of the bills, the John A Hauser Mental Health in Aviation Act, named for an aviation student who died from suicide in 2021, calls for a public information campaign to “destigmatize individuals” in the aviation industry who seek mental health care.
Finalyson, who loves his job, said he is doing “phenomenal” because he received the medical care he needed.
“The whole point of our movement,” he said, “is that once you get treated, you’re good to go.”

theguardian.com.title: Two people die trying to cross Channel as anti-migrant protesters clash with police in Gosport
theguardian.com.text:
Two people have died and two more have been injured attempting to cross the Channel in a small boat, French authorities have said, while anti-migrant protesters on England’s south coast scuffled with police as they opposed the rescue of nearly 150 more people on a second vessel.
Even though the number of small boat crossings has fallen in recent months, the incidents come amid growing unrest in some quarters partly been fuelled by far-right agitators.
Authorities in the Pas-de-Calais area said one man in his 30s and another in his 40s died during the overnight crossing from the French coastal town of Berck towards England’s south coast. Two women were taken to hospital after suffering burns over large parts of their bodies.
A spokesperson for the Pas-de-Calais prefecture said: “An investigation has been opened by the Boulogne-sur-Mer public prosecutor’s office to determine the circumstances surrounding the deaths. François-Xavier Lauch, the prefect of Pas-de-Calais, thanks all the services involved, particularly the firefighters, for their intervention and commitment during this operation.”
Anticipating the arrival of another boat, demonstrators gathered in Gosport, in Hampshire on Sunday night. It was the second time protesters had targeted the town amid rumours of rescued people disembarking there.
Several rescued people were seen arriving at a marina in Gosport after being transported onboard two RNLI boats late on Sunday evening. Their dinghy was shadowed by French rescue vessels while in the Channel until it was met by RNLI boats in English waters, according to ship tracking data.
The Home Office said 149 people were believed to be onboard. It said: “The Border Security Command works around the clock to protect our border. We have established contingency plans to make sure we can securely disembark, check and process all small boat arrivals. Migrants will be transported to short-term holding facilities in Kent, where they will be processed as normal and undergo stringent health, security and biometric checks.”
On Sunday, Hampshire and Isle of Wight constabulary said it had deployed officers to Gosport to “support our partners in the event of an emergency at sea”. Ambulances and coaches were also seen in the area.
The force imposed conditions under the Public Order Act and used powers prohibiting the wearing of face coverings.
Demonstrations were mostly peaceful, though there were reports of flares being set off and some scuffles with police.
There were similar scenes last month when protesters gathered in the area expecting migrants to arrive on a dinghy, but they were ultimately taken to Dover by sea.
Departures from so far west on the northern French coast have been rare in recent years, but it is the third such crossing in a month. In September, British rescue boats collected passengers off a dinghy that had spent about 30 hours at sea after setting off from Normandy.
The 51 people, who refused help from the French coastguard, arrived in Dover after being transferred to Border Security Command boats. It had been expected they would be taken to Gosport, with hundreds of protesters gathering after coaches and ambulances were seen in the area. Six people were arrested by officers that evening.
The provisional total for Channel crossings this year is 19,451. This is down 43% on this time last year and 23% below the figure at the same time in 2024.

theguardian.com.title: Mary Beard suggests ‘tweaks’ to British Museum’s handling of queues to see Bayeux tapestry
theguardian.com.text:
Mary Beard has intervened in the row about excessively long queues for the Bayeux tapestry by visiting the line and submitting a list of improvements to the British Museum.
Beard, 71, is a trustee of the museum and inspected the queue herself after visitors to the tapestry complained that they had to wait for hours for their turn to view it, and some were turned away with no guarantee they would get another time slot.
One visitor posted on social media that she had been waiting since she was seven to see the Bayeux tapestry, and had bought tickets only to be turned away after queueing.
The museum has since announced new measures to make the viewing of the tapestry, which has returned to England after 1,000 years in France, more accessible. This includes longer opening hours to prevent queues, a new audio guide to help people move along the embroidery, and additional signage and seating.
Beard, a celebrated classicist and TV presenter, told the Guardian she had visited to “chat to people in the queue”, adding: “The atmosphere was very good, with people who had come from everywhere. I thought some tweaks were necessary: more benches for old ladies like me, more guidance on wait times.”
She said she had some sympathies for the museum: “We had to expect some teething troubles – this isn’t like an ordinary exhibition, everyone has come to see the same one object! The important thing is to put those teething troubles right.”
Members of the public keen to see the Bayeux tapestry faced online queues of up to nine hours when tickets went on sale for the first time this summer. There were reports of 40,000 people queueing by mid-morning, with that figure ballooning to almost 80,000 by mid-afternoon. The next wave of public tickets for the tapestry will go on sale on 21 October at 10am.
Adult tickets cost £33 during peak times and £27 at off-peak hours, compared with its usual €12 (£10) fee to see the tapestry in its home in Bayeux, Normandy.
The British Museum’s handling of the exhibition has come under scrutiny after the Guardian revealed that the controversial tech billionaire Peter Thiel was given a private viewing of the tapestry. The Trump-supporting businessman’s public software company, Palantir, plays a controversial role in the British state.
Of the viewing, the museum’s chair, George Osborne, said: “It wasn’t like we expected anyone to know about it.” The museum’s director of development, Charlotte Appleyard, hosted Thiel at a VIP viewing of the tapestry before it opened to the public on 18 August.
When asked what the museum might have received in return, Osborne said: “The short answer is [Thiel] hasn’t offered any money, and were he to offer money, the board would consider it and have to take into account the pros, you know, receiving more income, and the reputational risks.”
A British Museum spokesperson said they were “delighted by the excitement” people had shown. They added: “We also know that some visitors have faced longer queues than we would have wanted, so we are introducing a series of measures to make the experience smoother and give more people the time they need to enjoy the tapestry.”

theguardian.com.title: Average five-year fixed mortgage rate hits 6% for first time in three years
theguardian.com.text:
The average cost of a five-year fixed-rate mortgage has hit the 6% barrier for the first time in three years, as jitters in the money markets make the loans more expensive for lenders to offer.
Figures from financial information provider Moneyfacts show the average is now 6.00%, its highest point since September 2023, while the average two-year fixed rate is not far behind at 5.98%, its highest since December of the same year.
In recent weeks most big banks and building societies have put up prices as turmoil in global bond markets has increased expectations of a base rate rise.
Meanwhile, borrowers in Great Britain have seen their choice of fixed-rate mortgages costing below 5% shrivel to only nine options, according to Moneyfacts. That marks a 99% plunge in the market since the start of last month, when there were 1,494 deals priced below that level.
There has been no change in the Bank of England base rate since December last year, but volatility in the bond markets has driven up the swap rates that affect the pricing of fixed-rate mortgages.
Rachel Springall, a finance expert at Moneyfacts, said the impact on rates had been “brutal”.
She said: “Average fixed mortgage rates rising back to three-year highs will be disastrous news for borrowers. Borrowers who were hoping mortgage rates would stabilise will be disappointed.”
The rise in prices is bad news for borrowers finishing existing fixed-rate deals who at the start of the year may have been looking forward to falling costs, as well as those hoping to take out a mortgage to buy a property.
Figures from the HomeOwners Alliance show the monthly cost of a £250,000 loan fixed at 6% for five years is £158 higher than the same-sized loan locked in at 4.94%, which was the average rate reported by Moneyfacts at the start of February.
There are already signs that higher mortgage costs are weighing down the housing market, with Nationwide building society last week reporting that annual price growth had halved in September.
Ian Harris, the president of the estate agents’ body NAEA Propertymark, said members were “seeing first-hand how sensitive buyers are to mortgage rates”, and the rapid disappearance of sub-5% deals would add further pressure to affordability.
He said: “For some buyers, even a relatively small increase in monthly repayments can mean they have to reduce their budget or step back from a purchase altogether. Equally, homeowners coming off fixed-rate deals may face significantly higher repayments, which could affect their decision to move.”

theguardian.com.title: UK reviewing whether to impose tariffs on Chinese car imports to align with EU
theguardian.com.text:
The UK is reviewing whether to impose tariffs on Chinese car imports to align itself with the EU and strengthen its case to be included in new legislation designed to protect the European manufacturing sectors including autos and chemicals.
It is understood the EU has raised the question of tariffs with the UK as part of the discussions on the “Made in Europe” legislation, known as the Industrial Accelerator Act.
The UK is an outlier in choosing not to put import taxes on Chinese vehicles, even as the US has shut them out almost entirely. Brussels believes the UK would have to introduce tariffs to create a level playing field to qualify for inclusion in the scheme and match the tariffs of up to 45% it has levied on Chinese cars since October 2024.
Imposing tariffs on Chinese cars would probably prompt a hostile response from Beijing and test Andy Burnham’s desire for a reset in the post-Brexit relationship with the EU.
It would also involve a lengthy World Trade Organization process. It took the EU 13 months between the launch of the investigation into state subsidies in production and transport lines and finally imposing tariffs in October 2024.
The UK has been lobbying hard to be included in the legislation, which will require manufacturers to procure components from the continent to protect against the growing presence of China in supply chains, particularly the auto and chemicals sector.
A government source pointed to comments from the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, last week, saying tariffs on Chinese EVs were “always kept … under close review”.
If tariffs were to be imposed, the move would be a break with the previous government policy. Keir Starmer’s government positioned itself as a strong ally to China, viewing it as an important source of economic growth rather than a risk to British manufacturing.
The UK has consistently argued it does not need trade barriers in the way Brussels does because it does not have the huge trade deficit – now running at more than £1bn (€1.18bn) a day – that the EU is struggling to contain.
China’s increasing trade with the EU – not only in finished products such as cars but also in components – is causing deep concern about cannibalisation of native industries in European capitals. The EU trade commissioner, Maroš Šefčovič, is visiting Beijing this Wednesday for talks over a reset in trade relations.
Experts said last week the UK car industry faced a “difficult trade-off”, with Chinese investment a potential “lifeline” for carmakers, while access to Europe would also be “crucial” for smaller manufacturers.
However, Nissan’s chair in Europe, Massimiliano Messina, recently said Europe “cannot have a Trojan horse where the Chinese are going to flood the market” through imports via Great Britain.
Nissan is in talks with the Chinese company Chery to manufacture cars in its Sunderland plant, but this would still align with the EU’s Made in Europe policy.
The EU views Chinese manufacturers based in Europe, employing EU staff, as less of a threat to its indigenous industries. Chinese brands made by BYD in Hungary, for example, will not be subject to import duties.
Mike Hawes, the chief executive of the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders, said any consideration of tariffs needed to be based on “robust evidence” and maintain a rules-based open and competitive market, adding: “Trade restrictions can have unintended consequences.
“The immediate priority is a pragmatic agreement recognising the UK as a trusted ‘Made in Europe’ partner as the exclusion of UK-built vehicles would severely damage both our highly integrated industries, jeopardising the €80bn trading relationship.”
Brands such as BYD, Leapmotor and Jaecoo more than tripled their share of the UK new car market in 2026, reaching 12% of sales, according to the latest industry figures.
BYD has almost doubled its share of the UK market in September 2026 compared with September 2025, with 5.75% of the market, according to figures from the SMMT released on Monday.
In the year to date, BYD’s share has gone up from 2.2% to 3.93%, with 68,000 BYD cars sold up to the end of September, closing in on BMW, which shifted 91,000.
Jaecoo’s share has rocketed, increasing by 223%, with 58,000 new cars sold in the year so far, while Leapmotor sales have soared by a phenomenal 765% – up from about 1,500 cars sold in 2025 to more than 13,000 in the year so far.
A UK government spokesperson said: “We have not put tariffs on Chinese EVs. We continue to engage closely with industry so that our approach reflects the sector’s and UK’s national interests.”

theguardian.com.title: Euro falls to 17-month low against dollar amid French debt fears
theguardian.com.text:
The euro has slumped to the lowest level against the dollar in 17 months amid growing concern France’s debt position could threaten the stability of the wider single currency bloc.
The single currency fell as much as 0.8% against the dollar in early trading on Monday to below $1.12, its lowest level since May 2025, before recovering slightly. It has slumped by about 1.2% this month, accelerating a drop of about eight cents against the greenback from a peak of $1.20 in January.
Investors said the sell-off in the euro was fuelled by concerns over France’s rising debt costs as the government battles to control its stretched public finances in the run-up to next year’s presidential election.
France’s blue-chip Cac 40 index of leading company shares fell by 1% on Monday, as markets elsewhere across Europe rallied. The FTSE 100 was up 0.2%, while Germany’s Dax was little changed.
Monday’s announcement of a snap election in Spain by the socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, after rightwing parties torpedoed emergency housing legislation last week has also fuelled eurozone uncertainty. Madrid’s benchmark Ibex 35 index rose by 0.5%.
“Europe is taking the spotlight at the start of the week, as fiscal and political concerns hit the bloc,” said Kathleen Brooks, the research director at XTB. “France is the epicentre of the concerns; however, Spain is also set to get ready for an early election, which is adding to investor worries.”
Amid a global sell-off in sovereign debt as the Iran war rattles markets, the yield – in effect the interest rate – on French 10-year government bonds last week hit the highest level since 2002, before dipping back on Friday.
This pushed the gap between France and Germany’s borrowing costs, an important measure of investor concern, to its widest level since 2012 at the height of the eurozone sovereign debt crisis.
Investors are focused on Paris’s fiscal position and concerns that the presidential election and a hung parliament – with Marine Le Pen’s far-right National Rally party gaining ground – could make it tougher for the government to curtail a yawning budget deficit.
The minority government of the French prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, announced plans last month for a €54bn (£45.8bn) savings drive to curb borrowing levels, setting the stage for a fierce political battle.
With President Emmanuel Macron’s centrist administration under pressure amid strikes and protests across the country, the budget measures involve cutting pensions spending and funding for government departments, excluding defence.
Lecornu said the savings would result in limiting a budget deficit of 5.5% of GDP this year to 5% next year. He warned that without action the shortfall between public spending and revenue could reach 6.5%.
However, investors fear political pressures could derail fiscal consolidation, threatening to push up borrowing and adding to France’s debt pile at a time of soaring government borrowing costs.
Analysts warned the stresses in the French bond market could spread to other countries in the euro area, stoking fears over a return to the dynamics of the 2010s sovereign debt crisis.
It comes amid concerns over the test facing the European Central Bank from mounting inflationary pressures from the war in the Middle East and the risk France’s debt problem spreads throughout the euro area.
Roberto Mialich, a currency strategist at the Italian bank UniCredit, said: “Investors still do not rule out riding a further decline of the euro, making a retest of $1.10 possible in the near term.
“This is also because growing political tensions across the eurozone (primarily in France and Spain) and fears of contagion across the European sovereign debt market are putting pressure on the euro.”

theguardian.com.title: Son of disgraced ex-president Jair Bolsonaro takes election lead in Brazil | First Thing
theguardian.com.text:
Good morning. Brazil’s presidential race will go to a second round after the far-right candidate, Flávio Bolsonaro, beat the incumbent leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, but failed to secure the outright majority he needed to avoid a runoff.
The 45-year-old son of the disgraced former president Jair Bolsonaro will go into the second round as strong favourite, likely to pick up votes from the election’s other rightwing candidates, including Ronaldo Caiado, who secured 2.1%, and Renan Santos, who won 2.2%. The second round will take place on 25 October.
- How have Bolsonarista politicians taken a grip on Brazil? Brazil’s far right put in an even stronger than expected showing, with a succession of Bolsonarista politicians winning congressional or gubernatorial races. They included Jair Bolsonaro’s second son, Carlos Bolsonaro, and his wife, Michelle Bolsonaro, who both won seats in the senate. Bolsonaro’s youngest son, Jair Renan Bolsonaro, was elected to the lower house of congress.
Woman in Cornell rape allegations case targeted with threats, her lawyer says
The woman who has alleged that she was drugged and raped by Cornell University students has been the target of threats, her lawyer said. Thomas Giuffra told CNN that people had threatened to silence or harm her if she did not withdraw her civil lawsuit alleging that several members of a Cornell fraternity had drugged and raped her in 2024.
Giuffra said he had also been threatened. “I’m not afraid of these people,” he said. “But the threats, the abuse to protect what’s going on, the status quo – these guys are disgusting. They should stay in their mother’s basement and stay out of the world.”
- What has been the latest response from Cornell University? In a video message, the Cornell University president, Michael Kotlikoff, said the school would take “a serious look at the role of fraternities and sororities in campus life”, adding: “At their best, these organisations can provide students with friendship, belonging, mentorship and a powerful sense of community. But being part of a group can never diminish individual responsibility.”
White House defends new press aide who posed with rifle in ‘Fuck Joe Biden’ shirt
Beni Rae Harmony revealed on Friday she was going to work for Donald Trump, just days after covering him as a correspondent for Real America’s Voice, a partisan rightwing outlet originally created as a video podcast platform for the president’s former adviser Steve Bannon. It then emerged she had posed for a holiday photograph in 2021 wearing a “Fuck Joe Biden” T-shirt and holding a rifle.
The White House deputy press secretary, Anna Kelly, defended the appointment, saying: “Beni Rae Harmony has been a trusted voice for the Maga movement as a White House correspondent. She will be an outstanding addition to President Trump’s communications team as an assistant press secretary – we look forward to having her onboard!”
US bombers pulled from RAF Fairford base after suspected terror plot
The US air force has pulled its bombers from RAF Fairford in England following an investigation into an alleged planned terrorist attack at the base. At least 10 B-1 bombers out of 12 flew out of the base on Sunday, including some that arrived on rotation less than a week ago, underlining the haste of the departure. According to reporting by US media, the withdrawal appears to be in response to fresh or renewed security concerns about safety on the base. Five British nationals were initially detained on suspicion of explosives offences and terrorism last weekend after three vans were found near the base. They were later released on bail.
- What are the latest developments in the Middle East? Yemen’s Saudi-backed government has announced the start of a new military operation to retake all territory held by the Houthis. The statement came just hours after the Houthis cut a vital supply route linking the besieged city of Taiz with the government’s interim capital, Aden. Yemen’s internationally recognised government has struggled to hold off Houthi territorial gains, even with the military support of Saudi Arabia.
In other news …
- The former prince Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor has launched legal action against British police over their raids on his property in connection with the Epstein files. It represents the first time a member of the British royal family has challenged the lawfulness of criminal proceedings against them since the trial of Charles I in 1649. He was executed.
- Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, a frequent target of criticism from Trump and from Israel, has announced a snap general election three days after rightwing parties torpedoed the emergency legislation his minority government had put forward in response to growing public anger over the country’s housing crisis.
- A US marine stationed on Japan’s southern island of Okinawa is accused of murdering a Japanese woman and has been arrested, police said.
- Donald Trump has named Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, to also serve as the new White House AI czar. Trump announced that Clayton would lead what the US president called “the Super Intelligence Force (SIF)”.
- More than 400 schools in France will be closed or partly closed on Monday as authorities brace for another week of student protests. A minister said 24 schools had been burnt or ransacked and 78 education staff members injured.
Stat of the day: Digger may lose $150m after Tom Cruise film bombs at the box office
Tom Cruise is used to success, but his appearance in Alejandro G Iñárritu’s critically panned satire doesn’t seem to have pulled in an audience. It took just $20m globally in its opening weekend, against a reported $150m production budget and $100m marketing spend.
Don’t miss this: Are rumors of lost gold spurring clandestine excursions into New York sewers?
Can it really be true that underground invaders of the city’s sewer system are lured by the promise of lost valuables? Adam Gabbatt investigates.
… or this: My sister Nicole married OJ Simpson – this is what I wish I had known
Since Nicole Brown Simpson’s murder in 1994, Denise Brown has devoted herself to the cause of ending domestic violence. Emine Saner interviews her.
Climate check: Extreme heat warnings issued for parts of southern California
The National Weather Service in the US has issued extreme heat warnings for parts of southern California, including Los Angeles, until Thursday. Burbank, a suburb north of Los Angeles, recorded 102F on Saturday, a few degrees shy of the October record for the region set in 1987.
Last Thing: Mexico debuts tiniest national guard recruit – Comando the chihuahua
Diminutive Comando stands just 8in tall and looks nothing like the powerful dogs usually associated with military or police units. However, the 13-month-old pup is being trained not just as a crowd-pleasing mascot but for search-and-rescue work as well.
